The ten high-rise buildings that still need “unsafe cladding” replaced have been revealed, with one being directly attached to a fire station. A meeting of the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority last month revealed there are still residential buildings of seven stories or more waiting for replacement works. The authority said they were “confident” they will meet the government deadline of December 31, 2029, for all high-rises to have their cladding replaced. This was set after the conclusion of the inquiry into the Grenfell Tower fire in 2017 when 72 people lost their lives in the fire which spread through flammable cladding. The inquiry concluded in 2025 and also set a deadline of December 31, 2031, for medium-rise residential buildings to have any unsafe cladding replaced. The combined authority was told that the buildings identified belong to private owners, whose responsibility it is to replace the cladding. A new bill was brought to Parliament this week which, if approved, will give councils more power to replace cladding themselves if the building’s owners fail to act. The Remediation of Unsafe Cladding Bill will also place a legal duty on owners to fix issues without delay or they may face criminal penalties – including a fine of up to £500k. A Freedom of Information request to the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority has revealed the buildings which are still waiting for unsafe cladding to be replaced. It includes all of the Parkside Place development – with Cambridge Fire Station on its lower floor – and the Parkside Terrace building is the tallest on the list at eight stories. All ten buildings are in Cambridge with the remaining being Petersfield House in Parkside Place, the Cyan Building, 1-32 Orchid Building and the Aqua Building on Glenalmond Avenue, Meade House on Mill Park, The Lauro Building on Aberdeen Avenue and The Triangle Blocks A, B and C on Warren Close. There are also 84 medium-rise residential buildings waiting for cladding to be replaced. A spokesperson for the combined authority said that even if a building is waiting for unsafe cladding to be replaced, it does not mean the building is unsafe to live in. They said: “There may be mitigating measures in place, such as changes to the fire alarm system so that everyone is alerted to a fire at the same time, and would all leave the building together (called simultaneous evacuation). “This will be determined by the external wall report completed by a qualified fire engineer.” They said that five buildings have had replacement works completed, two are currently having work done and work is set to start on 14 more buildings in the next two months. A further update will be presented to the combined authority’s growth committee in November. They said: “We are supporting responsible entities to meet their obligations on building remediation, and where they are not doing so, regulators will take appropriate action. “For any buildings undergoing remediation, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service has a webpage with fire safety advice for members of the public: Fire safety advice during building remediation.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Clinical hypnotherapist explains why driving can make people feel anxious
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire-based clinical hypnotherapist Dan Regan explains why driving can make people feel anxious As the evenings draw in, driving can become more uncomfortable for some people. Darker roads, headlight glare, wet weather and reduced visibility can all make journeys feel more difficult than they did during the summer. But driving anxiety certainly isn't limited to driving in the dark. One thing I've noticed from working with people with driving anxiety is just how differently it can affect people. Someone might be perfectly happy driving around Ely or on familiar local roads but avoid dual carriageways or motorways altogether. For someone else, it might be particular situations such as joining a fast road, overtaking, busy roads or driving somewhere unfamiliar. Some people may become anxious about almost any journey. And I've also worked with people who are comfortable driving themselves but become very anxious when they're a passenger and someone else is in control. The anxiety itself can vary too. For some, there's a constant feeling of tension or unease. Others might experience a racing heart, shaking, dizziness, feeling hot or other physical symptoms of anxiety. If someone has experienced a panic attack while driving, they can understandably become very worried about it happening again. And often the anxiety begins long before even getting into the car. You might start worrying about a journey hours or even days beforehand. You imagine the difficult parts of the journey, wonder how you'll feel and start thinking about what you'll do if the anxiety becomes too much. By the time you actually get into the car, you've already spent a lot of time practising feeling anxious about the journey. Avoidance can then creep in. Perhaps you choose a longer route because it avoids a dual carriageway, only drive at quieter times or ask somebody else to drive. You may stop travelling somewhere altogether because getting there feels too difficult. Those decisions can make perfect sense in the moment because they reduce the anxiety. But repeatedly avoiding something because of anxiety can reinforce the idea that it was something you needed to avoid. Gradually, your world can become a little smaller. Driving anxiety can affect much more than simply how comfortable you feel behind the wheel. It can affect work, seeing friends and family, days out, holidays and your independence. That's why I tend to look beyond simply trying to make someone “feel confident” about driving. I'm interested in the patterns that have developed around it. For example, what are you imagining before a journey? What are you paying attention to while you're driving? What are you doing to try to prevent yourself from feeling anxious? And what have you gradually started avoiding? Those patterns can become very well practised, but that doesn't mean they have to stay that way. So if driving has become more uncomfortable as the nights draw in, it may be worth noticing not only how anxious you feel, but also what you're doing in response to that anxiety. And if your driving has gradually become restricted to certain roads, routes or situations, remember that those patterns can change. You don't necessarily have to accept those restrictions as your new normal. Dan Regan is a clinical hypnotherapist specialising in anxiety, based in Ely and Newmarket. You can find more anxiety help and information at danreganhypnotherapy.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire-led study to recruit 7,500 people to improve psychosis care
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major research programme to improve early intervention in psychosis is being led by Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. The Early Intervention Mission, spearheaded by Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust (CPFT), is a UK-wide study focused on early identification, monitoring and personalised care for individuals experiencing a first episode of psychosis. Symptoms of psychosis can include hallucinations, hearing voices, delusions and disorganised thinking. Professor Graham Murray, consultant psychiatrist at CPFT and professor of psychiatry and neuroscience at the University of Cambridge, said: "This research will help us understand who is at risk of early psychosis and how best to target preventative treatment and tailor personalised mental health care to meet their needs. "Working with expert colleagues across the UK, we’re on a mission to use new digital technologies, electronic health records and genetic data to improve care and treatment, and support recovery. "Effective early intervention can give people a much better quality of life." The study aims to recruit up to 7,500 people in the early stages of psychosis, along with up to 500 healthy control participants. Participants identified through health service records will be invited to take part remotely via NHS England’s DigiTrials service. Where suitable, individuals may be asked to attend an initial research visit to provide a blood or saliva sample and complete questionnaires and cognitive tasks. Those with psychosis will be followed every six months for up to three years using digital questionnaires. Data collected will be stored securely in the Mental Health Mission Trusted Research Environment and will be used to investigate factors such as immune markers, genetics and social influences on the development and progression of psychosis. The study is informed by individuals with lived experience and intends to create a long-term, representative resource to support future clinical trials and personalised treatment approaches. It is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research Mental Health Translational Research Collaboration Mission.

A man accused of a mass stabbing on a train in Huntingdon, and separate attacks earlier that day in London and the day before in Peterborough, has pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder and is due to stand trial next week. Passengers and staff were injured on a service from Doncaster to London on November 1 after it left Peterborough, leading to an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon railway station. Anthony Williams pleaded guilty at Cambridge Crown Court today. (Image: Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire) At a pre-trial review hearing at Cambridge Crown Court today (October 19), Williams pleaded guilty to 14 new counts, 12 of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent. He was also rearraigned on seven counts to which he had previously pleaded not guilty. Williams pleaded guilty to affray at a barber shop in Peterborough on October 31 and the theft of knives from an Asda store in Stevenage on October 31. He pleaded guilty to possessing a bladed article in a public place at a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk, the Rail World car park and Queen’s Walk in Peterborough on October 31. Williams pleaded guilty to 14 new counts, 12 of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent. He pleaded guilty to possession of a knife on a train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on November 1. He also pleaded guilty to the assault occasioning actual bodily harm of a male police officer in custody on November 2. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Optometrists prepare for second Ghana trip to provide free eye care in rural villages
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A team of optometrists is preparing for a life-changing journey to Ghana. The group, from St Neots, Bedford, Dunstable, and Biggleswade, will travel to the Ashanti region of Ghana this November to deliver essential eye care in rural communities. They will spend two weeks in the village of Gyetiase, providing free eye tests and glasses with the support of charity Ashanti Development. Shivam Patel, ophthalmic director at Specsavers in St Neots, said: "We would love the local community to get behind us again by donating any old or unwanted glasses they no longer need. "Every pair we can take with us gives us another opportunity to help someone see more clearly. "Something that may have been sitting unused in a drawer here can genuinely help transform another person’s daily life." This will be the team’s second visit to Ghana. During their previous trip, they examined 1,333 people, distributed more than 1,000 pairs of glasses, and helped fund 72 cataract surgeries. Access to eye care can be extremely limited in rural areas, and for many people this will be their first eye test. Specsavers customers are being encouraged to donate old or unwanted glasses, which will be distributed during the visit. A major focus of the trip is raising funds for cataract surgery. A specialist surgical team will join the project in its second week to operate on patients identified during initial screenings. Shivam said: "Whether someone donates a pair of glasses, contributes a few pounds to the fundraising appeal or simply helps us spread the word, every bit of support matters." Glasses donations can be made at Specsavers St Neots, 13 High Street, St Neots, Cambridgeshire, PE19 1BU. To support the fundraising appeal, visit www.gofund.me/80505b29f.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Meet the medical tattooist who helps surgery and cancer patients reclaim confidence
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A permanent make-up artist from Cambridgeshire is using her skills to help people heal after surgery, trauma, and cancer treatment. Ely-based Helen Honey runs The Brow & Body Studio, which offers medical tattooing, scar restoration, areola reconstruction, and camouflage services from her private studio. She said: "It helps not only repair the body but restore people's confidence, whether they're recovering from an accident, surgery or trauma." Her decision to expand into medical tattooing followed the loss of a close family friend to cancer in 2020, which prompted her to consider how her skills could support those dealing with more than just cosmetic concerns. After extensive research, she undertook specialist training in areola reconstruction, scar and stretch-mark restoration, and scar camouflage. Helen working in the studio (Image: Helen Honey) Ms Honey said: "I am so grateful to be able to be a part of each patient's healing journey. "My friend had to make the life-changing decision of having a voluntary double mastectomy after being diagnosed with the BRCA gene. "I had the honour of helping her through part of her cancer journey by doing 3D areola tattoo restoration, something that is no longer available on the NHS." Her services include MCA (Multi-Trepannic Collagen Actuation), an inkless needling technique that uses medical-grade needles to create micro-trauma, stimulating collagen production and helping to improve the appearance of scars, burns, and stretch marks. Clients have included individuals recovering from mastectomies, breast augmentation, body contouring surgery, burns, gender-affirming procedures, and significant weight-loss journeys. Each treatment takes place in Ms Honey’s private studio in Ely, which she believes offers clients a safe and comfortable environment to share their stories and begin their healing journey. A patient's before and after photos (Image: Helen Honey) She said: "Many clients arrive anxious or self-conscious, carrying difficult memories, and a private, one-to-one setting gives them space for the kind of sensitive conversation that rarely happens in a busy salon." Ms Honey’s work was recently recognised at the 2026 UK PMU Awards, the UK’s largest permanent make-up awards event, where she was named a top 10 finalist in the Medical Artist of the Year category. She said: "It was the most educational and emotional weekend. "I'm so grateful for the recognition, as it's so complicated but so emotionally rewarding." Her skills recently helped a Cambridgeshire man regain confidence after life-saving surgery left him with a large abdominal scar and no belly button. Following several sessions of MCA to soften the scar tissue, Ms Honey used medical tattooing techniques to recreate a realistic, three-dimensional belly button. Her journey into permanent make-up began after she left a long corporate career to pursue a career that offered greater work-life balance. What started as a creative venture soon became a mission to help others through restorative and medical tattooing. She continues to expand her expertise and is set to introduce laser tattoo removal to her list of services from the end of October. Ms Honey said: "I just want people to know what I can do for them. "To be able to make people happy and confident in themselves again – this job enables me to do just that." In recognition of Breast Cancer Awareness Month, she is offering 20 per cent off areola tattooing services until the end of October, with all consultations provided free of charge. Appointments can be booked by emailing thebrowandbodystudio@gmail.com. Ms Honey’s work highlights the growing impact of medical tattooing, not just in cosmetic enhancement but in supporting emotional and psychological recovery. By combining technical skill with compassion, she is helping individuals reclaim confidence and comfort in their bodies after life-changing events. The Brow & Body Studio continues to evolve, now offering a wider range of restorative and aesthetic treatments designed to support healing and self-esteem. Ms Honey said: "This work goes far beyond beauty. "It's about giving people the chance to feel whole again."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drum and bass pioneer Goldie to perform at Cambridge Junction
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drum and bass pioneer Goldie is set to bring his legendary sound to Cambridgeshire. Hosted by promoter Warning, the Metalheadz founder and influential DJ will take to the decks at the Cambridge Junction on the evening of November 11. Goldie, an English music producer, DJ, graffiti artist and actor, first gained recognition through the UK graffiti scene before becoming a pioneering figure in the 1990s jungle, drum and bass and breakbeat hardcore movements. Through projects including Rufige Kru and Metalheads, and as co-founder of the influential Metalheadz label, he helped shape the sound of modern drum and bass. His landmark 1995 album Timeless reached No. 7 in the UK charts and remains one of the genre's defining records. Beyond music, Goldie has enjoyed a successful acting career, appearing in films including the James Bond blockbuster The World Is Not Enough and Guy Ritchie's Snatch, as well as the BBC soap EastEnders. More than three decades after helping define Britain's underground electronic music scene, Goldie remains a major force in dance music, renowned for his high-energy DJ sets and deep knowledge of the culture he helped create. The event is expected to attract drum and bass fans from across the region, with Warning continuing its reputation for bringing some of the genre's biggest names to Cambridge. Tickets are now available online

Cambridgeshire Constabulary’s Rural Crime Action Team (RCAT) made 26 arrests and disrupted organised criminal activity between April and September. They recovered 48 stolen vehicles, trailers, plant machinery and other assets valued at more than £699,000. Sergeant Tom Nuttall, who leads the team, said: "Many people know RCAT as the force's hare coursing team, but that is only one aspect of what we do. Read more Health and safety investigation launched after boy falls from double-decker bus Fenland councillors claim planning rules changes will weaken local democracy Details emerge after police chase 'stolen' van from Peterborough to March Fenland launches £40,000 culture fund with grants of up to £2,000 Man indicates guilty plea after spaniel killed and woman injured in dog attack "Every day, our officers provide specialist support across Cambridgeshire, from pursuing dangerous offenders and recovering stolen property to locating missing people and assisting with major incidents. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP calls for social care savings limit to rise from £23,250 for disabled people
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Ian Sollom MP has called on the Government to overhaul social care funding rules which he says are preventing thousands of disabled people from saving for their future and living more independently. The MP for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire has launched a campaign ahead of this month's Autumn Budget, urging the Health Secretary to review the adult social care capital limit after being contacted by constituent Maxwell McKnight, 22. Under current rules, people receiving social care who have more than £23,250 in savings, investments and property can be required to pay the full cost of their care. The upper limit was last increased in 2010/11. Mr Sollom argues the threshold effectively creates a "savings trap" for working-age disabled adults, preventing them from building financial security, saving for a house deposit or planning for the future. Read more £30m Huntingdon Sport and Health Hub construction to begin this month Little Paxton Parish Council named Council of the Year 2026 Council removes agricultural tie from Huntingdonshire bungalow after 40 years Two covered padel courts could be built on hotel grounds According to research cited by the MP, published by The King's Fund, the upper capital limit would now stand at around £35,600 had it risen in line with inflation since 2010/11. Mr McKnight, a wheelchair user who requires round-the-clock care, recently graduated with a first-class degree and now works full-time in central London. He also advocates for disabled people through his online platforms and serves as a trustee of a national disability charity. Mr Sollom said: "Young people like Maxwell have done everything the Government has asked of them under difficult circumstances - studied, worked hard, paid tax - and yet they are being punished by a savings trap which has not been changed for over 15 years. "There are credible solutions out there that would free young people a lifetime of expensive care costs, and it was deeply disappointing that the Government scrapped the reforms needed to do this back in 2024. "I am calling on the Health Secretary to engage with disabled young people like Maxwell and urgently put forward solutions to end the savings trap." Mr McKnight said the existing rules make it difficult for disabled people with complex care needs to build financial security despite being encouraged into employment. He said: "I've worked incredibly hard to graduate from university and build a career. As someone who's driven and determined not to let my disability define what I can achieve, it's incredibly difficult to accept that, in many ways, I could be financially better off being unemployed. "The government wants more disabled people in employment, yet the very system that's supposed to support us makes it almost impossible for those of us with complex needs to build financial security. "I don't want special treatment. I want the same opportunities as my peers to save for a home, build a future and enjoy the rewards of working hard." As part of the campaign, Mr Sollom has requested a meeting with the Health Secretary and has urged the forthcoming Casey Commission on adult social care reform to examine the challenges facing working-age disabled adults seeking to save money and purchase their own homes. The MP has also pointed to previously proposed reforms, including measures in the 2014 Care Act and recommendations from the Dilnot review, which would have significantly increased the capital threshold but were ultimately not implemented.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 50 foster carers have been honoured for their service and dedication to children in care. The awards ceremony, held on October 2 at Burgess Hall in St Ives, celebrated carers from across Cambridgeshire who collectively contribute more than 450 years of fostering. Councillor Edna Murphy, chair of the children and young people’s committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said at the event: "Tonight is about saying a huge thank you to our foster carers and recognising the incredible difference they make to children's lives. "It is often the quiet, understated things that matter most to children: being there to listen, helping with homework, providing comfort during difficult times and giving children the confidence to believe in themselves. "These moments may seem ordinary, but together they can be genuinely life changing and life enhancing." The Foster Carer Awards are organised by Cambridgeshire County Council to honour the impact foster carers have on young lives. This year, 45 fostering households were recognised for reaching service milestones of five, 10, 15, 20, and 50 years. The theme for the evening was Around the World in 80 Days, with guests arriving in colourful fancy dress and enjoying food, refreshments, and dancing. Many carers were praised for offering stability, encouragement, and a sense of belonging to children in care. The High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire, Francis Burkitt DL, said: "I feel very privileged to have attended the awards this evening and to have met so many impressive and loving foster carers and heard their stories. "The support, stability and encouragement they provide helps children and young people thrive, often during some of the most challenging periods of their lives. "Their commitment is truly inspiring, and these awards are richly deserved." Anyone interested in becoming a foster carer in Cambridgeshire is encouraged to contact the council’s fostering team.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We visited the new Hickory's Smokehouse in Cambridge that boasts Deep South menu
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: One of Cambridgeshire's newest restaurants opens its doors tonight, and diners are in for a finger-licking treat. Offering the taste of the American Deep South, Hickory's Smokehouse on Milton Road, Cambridge, does barbecue as you have never tasted before. We were invited to preview the restaurant, housed in the renovated former Milton Arms pub, on Wednesday evening. You are greeted by the smell of delicious smoky meat as you walk into the building, which is reminiscent of an old American bar in some Southern state, and it's enough to get those taste buds going. The Southern Sharer is just made for sharing, and the perfect starter. The venue has been completely stripped and refitted, with impressive results. Booths with upholstered seating and well-spaced wooden tables give diners a sense of comfort and privacy. The interior is rich in detail, helping create an authentic stateside feel. And the staff are some of the most welcoming I have ever encountered in any restaurant anywhere. My friends even commented on the warm welcome we received, and the enthusiasm of every staff member we encountered, from the friendly bartender to the waiting team. The evening let staff practise serving, the kitchen handle a packed restaurant and invited guests sample the menu, while families could use a cinema room showing children’s films with free popcorn. The entrance bar has the feel of a traditional saloon and serves drinks including Hickory’s own beers. Tailgator, a lager brewed in Scotland, is among them. The menu is packed with choice, including vegetarian and vegan dishes, but Hickory’s is primarily about the meat. And wow, what meat. There were four of us, and we were offered taster dishes of one of Hickory's specialities, slow-cooked smoked brisket, and it is to die for - simply melt-in-your-mouth delicious. The food was tasty, filling, and served with real Southern hospitality. We opted for a small starter, so we went for the Southern Sharer between three of us, and one of us chose the chicken in the basket as well. The platter came with bourbon-glazed smoked sausage, cowboy-buttered corn, smoked wings, celery, beer fondue and a selection of dips. Also on the platter were frickles, and if you have never tasted a frickle, then you have missed a treat. They are battered, deep-fried gherkins, and they are delicious. On to the mains, and we went for a variety. The interior of Hickory's Smokehouse, Cambridge has been designed with comfort and style. (Image: Neil Cooper) One of us chose the classic Gumbo - a hot and spicy southern stew served with rice, black beans and scallions alongside a baguette. It included smoked pulled chicken with pork, jalapeño, and cheese sausage. Verdict: hot, tasty and filling — ideal for stew lovers. Another of us chose the bird in the herd - Tennessee bourbon-gravy-glazed smoked beef baby back ribs, Kansas-style barbecue-sauced wings and cowboy buttered smoked chicken, all served with slaw and fries. The Gumbo was a tasty, hot treat and perfect for stew lovers. (Image: Hickory's Smokehouse) It was a mountain of food, but it went down a treat. A Hickory's Cobb salad with chicken was another choice, and this is like no salad you have had before. It combines crisp lettuce with Kansas caviar — black beans, sweetcorn, red and yellow peppers and spring onions — plus blue cheese, a soft-boiled egg, avocado and Cheddar. My friend found this a challenge to finish as it was so filling. Hickory's offers a range of alcoholic and non-alcoholic cocktails, including a variety of Margaritas. (Image: Hickory's Smokehouse) Finally, I chose the Texas-style sliced brisket. If you think you have tasted brisket before, think again. This was smoked low and slow for 16 hours and served with a pot of bourbon gravy. It was utterly delicious, and just melted in the mouth - I can't recommend this enough. With the top buttons on our trousers already undone, it was time to move on to desserts, but we were so full there was only one option, and that was to share a couple of desserts between us. The bar area is a welcoming space as you enter the restaurant on Milton Road. (Image: Neil Cooper) We chose banana-pudding cheesecake in a jam jar and vegan ice cream. Shared between two, they were a fitting end to a filling but delicious meal.One of the highlights of the evening was the arrival at our table of a Pitmaster margarita cocktail. Served in a glass dome filled with smoke, it was one of the most theatrical drinks I've ever had. The designated driver tried a couple of the sodas, including the refreshing raspberry and mint, which was sweet and tangy and very refreshing. The Southern Sharer is just made for sharing, and the perfect starter. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Another of us tried the Sierra Nevada beer and said it hit the spot. Hickory's ethos is one of Southern hospitality, and the staff certainly delivered that on Wednesday evening; they were welcoming, chatty, and willing to please. A quick tot-up of our bill saw a total of around £140 without drinks, but for three courses, for four of us, and for the quality of the food, we thought it was worth it. Would we go again? Yes, definitely, but we may have to wait a while for the excess of the evening to go down first. Verdict: 5/5 for food, service and ambience - why not give it a try? The Cambridge branch is the second Hickory's to open in Cambridgeshire, following the Peterborough restaurant's opening in June.

Captain Dan De’Ath opened the scoring after a strong driving move had taken the hosts towards the line. For much of the opening twenty minutes, neither side found fluency as gusts made passes dip, spill and swerve in flight. Ives then tightened their attack, with Henri Cole and Torv Romeis crossing for tries in quick succession. Connor Newsome secured the try bonus point before half-time, stretching over with two defenders attached after the ball moved swiftly across the field. Cole added his second try early in the second half, forcing his way over after a quickly taken penalty. As Peterborough tired, De’Ath completed his hat-trick with two late tries, before Josh Meadows finished the scoring with a fine solo effort after Mickey Drake took a quick tap. Mandley converted the late score and Ives secured a convincing win, although the performance never reached the heights suggested by the margin. Director of rugby Duncan Williams described the performance as disciplined rather than entertaining and welcomed another five-point haul. The result confirmed their unbeaten start after three rounds. The Bulls now turn their attention to next week’s encounter at St Neots, where they will seek to maintain their perfect league start.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A dazzling display of shooting stars is set to light up the night sky in the UK this month. The Orionid meteor shower, known for its fast, bright meteors, will peak in the coming week. The Orionids are visible each year between October 2 and November 7. Here is how they can best be viewed in the UK. A post shared by Royal Museums Greenwich (@royalmuseumsgreenwich) The Orionids are an annual event, towards the end of each year. However, they are considered "extra special" by many, as they are actually pieces of Comet 1P/Halley, famously known as Halley's Comet. As explained by the Royal Museums Greenwich: "A meteor is a piece of space debris that burns up as it enters the earth’s atmosphere creating a ‘shooting star’. "Certain times of the year are known for spectacular displays and these are generally associated with comets that have passed by after spewing fragments in their wake." While Halley's Comet only flies by Earth once every 75 to 76 years, the annual shower provides some compensation for those who may miss that once-in-a-lifetime event. Meteors from the Orionid shower can be seen with the naked eye from all parts of the sky, though they appear to originate from the constellation Orion. Stargazers are advised to find a dark, open area away from city lights. This year, the shower will peak on the night of October 21 and continue into the early hours of October 22. However, a waxing gibbous moon will add extra light to the sky on October 21, which could make the meteors harder to spot. Recommended reading: RMG says: "Hunting for meteors, like the rest of astronomy, is a waiting game, so it's best to bring a comfy chair to sit on and to wrap up warm as you could be outside for a while. "You will need to allow your eyes to adjust to the dark." No special equipment is needed to enjoy the display. Have you ever spotted a meteor shower before? Let us know in the comments below.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP State Pension age row deepens as 80,000 demand retirement at 65
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 80,000 people calling for the State Pension age to be cut to 65 have been dealt a blow after the Government confirmed it has no plans to lower it. The petition is approaching the 100,000 signatures needed for Parliament to consider debating the issue. Supporters argue that people aged 65 to 67 can struggle to keep working because of ill health, caring responsibilities and limited job opportunities. For those forced to stop working early, the gap before their State Pension begins can be costly. Tim Grimsditch, managing director of financial advice platform Unbiased, said: “The Government has consistently rejected calls to lower the State Pension age, and the Third State Pension Age Review is currently underway to determine what the age should be in future decades. "There’s a difficult balance here: the State Pension is one of the largest items of public spending, and allowing people to claim it earlier would mean paying it to more people for longer. Both sides of this are serious arguments.” The petition can be viewed on the UK Parliament petitions website. The State Pension age is rising from 66 to 67, with the change due to finish in March 2028. It affects people born between March 1961 and August 1977. Legislation already exists for it to rise to 68 later. Private pensions can generally be accessed from 55, rising to 57 in April 2028. Anyone who stops working before claiming their State Pension may need to fund the gap themselves. Grimsditch said: “The practical issue for most people isn’t the State Pension age itself - it’s the gap before it. Private pensions can generally be accessed from 55, rising to 57 in April 2028, while the State Pension now arrives at 67. "Someone who stops working at 63 through ill health or caring responsibilities is funding four years entirely from their own provision. "That’s the question the petition is really about, and it’s worth planning for regardless of what happens to it.” The full new State Pension is £241.30 a week, or £12,547.60 a year. The amount people receive depends on their National Insurance record, so checking your State Pension forecast can help you understand what to expect. Grimsditch said: “It also matters because the State Pension alone was never designed to cover everything. The full new rate is £241.30 a week, or £12,547.60 a year, and what you actually receive depends on your National Insurance record.” Recommended reading Workplace and personal pensions, savings and investments can provide extra retirement income. Pension contributions can benefit from tax relief, while money held outside a pension can offer another source of funds. Grimsditch said: “Building additional income can mean a workplace or personal pension, where tax relief gives contributions a boost, or savings and investments held outside a pension. One change worth noting if you’re considering a cash ISA: the annual limit for under-65s falls to £12,000 from April 2027.” He urged people approaching retirement to review their finances and work out how much income they will need. He said: “If you’re within a decade of stopping work, the useful steps are checking your State Pension forecast, reviewing pensions you’ve accumulated along the way, and working out what income you’ll actually need. "Decisions about when to access a pension, how much to draw, and what to keep invested make a substantial difference to how long the money lasts - and that’s where a qualified financial adviser earns their fee. It’s never too early, or too late, to start.”

HRH The Princess Royal speaking with Magpas Air Ambulance's Advanced Paramedics in Critical Care (Image: C1 Media) "We are always proud of our medical team members, who are there for our communities, families and loved ones, should the worst happen. "But also of the supporters who are vital to enabling the medical team to respond when every second counts. "We’re truly grateful for HRH The Princess Royal’s recognition of everyone who helps to save lives and for her wonderful support of Magpas Air Ambulance." HRH The Princess Royal addresses attendees at Magpas Air Ambulance's headquarters (Image: C1 Media) The event brought together those involved in recent emergency responses, including the Bedford train collision and the incident at Huntingdon station. Magpas was the first medical resource on scene in Huntingdon and the first air ambulance service to land at the Bedford train collision. HRH The Princess Royal met emergency services partners from across the region who work together at the scene of major incidents  (Image: C1 Media) During her visit, The Princess Royal observed real-time demonstrations of advanced treatments delivered by the Magpas clinical team and learned more about the charity’s efforts to train communities in bystander CPR.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare King Charles 50p sells for more than 200 times its face value
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare 50p coin has fetched more than 200 times its face value after an online auction. The Atlantic Salmon piece drew 37 bids on eBay before being snapped up for £123. Released by the Royal Mint in 2023, only 200,000 copies of the coin were ever produced. The coin celebrates British wildlife and the accession of King Charles III, depicting the Atlantic salmon as a priority conservation species in UK waters. King Charles Salmon 50p sells 8 times face value. (Image: eBay) The reverse features a leaping Atlantic salmon alongside the King Charles III royal cypher, while the obverse bears the official uncrowned portrait of King Charles III by Martin Jennings. It is officially ranked by the Royal Mint as the rarest 50p coin in active UK circulation, having ended the 15-year reign of the 2009 Kew Gardens 50p. With just 200,000 released into banks and post offices, finding one in loose change remains exceptionally rare. The 50p piece provides a distinct heptagonal canvas for coin designers. With a diameter of 27.5mm, it is the largest British coin in circulation and offers space for commemorative artwork. Rarity serves as the primary factor driving collector demand and market prices. Low mintage figures mean fewer examples exist to buy or trade. Coin condition also plays an important role, with well-preserved specimens securing higher prices. Collectors also prize unusual design errors and striking flaws that escape the mint. Sales avenues can influence the price realised for a rare coin. Sellers often turn to competitive online bidding on eBay to test market demand. Others prefer formal valuations from professional coin dealers to establish a certified market value. Royal Mint mintage figures confirm the rarest 50p designs to enter general circulation: The 2023 Atlantic Salmon coin holds the title as the rarest 50p design in circulation. Anyone checking their loose change is urged to keep an eye out for these scarce editions.

Located in Peterborough, the new Amazon facility is the company’s first new building in the city in 15 years and is now the largest of its kind in Europe. The 690,000 sq ft site represents a major shift in Amazon’s logistics network, designed to store and distribute high-demand products to around 20 fulfilment centres nationwide rather than shipping items directly to customers. Staff at the new Amazon Peterborough site (Image: ©UNP Tim George) Tomislav Batinic, site leader at Amazon, said: "This site is a complete re-invention of how we run part of our logistics operation, and a historic moment for Amazon. "It is the first of its kind in the UK and the largest in Europe, and it is fitting that it is happening in Peterborough — a city with real history. "Products arrive from suppliers at one end and head out to fulfilment centres across the country at the other, all under one roof. "This type of site will be the template for how we run our operations in the years ahead, so it is a privilege to be the one introducing it. "We have called our team 'Team Founders' to mark how historic this moment is — and we are not just launching a building, we are laying the groundwork for something that will grow and endure long after Day One."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Horror play 'fails to deliver a genuinely chilling experience' says Cambs reviewer
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: We went to Blackout: Fear Loves An Audience, which was marketed as a hauntingly immersive theatrical experience, and this is what we thought During its recent run at The New Theatre in Peterborough, the play attracted an audience anticipating a high-impact, two-act horror experience. The set design was ominous, establishing a chilling atmosphere before the show began. A flickering ghost light, a prominent ticking grandfather clock and as the thick stage smoke cleared, a centrally positioned chair equipped with handcuffs came into view. Before anyone could discuss what could be seen, the theatre was plunged into darkness, promoting a palpable reaction from the stalls. The production placed the audience as silent observers of actors rehearsing the play "The Devil's Daughter" within an old haunted venue. The reliance on the venue's existing environment to create immersion 'pulling you into to the play itself' proved ineffective, particularly given the theatre’s modern refurbished building. The play itself, which evolves to reveal the actors' own ghostly experiences, is slightly comical, yet the script relied heavily on profanity to achieve it's intended impact. While the production had the potential to deliver significant suspense, it ultimately failed to achieve the objective. The post-show feedback suggested that the experience did not meet the expectations of those seeking a genuinely chilling performance.

Fresh plans have been submitted to turn a former RAF Association club into new homes after a previous application was refused. OTAA St Neots Property Ltd wants to convert the Grade II-listed building at 44-46 Huntingdon Street, St Neots, into eight homes and build a three-bedroom house at the rear. The move comes after similar plans were refused earlier this year. In February 2026, the council turned down proposals for the conversion of the building into seven homes, alongside the construction of two bungalows at the rear. Before the refusal, planning officers had raised concerns about harm to the listed building and conservation area, flood risk, privacy and inadequate waste storage. That application hoped to restore the property back to its historical use - a series of residential units called The Limes. Similar plans for the club were refused by the council in February Later, the building became established as a pub for the town's Royal Air Force Association. The private members club closed its doors in 2023 after declining membership, and the building was handed back to RAFA, standing vacant ever since. The new plans would restore and convert the historic building into eight homes, with a detached house at the rear. There are also plans for landscaping works, parking facilities, cycle storage, and drainage improvements. The new plans involve creating eight homes within the existing building and a detached home at the rear A heritage assessment submitted with the application concludes the proposals would cause "less than substantial harm" to the listed building but argues this would be outweighed by public benefits, including restoring the deteriorating asset and securing its long-term future. The design team says the scheme would improve the building with repairs to its windows, roof and exterior finishes. New landscaping would replace much of the existing hardstanding, with private gardens, hedgerows and trees added across the site. Five more car parking spaces would be added according to the plans, bringing the total number at the site to 11. There are also 24 new cycle spaces proposed. Full details on the application can be viewed using the Huntingdonshire District Council planning portal.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: More than 5,500 EV charge points planned across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of new electric vehicle charging points are set to be installed across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. The £5.4 million project, funded through the Government’s Local Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (LEVI) scheme, will deliver more than 5,500 charge points across the region, with 1,058 planned for Peterborough. Paul Bristow, Mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, said: "Our commitment to delivering 930 chargers is unlocking many more times that number, which is exactly what I want our funding to do. "If you've got a driveway, charging an electric car is more straightforward. "If you haven't, it's been a real barrier, so this funding will help put EV charging within reach for more people." The scheme is designed to support residents without off-street parking by providing accessible charging options close to home. The chargers will be installed on residential streets and will include two sockets per unit. A 15-year contract has been awarded to Believ by Peterborough City Council. In Cambridgeshire, 4,527 charge points will be installed, while Peterborough will receive 1,058. Councillor Angus Ellis, cabinet member for environment at Peterborough City Council, said: "This is a significant chance to accelerate our city’s transition to cleaner, greener transport whilst improving access to EV charging for residents who do not have off-street parking. "The move ties in with our ongoing work to reduce carbon emissions and we will use grant funding to unlock substantial private sector investment, delivering a much larger and more accessible charging network than could be achieved through public funding alone." The project supports the region’s 2040 target of ensuring 80 per cent of households without off-street parking are within a five-minute walk of a public charge point or able to charge on-street from a domestic charger. Delivery of the new infrastructure is planned to begin in 2027, subject to the remaining statutory procurement stages.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Warnings of ‘incredibly serious’ water shortage if supply concern not taken seriously
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Warnings have been raised the region could face an ‘incredibly serious’ water shortage if supply concerns are not taken seriously. South Cambridgeshire District Council raised the alarm after it emerged a water credits system is no longer being actively progressed. The £4.5m scheme was announced in 2024 to offset the pressure on Cambridgeshire’s water network caused by new housing developments. At a scrutiny meeting last month, representatives of the newly-launched Greater Cambridge Development Corporation said they were still working on “what shape” the system could take but it was not being “actively progressed”. Cllr Dr Richard Williams said:  “I think we were all very surprised to hear that the water credits system is no longer a priority for the water scarcity group. “We should make it very clear that the water shortage in Greater Cambridge is incredibly serious. “We all saw it in the summer with the drought that we experienced. “If we have another few summers like that I think Greater Cambridge could have a very serious water problem. But we can all see the impact on the natural environment around us.” “We need really serious action – we need it now.” The Conservative councillor asked South Cambridgeshire District Council to support a motion expressing “alarm” at recent statements made “from more than one agency” which suggest “water supply is no longer regarded as an immediate concern in Greater Cambridge”. Cllr Chloe Wills-Eve asked how this could be the case while a hosepipe ban which came into effect in July is still ongoing. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “How can water no longer be considered an immediate concern when existing residents are being asked to restrict their own usage? “I’m not opposed to development but it must be sustainable. “Before planning powers transfer to the Dev Co we need clear answers and a credible, deliverable plan.” Cllr Laurence Damary-Homan said: “I don’t even know how I can go about describing what I felt when I heard the development corporation’s comments on water in this area. “Every single one of us in this room knows how serious an issue this is.” The Liberal Democrat councillor said it was “beyond belief” that they were not taking water supply issues as “seriously as they need to be”. Cllr Anna Bradnam said it was “extremely worrying” that the development corporation was no longer treating the credits scheme as a priority. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “Water credits was the way our concerns about water supply were going to be answered. “That was to give us comfort to cover the decisions that we were making as planning committees. “I think it’s going to be difficult for us to make decisions going forward.” Cllr Heather Williams said they were unable to object to planning applications based on water supply because the credits system was promised. The Conservative councillor said: “It does make me think what’s happened to those planning consents that are already out there, that were made on the basis of water credits coming through. “What this council has done, unintentionally, is made an already very difficult situation worse because of the lack of accurate information that was given at the time. “Everyone needs to try and really emphasise the need to sort this out quickly and we also need the backup to be able to say no to development if these matters are not resolved.” The motion passed unanimously.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Flagship Drive Project launched to tackle high-risk domestic abuse in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A flagship scheme is being rolled out to reduce domestic abuse in Cambridgeshire. The Drive Project, launched through a multi-agency partnership, will focus on changing the behaviour of high-risk perpetrators across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. Darryl Preston, police and crime commissioner for Cambridgeshire, said: "Victims are at the heart of everything I do as Commissioner. "The roll out of this flagship project will support the work already underway across Cambridgeshire to manage risk and break the cycle of abuse to protect victims and ensure perpetrators are rightly held accountable for their actions." The programme will be delivered by Red Snapper Managed Services and is supported by Cambridgeshire County Council, Peterborough City Council, Cambridgeshire Constabulary, and the Probation Service. Case managers will work one-to-one with high-risk perpetrators over several months, aiming to change their behaviour through close monitoring and disruption tactics. The scheme will take a tailored approach based on individual risk levels and will involve co-ordinated action across multiple agencies. Survivors will also benefit from additional support, with two new posts created to strengthen the work of independent domestic violence advisor (IDVA) services in the county. The project is funded by the Home Office following a successful bid by the commissioner’s office. It forms part of the government's Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) Strategy. Jonathan Hussey, managing director of Red Snapper Managed Services, said: "We are proud to have been chosen to deliver the Drive Project in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. "Drive holds the people causing harm to account, disrupting their behaviour and, wherever possible, changing it for good. "Our team will be working with the highest-risk individuals in the county, and we look forward to seeing the difference we can make alongside local services." Perpetrators will be identified and referred to the scheme via multi-agency arrangements.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New Milton police station opens with 24-cell custody suite and modern facilities
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new police station has officially opened in Milton. Located next to Milton Park and Ride, the two-storey facility is designed to improve public services, manage growing demand, and support officers and staff with modern infrastructure. It replaces the outdated Parkside Police Station. Chris Balmer, Chief Constable of Cambridgeshire Constabulary, said: "The opening of Milton Police Station is a significant moment for Cambridgeshire Constabulary and for the communities we serve. Officers and staff have moved into the purpose-built police station (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) "This modern, purpose-built facility gives our officers and staff the environment, tools and capacity they need to meet rising demand, respond more efficiently, and provide a high-quality service to the public for many years to come. "It represents a major investment in community safety and in our frontline people." The station includes a 24-cell custody suite—double the previous capacity—alongside interview rooms, medical facilities, and secure holding areas. It also features open-plan offices, space for investigative work, and areas for cross-force and multi-agency collaboration. Sustainability features include air source heat pumps, solar panels, and electric vehicle chargers. The building has achieved an A rating for energy efficiency. Darryl Preston, Police and Crime Commissioner, said: "As a former police officer who regularly worked out of Parkside Police Station, the Milton facility offers a more modern working environment for police officers and staff. The new station includes a 24-cell custody suite and modern facilities (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) "It’s better access to our roads network will enable the Constabulary to meet the demands of our growing population, particularly in the south of the county. "I would like to thank everyone involved in the development – from the constructors, Wilmott Dixon to our Estates and IT Team who have worked tirelessly to make this happening." Plans for the new station were submitted in September 2020. Following an archaeological investigation, construction started in January 2024. The new facility replaces Parkside Police Station, built in the 1960s.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs Typo store to close as stationery retailer ends UK trading
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A high street stationery store in Cambridgeshire is set to close as the retailer plans to end trading in the UK. Typo, owned by Australian group Cotton On, will close all its UK stores and end online trading by early 2027. As a result, the Typo store in Cambridge, located at 2 Lion Yard Shopping Centre, is set to close down in the next few months. A Cotton On Group spokesperson said: "After careful consideration we are closing Typo’s operations in the United Kingdom, with all stores and online trading to close by early 2027. "We recognise the impact of this decision on our Typo UK team who is already aware of this, and our priority is to support our people through this transition. "Over the past two years, we’ve taken steps to reshape Typo’s global operations and footprint to operate more sustainably, setting the brand up for a stronger long‑term future. "With the launch this year of our new Typo concept in Australia, South Africa and Malaysia, we’ve seen exciting momentum globally and remain incredibly optimistic about the brand’s future. "However, despite the efforts of our teams, ongoing high rent and operating costs, combined with softer sales, mean there is no sustainable path today for Typo in the UK. "Cotton On, Cotton On Body and Cotton On Kids will continue to operate through online and wholesale channels in the UK, and we remain confident in their long-term growth." The retailer, which launched in the UK in 2016, has operated stores in major shopping centres across the country, including London. A specific date for the closure of the Cambridge store has not been confirmed yet. The online store for UK customers is also expected to close by next year.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Robbers who attacked group of boys before stealing child’s bicycle pictured
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two men who attacked a group of boys before they stole a child’s bicycle in Peterborough have been convicted. Declan Hyland, 29, Imran Ali, 41, and another man ambushed the youngsters at about 5pm on April 18. They blocked the path of the teenage boys, two of whom were on bikes and the third a scooter, between Ivatt Way and Bourges Boulevard. They then pushed the boys off the bikes and repeatedly punched them, using keys held within their knuckles as improvised weapons. The boys tried to defend themselves, but Ali managed to ride off on one of the bikes - a Carrera worth about £600. He was closely followed by Hyland, who shouted an insult at the boys as he fled. The victims received minor injuries, including cuts caused by the keys that were used as weapons. Detectives reviewed CCTV footage from the area, resulting in Ali being identified and arrested. A media appeal was circulated with images of the two other men, resulting in Hyland being identified and arrested. The third man was not identified. Hyland, of no known address, admitted robbery and two counts of attempted robbery. Ali, also of no known address, denied the same counts but was found guilty following a trial at Cambridge Crown Court last month. On Monday (October 12) at the same court Hyland was jailed for five years. Ali will appear at Cambridge Crown Court on October 19 for sentencing. DC George Corney said: "This was a nasty attack on three teenage boys that understandably left them extremely shaken. "For three men to attack and rob a group of young boys, who admirably tried to defend themselves, really is cowardly. "I’d like to thank the public for helping us identify Hyland and therefore bringing him to justice." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Plans to redevelop Hinchingbrooke Hospital have taken a major step forward. This follows an agreement in principle to acquire land as part of a major hospital redevelopment programme. North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust has reached agreement in principle to acquire around six hectares of former Cambridgeshire Constabulary land, which will be used to support the redevelopment of Hinchingbrooke Hospital. Deborah Lee, senior responsible officer for the Hinchingbrooke Hospital Redevelopment, said: "Reaching agreement on this land acquisition is a major milestone for the Hinchingbrooke Hospital Redevelopment Programme. "Securing this site will allow us to deliver the vital infrastructure needed to support our plans for a modern hospital that meets the needs of our patients, staff and communities for decades to come." The land will be used for critical infrastructure, including a new access road, around 682 parking spaces, environmental mitigation works, and low-carbon energy infrastructure. These improvements are subject to planning approval. A public exhibition showcasing the latest plans will be held in the Garden Restaurant at Hinchingbrooke Hospital on Saturday October 17 from 10am to 2pm. The project aims to address challenges posed by ageing hospital infrastructure and to support the healthcare needs of a growing population in Huntingdonshire and nearby areas. The acquisition is also expected to improve access to the hospital and reduce congestion in the surrounding area. Darryl Preston, police and crime commissioner, said: "As owner of the police estate in Cambridgeshire, I have a duty to ensure that land no longer needed for policing purposes is used in a way that delivers the greatest benefit to the public. "Once finalised, this sale will help improve access to local healthcare facilities, providing a positive outcome for residents and the wider community." The transaction is still subject to legal completion and final approvals. This includes the return of land to the police and crime commissioner from National Highways after the completion of the Views Common scheme.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts leaseholder furious over 'unacceptable' bill increase and payment issues
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire leaseholder says he has lodged a complaint with a major social housing provider after an 'unacceptable' 90% bill increase and other payment issues. Blazej Kalinowski, who rents under a shared ownership scheme with Places for People, said that his building insurance suddenly doubled with little explanation. When he signed up with the company in November 2024, he paid £20 a month in insurance on his two-bedroom property in Huntingdon. But he was surprised when this year the bill nearly doubled. Blazej said: "I understand that prices will go up every year as you can expect that. "However I was a bit shocked this year in April when it suddenly went from £20 to over £40." He claimed that the company Places for People get to manage the property also failed to collect his rent one month and the following month only took around £30 out of the full £500 bill. Blazej said: "The third month they took nearly £900 for two rents altogether. "I'm a single father who's coparenting two children, you can imagine on one salary it's a bit tricky these days. "Why do I have to chase about payments, why are they collecting money in random amounts whenever it suits them instead of as its supposed to be on the first of each month?" Blazej has raised a complaint with Places for People, but said the response from stage 1 was that they couldn't see any wrongdoing from the company. He added: "For me, a nearly double increase is completely unacceptable. "What worries me is that this may not just affect me, but thousands of people around the country because Places for People have a lot of properties. "At the end of the day, we are in such a financial state that everyone is looking for savings. "So this increase, I can manage it but it's a huge burden on my monthly expenses." Blazej has two children and the price increase and inconsistent rent bills are costs he would much prefer to spend on activities with them. He also fears the bills will continue to rise with little explanation. He said: "If I managed a property and I saw that my client would be paying nearly 90% more on house insurance from one year to another, I would question why that was happening and how can that be justified." Ben Obese-Jecty, MP for Huntingdon, raised concerns about Places for People with Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook in Parliament on September 7. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "I have received over 70 complaints from tenants in my constituency who are resident in Places for People properties about its failure to maintain its obligation to fix the property and carry out basic maintenance. "Are the Government aware of whether this is a more widespread problem, and is there anything they can do to encourage Places for People to fulfil its obligations?" Mr Pennycook responded that Places for People will have no doubt heard the complaints raised. He added: "Social housing providers are regulated on the basis of consumer standards, and they are inspected on that basis. "We have introduced Awaab’s law, which provides that landlords have to fix hazards within specified time limits. "If he wants to write to me with further information about the development in question, I will be happy to look into it." “We aim to keep service charges as low as possible but costs to run buildings - particularly insurance - are continuing to rise. A spokesperson for Places for People said: “At the start of each financial year, insurance charges are estimated using the best information available at that time. "Once the final premium is confirmed, a review is carried out to ensure customers are charged only the actual cost. "In this case, that review resulted in a deficit on Customers’ accounts. Due to the difference between the estimated and final cost, a shortfall arose and a balancing charge has been applied to customers’ accounts. “With regard to the Customer’s rent payments, we acknowledge that the issues they experienced did not meet our usual standards. "We are working closely with the customer to resolve these issues and can confirm that their account has now been updated.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: UK destination named among 'fastest-growing' travel spots for 2027 in new report
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Escapism, adventure and a touch of nostalgia are set to shape the way we travel, according to a new travel trends report. Expedia and Hotels.com have launched their latest travel trends report, Unpack '27: The Trends in Travel, revealing the top destinations and emerging travel behaviours expected to define 2027. The report combines first-party data, a survey of 26,000 travellers and social listening to identify a shift towards more intentional, personalised journeys. Ariane Gorin, chief executive of Expedia Group, said: "Travel is about creating memories, and Unpack '27 uncovers the destinations and experiences shaping those moments. "In 2027, travellers are being more intentional in choosing their next adventure, seeking experiences that are more personal and purposeful to them. "We’re making it easier to discover, plan and book the right trip, so travellers can spend less time managing the details and more time enjoying the moments that matter." Among the fastest-growing destinations globally, Chichester in the UK featured on Expedia’s 2027 Destinations of the Year list, alongside South Lake Tahoe in California, Hyogo in Japan, and Punta del Este in Uruguay. The report highlights the growing appeal of “Un-Adulting” getaways—child-free escapes packed with playful, nostalgic activities. More than half of travellers (57%) said they are likely to book such a trip in 2027, rising to 711% among Gen Z and Millennials. British travellers described these experiences as "having fun and enjoying a carefree day out" (74%), a way to spend "quality time with loved ones" (64 per cent), and a break from "everyday responsibilities" (60%). Hotels.com identified a surge in “Trip Snacking”—short, one-night stays designed to fit around busy schedules and limited budgets. Nearly eight in 10 travellers (79%) plan to book a one-night stay in the coming year, with numbers rising to 83% among younger generations. For British travellers, top reasons for these mini-breaks include attending concerts or sporting events (49%), celebrating milestones (42%), or simply needing a quick reset (23%). Atmosphere is becoming increasingly important, with 56% of travellers booking hotels for their atmosphere or aesthetic appeal. A growing number (65%) are specifically interested in “Gothic Getaways”—dramatic, moody stays featuring neo-Gothic architecture, castles and dark, immersive interiors. These experiences are especially popular among Gen Z and Millennials, with 71% expressing interest. Social media mentions of Gothic architecture and travel have risen by 38%, and global demand for castle properties on Hotels.com has grown by 20%. Film and television continue to influence the way we travel, with nearly one in five travellers booking trips to destinations featured on screen. UK respondents reported spending an average of £600 on these “Set-Jetting” trips, with the figure rising to £629 for those travelling with children. New seasons, sequels and franchise extensions mean that this travel trend is likely to continue well into 2027. Almost half of travellers surveyed said they had researched or booked trips to locations from upcoming shows or films, a figure that jumps to 58% among younger travellers. Expedia’s 2027 trend report paints a picture of travel that is increasingly playful, purposeful and influenced by the worlds of entertainment and design.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: UK households could be owed up to £180 TV Licence refund - how to claim money back
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Households who do not watch live television could claim a TV Licence refund of up to £180. Anyone with a valid licence who no longer watches live broadcasts or BBC iPlayer can apply to cancel their cover and get money back. TV Licensing calculates refunds based on the number of complete unused months remaining before the licence expires. Applicants must have at least one full month left on their licence to qualify, meaning refunds can cover between one and 11 months. Official guidance states: "Any refund due is calculated in unused months. You must have at least one complete month left on your licence that you won’t need before it expires. "So, you could get a refund for between one and 11 months, depending on how long you have left on your licence." TV Licensing aims to process and issue approved refunds within 21 days of receiving an application. Payments are issued either by cheque or directly into a bank account through a BACS transfer. Households cannot claim a refund if there is less than one month between the cancellation date and the expiry date. A TV Licence is legally required to watch or record live television on any channel or service, including Freeview, Sky and Virgin Media. Cover is also required to watch live programmes on streaming services such as Amazon Prime Video, ITVX, YouTube and Netflix. Anyone using BBC iPlayer must also hold a licence, whether watching live, catch-up or on-demand content. Viewers do not need a licence to watch on-demand programmes on services like Netflix, Disney Plus or Amazon Prime Video, provided they are not broadcast live. Watching DVDs or on-demand clips on video websites without live broadcasts also does not require a licence. Households may also qualify for a free TV Licence if someone living at the address meets specific criteria. Residents aged 75 or over who receive Pension Credit can claim a free licence rather than paying the annual fee. Guidance from TV Licensing confirms: "Free TV Licences are only available if you’re 75 or over and you, or your partner living at the same address, are receiving Pension Credit." Eligible residents can apply online or by calling 0300 790 6117 between 8.30am and 6.30pm on weekdays to request a paper form. Those applying for a free licence do not need to cancel their existing Direct Debit, as TV Licensing will cancel payments automatically and issue any refund owed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Eligible people across Cambridgeshire urged to get free NHS winter vaccines
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: NHS Central East is encouraging people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough to check whether they are eligible for free NHS vaccinations and take up the offer to help protect themselves this winter. As we head into the colder months, viruses such as flu, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) spread more easily as people spend more time indoors and in close contact with others. These illnesses can lead to serious complications, particularly for older people, pregnant women, young children and those with certain health conditions. Vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to protect yourself, your family and your community. It can help reduce the risk of serious illness, hospital admission and pressure on NHS services during the winter months. This winter, a range of free NHS vaccinations are available to help protect those most at risk from serious illness: Flu vaccine: available for adults aged 65 and over, pregnant women, 2-3 year olds, school-age children, people with certain health conditions, carers, homeless people and frontline health and care workers. COVID-19 vaccine: available for people aged 75 and over, older adult care home residents and those with weakened immune systems. RSV vaccine: available for pregnant women, adults aged 75 and over, residents in adult care homes and people aged 65 to 74 with a weakened immune system or certain long-term lung conditions. Pneumococcal vaccine: available for people aged 65 and over and some people with underlying health conditions. Depending on the vaccine, eligible people may be able to receive their vaccination at a GP practice, community pharmacy, maternity service, care home or local vaccination service. People eligible for flu or COVID-19 vaccinations can book through the NHS App or National Booking Service and may also receive an invitation from their GP practice. People who think they may be eligible for an RSV or pneumococcal vaccine should contact their GP practice to check their eligibility and arrange an appointment. Cali Makewell, strategic vaccination lead for NHS Central East, said: "Winter viruses such as flu, COVID-19 and RSV can cause serious illness, especially for people who are more vulnerable to infection. "Getting vaccinated is one of the simplest and most effective ways to protect yourself and those around you. "We encourage everyone who is eligible to take up the offer of their free NHS vaccinations. By getting vaccinated, you are helping to protect your own health while also helping to reduce pressure on NHS services this winter." People can find out more about winter vaccinations, check their eligibility and learn how to book on the NHS winter vaccinations webpage Winter vaccinations and winter health - NHS.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New busway approved between Waterbeach and Cambridge
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new busway has been approved despite fears that issues with current routes are “damaging public trust”. The Waterbeach to Cambridge Transport Scheme (W2C) will create a new guided busway route linking Waterbeach New Town with Cambridge. Cllr Anna Bradnam, county councillor for Waterbeach, said the project had been “a long time” in the works and many concerns had been “worked through and resolved”. The Lib Dem councillor said she thought it would be “an extremely important transport link to Cambridge” which is needed with the 11,000 planned homes in the new town. Cllr Darren Green, of Romsey, said he saw “both sides of busways” as either “value-for-money mass transit” or a “cut-price solution”. The Green councillor said: “As far as I can see, there’s not been any progress in trying to solve the problem of how buses may progress through the rush-hour traffic in the morning. Our busways will essentially just hit the same traffic that everyone else is stuck in as soon as they reach Cambridge. “I think now is the time to really question whether Cambridge deserves a better solution for its public transport issues than busways.” Cllr Alex Bulat, of St Ives South and Needingworth, said she would vote for the motion but warned existing busways must be improved to “restore public perception”. The Labour councillor said the Cambridge to St Ives route is “sadly, not currently a success anymore” as it’s “not a commercially viable route”. She said: “What happens on the ground is actually damaging public trust in this type of public infrastructure. “Because people in St Ives, and beyond, face endless delays to travel, commuters are going back to their cars day after day.” Cllr Rory Clark, of Castle, said the busway would give young people and those who don’t drive the ability to move around the county. The Lib Dem councillor said: “I’m sure we would all love a fully fledged light rail system around Greater Cambridge and, indeed across the whole county, but we have to be realistic about the money we have on the table. “Letting the perfect be the enemy of the good isn’t a reason to further exclude young people in Cambridgeshire.” Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of the highways and transport committee, said there was “no shortage of ideas” for public transport in Cambridgeshire. The Lib Dem councillor said: “The most frustrating thing about this is everyone with their own idea nearly always wants to vote against someone else’s idea because it might mean that their idea then becomes less successful. “It just goes round and round in circles – everyone knows that we need to do something and I think that is the really important thing. Making sure that we really do start addressing the issues rather than kicking the issues into the long grass.” The council approved the scheme with 40 votes in favour, eight against and seven abstentions.
