summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Zoo experts warn visitor behaviour risk can never be eliminated after tiger death
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Public safety is an “integral part” of standards regulating zoos in the UK, but risks linked to “unpredictable behaviour” from visitors can never truly be eliminated, experts have said. Concerns were raised after a man was fatally attacked by a tiger when he entered an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park on Saturday. The incident took place months after a three-year-old boy was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure at Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire. Dr Campbell Murn, a former member of the government’s expert committee for zoos and a lecturer in Conservation Science at the University of Reading, said such incidents remain rare, but strengthened regulations could help mitigate risks further. He said: “There’s an enormous amount of effort that goes into the securing of public safety for people who are visiting zoos, in addition to the weight that’s given to animal welfare in those settings as well.” “So it’s certainly something that is a very big and integral part of the zoo standards in this country.” He added that, in zoos that have dangerous wild animals, enclosure design follows set regulations, and staff are trained in emergency responses. “Their training is updated regularly, and they have immediately known and very rapid protocols to respond to emergency incidences, whether it’s an escape in the zoo or whether in very rare situations like this,” he said. “There’s a lot more extensive safety systems involved with dangerous wild animals,” he said. “There’s very clear standards that indicate the size and height of particular enclosures for dangerous wild animals.” Registered zoos across the country undergo regular inspections to ensure compliance with the Secretary of State’s standards of modern zoo practice, Dr Murn added. While some of these zoos “probably need to come up to speed”, Dr Murn said he does not believe the incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park was contributed to by a safety failure. Flowers left at the entrance of Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster (Image: Dave Higgens/PA Wire) He said: “It seems that in this case it was not possible to get there before the visitor was injured and subsequently died.” He also said the question of how to mitigate the risk of a visitor entering the enclosure of a dangerous wild animal was “difficult”. “Even the most elaborate enclosure, if they really want to get in, they’re going to find a way,” Dr Murn said. “What could be changed is to prevent the ease with which that can happen.” “If it was made much more difficult, then that would minimise or reduce the risk further, but it’s never going to truly eliminate it.” He added: “There are some zoos in this country that I don’t think are up to standard, and the process of phasing those out or improving the standards in those zoos is slow.” “There is a process in place, but it can’t happen overnight.” “So, I strongly would support the strengthening of regulations further.” A park spokesperson has said the tiger who attacked the man is safe and well and will not be euthanised following the incident (Image: Dave Higgens/PA Wire) Dr Paul Rose, a member of the UK Zoos Expert Committee (ZEC) and lecturer in animal behaviour at the University of Exeter, said zoos do take into account risks linked to unpredictable behaviour from members of the public in their safety protocols. “Public behaviour can be unpredictable as we all know,” he said. “There will be mitigation in place, such as high fencing, stand-off barriers, signage and explanation and a code of conduct for how to behave at the zoo — and for visitors to take responsibility for their actions.” “Risk assessments will also be undertaken regularly.” “However, a risk of unusual human behaviour will always remain.” “The majority of visitors behave in a way respectful of the animal and environment at the zoo, but there is always a risk of rogue or unusual behaviour and this will continue to be risk assessed and part of zoo personnel training.” Yorkshire Wildlife Park remained closed on Monday as investigations continue into the death of the man. Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on October 10 when the man entered the enclosure. A man died after suffering serious injuries in a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park (Image: Dave Higgens/PA Wire) He was pronounced dead at the scene, South Yorkshire Police said, adding that his family have been informed. The three-year-old boy who suffered serious injuries at Johnsons of Old Hurst was discharged from hospital in late August. The Cambridgeshire zoo said in a previous social media post it was “alerted to reports that a child had allegedly been thrown into one of our crocodile enclosures” on June 18. A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder following the incident and was later bailed as police said he was “assessed as not being fit for interview”. Police were called to Johnsons of Old Hurst zoo in June after a toddler ended up in the crocodile enclosure (Image: Joe Giddens/PA) The suspect in the case reportedly has learning difficulties and had been on a trip with carers, and an investigation has been launched into his care. In October 2016, a large silverback gorilla escaped from its enclosure at London Zoo, with armed police called to the central London attraction while keepers desperately tried to recapture the loose animal. Visitors were evacuated and London Zoo later said they were “never in any danger.” Malcolm Fitzpatrick, curator of mammals at the zoo, described the escape of Kumbuka as a “minor incident” in which the male gorilla got into a secure keeper area that was not open to the public. At the same attraction in 1992, a man was mauled by a lion after he climbed into a fenced enclosure. He was airlifted to hospital with a “very deep chest wound” after zoo staff fired CO2 extinguishers and gunshot to distract the animals. Other examples include a string of incidents at zoos owned by the late conservationist John Aspinall, with five keepers killed between 1980 and 2000. Three were killed by tigers, two were killed by elephants and both keepers and visitors also suffered injuries over the years.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cancer service celebrates 10 years as annual visits rise to 10,000
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A cancer support centre in Peterborough has celebrated its 10th anniversary. The Cancer Wellbeing Service, based at Peterborough City Hospital, supports around 10,000 people each year, up from 6,000 when it relaunched in 2016. Lisa Deacon and Rebecca Hardy, joint service managers, said: "We are so incredibly proud of the service we offer and the wonderful staff and volunteers who deliver that service. "The Centre has been supporting people in its current format since 2016, since undergoing a major transformation to meet the changing needs of cancer patients. "In the first year, we had 6,000 visits – and that number has almost doubled in 10 years. "We are a free service available without referral to anyone affected by cancer and hold hands with the Trusts cancer unit." To mark the milestone, North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust staff and volunteers were invited to a birthday breakfast as a thank you for their hard work and dedication. Professor Steve Barnett OBE, chair of the trust, said: "The Cancer Wellbeing Service and its wonderful gardens are a jewel in the crown of our services. "The feedback we receive from patients and their families is exemplary. "And while the building is beautiful, what is even more beautiful is the care and compassion shown to all the service users." The centre originally opened in 1992 as the Robert Horrell Macmillan Centre, operating primarily as a day unit for patients already receiving hospital care. It was purchased for £850,000 through fundraising efforts by the local Macmillan team, who later handed it over to the hospital. Today, the centre offers support to people living with cancer, including those newly diagnosed, in treatment, recovering, or experiencing long-term effects. It also supports families, friends, and healthcare professionals. Services include one-to-one and group sessions, information and advice, art therapy, complementary therapies, and counselling.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP State Pension Age row takes new turn as Government responds to campaign
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Government has rejected calls to lower the State Pension age in a major update to a petition arguing that older workers should be able to retire earlier to free up jobs for young adults. The campaign, created by Helen Grice, has attracted 16,749 signatures and calls for the State Pension age to be reduced so more young people can get a foothold in the jobs market. But in its response, published on October 12, the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said: “The Government has no plans to lower the State Pension age.” The petition argues that making people work for longer means there are fewer jobs available for younger adults who are struggling to find employment. It says lowering the State Pension age could encourage older workers to retire, giving employers the opportunity to recruit younger staff while allowing people who have worked throughout their lives to enjoy their retirement. However, ministers have defended the current approach, pointing to rising life expectancy and the financial challenges of supporting an ageing population. The Government said: “We are fortunate today that more people are reaching old age: life expectancy has risen rapidly over the past century, driven by breakthroughs in medical treatments and generally healthier lifestyles.” It added that men aged 66 in the UK in 2026 could expect to live, on average, another 19.3 years, while women of the same age could expect a further 21.9 years. The DWP said State Pension age policy must reflect the fact that people are living longer, with some increases necessary to maintain fairness between generations, protect public finances and ensure the State Pension remains sustainable. The response comes as the Government's Third State Pension age Review gets underway. The review will consider what State Pension age is appropriate for future decades, weighing up a range of evidence, including an independent report from Dr Suzy Morrissey. While ministers have ruled out a reduction for now, they also acknowledged the difficulties facing young people trying to get into work. The Government said around one million young people are not in education, employment or training. It said it is investing an additional £2.5billion by 2029 in the Youth Guarantee and the Growth and Skills Levy, with the aim of supporting almost one million young people and creating up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn. The measures include expanded Youth Hubs, more intensive support through Jobcentres, additional work experience and training, a £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant and a £2,000 apprenticeship hiring payment for employers. The plans also include a fully funded six-month job for long-term unemployed people aged 18 to 24. Recommended reading Despite the Government's response, the campaign is still open for signatures. The petition, titled Lower the State Pension age to free up jobs for young adults, was published on June 25 and will close on December 25, 2026. It has passed the 10,000-signature threshold required for a Government response, but has yet to reach the 100,000 signatures needed for it to be considered for a debate in Parliament. The petition's central argument is that allowing more older workers to retire could create opportunities for younger people who are currently out of work. The Government's response makes clear that it does not plan to lower the State Pension age, instead pointing to its youth employment measures and the ongoing review of the age at which people can claim their State Pension.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The one thing Brits can't stop talking about as autumn Budget draws closer
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Brits spend 20 hours a month talking about money, making personal finance the nation's number one topic of conversation ahead of the Budget. Household bills, spending habits and savings are among the issues dominating discussions, with people dedicating a further 15 hours every month to talking about the wider economy. But the figures also reveal the toll money worries are taking, with one in four adults (25%) worrying about their household finances every day. More than six in ten (61%) feel anxious about money at least once a week, while more than two thirds (68%) say financial concerns keep them awake at night, according to research from Utility Warehouse. The findings come as households await the Chancellor's Budget announcements later this month, with millions hoping for clarity on what changes could mean for their wages, savings and monthly outgoings. Keeping on top of household finances has become a regular part of everyday life, with the average Brit spending an hour and a half a week on financial admin. That includes checking bank balances, paying bills and moving money between accounts, as well as keeping an eye on energy costs. The research found that: With household budgets under pressure, these routine tasks can be an important way for people to track where their money is going and spot potential savings. Younger adults are increasingly using digital tools to keep tabs on their finances, with Gen Z more likely to turn to banking apps and artificial intelligence. More than half (53%) of Gen Z respondents use banking apps to monitor their money, while 14% use AI. Older generations, meanwhile, are more likely to check their bank accounts regularly, with 66% doing so, or write down their spending in a notebook, a habit reported by 18%. Despite embracing digital tools, younger adults are not immune to financial pressures. While 36% of Gen Z respondents said they had a clear budget to track their spending, 11% admitted they often struggled to stay on top of their finances. More than one in five (21%) said they had dipped into their savings to cover everyday spending. Recommended reading: The findings highlight how financial concerns extend beyond balancing the books, with many adults worrying about their finances on a regular basis. One in four respondents said they worried about household finances every day, while 61% experienced anxiety about money at least once a week. The fact that 68% said money concerns kept them awake at night also points to the wider impact of financial pressures on everyday life. With bills, savings and spending all competing for attention, the run-up to the Budget is likely to bring renewed focus on household finances. The research was released by Utility Warehouse as part of its Chancellor of the Home campaign, fronted by brand ambassador Cat Deeley.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £14m approved for 16 active travel schemes across Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than £14 million has been approved for active travel schemes across Cambridgeshire. The funding, secured through the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority from the UK Government’s Local Transport Consolidated Settlement fund, will support 16 projects over the next four years. Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways and transport committee, said: "Active travel remains one of our top priorities, so I’m delighted we’re approved a programme today, supported by fresh funding from Active Travel England, which will benefit diverse communities across Cambridgeshire over the next four years and beyond. "Whether schemes are linking homes, schools, employment centres, leisure venues or travel hubs – when active travel is a reliable option for local journeys it leads to safer streets, less isolated and more interactive communities, cleaner air and better health." Among the schemes to receive funding are widening the existing shared-use path from Great Stukeley to Alconbury Weald, improving links to Huntingdon Station, and a shared-use path connecting the A505 to Granta Science and Technology Park. Other projects include a new footpath on Cromwell Road in Wisbech and an active travel route between Ely and Soham, which will connect to the National Cycle Network. The council also allocated £80,000 per year for its School Streets programme, which aims to improve walking and cycling access around schools. In a separate decision, councillors agreed to reallocate £890,000 in funding from the Whittlesford-Duxford scheme to a new crossing at the A14 Histon interchange, pending approval from Active Travel England and the combined authority. This crossing is designed to improve safety for students travelling between Cambridge and Histon, including those attending Impington Village College. A further £2.776 million in revenue funding has also been earmarked for behaviour change schemes, such as Bikeability courses for schools, adaptive cycle training, and community cargo-share hubs.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: All we know after 'trespass' at RAF base in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire found itself thrust into the national spotlight last week after counter terror police revealed they were probing alleged trespass offences at an RAF base. Security patrols by Ministry of Defence Police at RAF Molesworth identified an abandoned vehicle at 10pm on Wednesday (October 7). Officers from Cambridgeshire Constabulary attended and further searches of the area later revealed a small breach in the perimeter fence. At 2am the next day, two men, aged 36 and 32, were arrested inside the base perimeter. Here's everything we know so far. The pair were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage and taken to a police station. They were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023. The Latvian nationals living in the UK have since been released on bail with strict conditions, it was announced on Friday October 9. Officers carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation. the abandoned vehicle was recovered by police and taken to a nearby location. While undergoing further searches, concerns over the vehicle led to the deployment of specialist ‘EOD’ officers to carry out additional checks. As a precaution, a cordon was put in place, which impacted local roads in the Glatton area, including part of the A1(M). However, after assessment by specialist officers, nothing of concern was found and all cordons were lifted. The incident is now being investigated by officers from Counter Terrorism Policing. Commander Helen Flanagan, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but there is nothing from our investigation so far to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week. "Our investigation continues and we are working closely with colleagues from the Ministry of Defence Police and Cambridgeshire Constabulary on this. "A key line of enquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity. “Meanwhile, I would encourage the public to remain vigilant and if you see anything of concern, then to contact police." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 29 Filipino nurses mark 25 years of service at Hinchingbrooke Hospital
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A group of Filipino nurses have been honoured for 25 years of dedicated service at Hinchingbrooke Hospital in Huntingdon. The nurses, who first arrived in the UK in 2001, have spent a quarter of a century caring for patients and supporting colleagues across the trust. Many remain part of the workforce, having built careers, friendships, and families in the community. Menchie Lynn, clinical site matron and one of the original arrivals, said: "We've had a lovely time marking our 25-year milestone together. "It has been wonderful to celebrate. "The difficult and heart breaking moments were when we left our families behind. "But we are still glad to be here and serve the community of Huntingdon and Cambridgeshire." To mark the occasion, the hospital hosted an afternoon tea where nurses received long service certificates, commemorative badges, and vouchers. A special video reflecting on their journey over the past 25 years was also shared. Hannah Coffey, chief executive of North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust, said: "We celebrated not only the many years of service, but the countless lives that have been touched along the way and the lasting legacy that has been built. "Our Filipino nurses have cared for patients and families with dedication, compassion, and excellence through changing times." Of the 60 nurses who joined Hinchingbrooke Hospital in 2001, 29 stayed. Some have retired, while others have moved to different hospitals or abroad. Ms Coffey said: "We reflected together on the courage it took to leave everything familiar behind to start a new life in the UK. "This celebration is an opportunity to thank each and every one of them for their outstanding contribution to healthcare and to our Trust." Some of their children have even gone on to work within the Trust, continuing a legacy of care across generations.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs foodbank raises £15,000 after van stolen and stripped for parts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire foodbank charity has raised £15,000 in a week after its van was stolen and stripped for parts. Cambridge City Foodbank reached its fundraising target in less than a week after damage to one van put its operation at serious risk. Police were called at about 2.20pm on October 7 after a foodbank vehicle was reported stolen from Nuffield Close, Cambridge. Police recovered the vehicle in the early hours of October 8, but parts were missing. The foodbank's van was recovered but parts were missing (Image: Cambridge City Foodbank) A police spokesperson said: "Investigations are ongoing and anyone with any information or relevant dashcam or doorbell footage is urged to report this to police." Cambridge City Foodbank provides emergency and affordable food to people in need, using vans to transport donations and food parcels. The independent charity launched an appeal for a replacement vehicle, saying the incident put its operation "at serious risk". But people across Cambridgeshire rallied behind the foodbank, which exceeded its £15,000 target in less than a week. Stephen Thornton, Chair of Trustees at the foodbank, said: "When our van was stolen, we were at real risk of our operations grinding to a halt, and not being able to provide food for the people in Cambridge who needed it. The foodbank hit their fundraising target of £15,000 in just a week (Image: Cambridge City Foodbank) "But what happened next has left everyone at Cambridge City Foodbank both humbled and inspired. "We have been absolutely blown away by the response to what was a tragic and heart-breaking situation and, in less than a week, our appeal has hit our target of £15,000." The charity can now source a replacement van and continue providing food for people in need. The charity called the situation "tragic and heart-breaking" (Image: Cambridge City Foodbank) The charity said further donations through its JustGiving page would support the foodbank’s wider work. Mr Thornton added: "Every single donation, whatever its size, has made a huge difference to our charity and every person we serve and, while words can’t really express the sense of gratitude we have for your incredible support, as Chair of Trustees, I extend my sincere thanks to each and every one of you."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Three friends from Cambridgeshire have scaled the highest peak in North Africa. James Baker, 35, from Ramsey, Paul Mallinson, 65, from Houghton, and Tamar Mullard, 45, from Whittlesey took on Mount Toubkal in Morocco. Their five-day ascent raised more than £9,000 for Sue Ryder’s palliative, end-of-life care, and bereavement support services. Paul, Tamar and James (Image: Sue Ryder ) James said: "There is no doubt that the challenge was hard – in fact by far the hardest thing I have ever done – and exhausting." He said the trek was in memory of his father, Peter, who died from oesophageal cancer at the age of 54. James said: "Even though Dad was only in a hospice for two days, those two days were completely different from his time hospital. The hike (Image: Sue Ryder) "The hospice staff were amazing." Paul said the climb, which totalled 70,000 steps and 34 miles, was tougher than he had anticipated. Paul said: "At 70,000 steps and 34 miles, the climb and descent was longer than I expected, and I had to keep reminding myself why I was doing it." Paul and James (Image: Sue Ryder) The men held several fundraising events before the trek, including a bake sale and live auction at The Three Horseshoes in Houghton, which raised more than £2,000 in a single day. James  said: "We want to say a huge thank you to everyone who has supported us with our fundraising." James' dad Peter (Image: Sue Ryder) While Mr Mallinson considers his next fundraising challenge, Mr Baker and Ms Mullard are already discussing a climb of Mount Kilimanjaro in 2028. The trek was part of Sue Ryder’s 2026 challenge events. Donations can still be made through their individual JustGiving pages.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire MP has called for renewed action to phase out animal testing. Huntingdon MP Ben Obese-Jecty raised his concerns at the Conservative Party Conference during a meeting with Isobel Martin of Animal Free Research UK. They discussed the Government’s failure to deliver its manifesto pledge to phase out animal testing. MBR Acres, a facility that breeds dogs, specifically beagles for scientific, medical, and veterinary research in the UK, is in Mr Obese-Jecty's constituency. Read more Man bailed after protest camp outside puppy breeding facility cordoned off Convicted paedophile found with indecent images sent back to prison Huntingdon Town Council given go ahead to fly Pride and Pan-African flags Swimming pool plans for industrial unit refused over parking and safety concerns Counter-terror police investigating after two men arrested at Cambs RAF base Owned by Marshall BioResources, it can breed up to 2,000 dogs a year and sells them to laboratories for testing. The MBR Acres site at Wyton is the focus of ongoing protests, highlighting concerns over animal welfare and the ethical implications of animal testing. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "MBR Acres continues to be a focus for campaigners as the Government continues to use legal action on individuals to prevent campaign interference against it. "The Home Office continues to issue licences for animal testing despite the Government’s pledge and publication of the Replacing Animals in Science strategy later this year last year." He also questioned the effectiveness of the Home Office’s Animals in Science Regulation Unit, particularly its lack of regular unannounced site audits. The concerns come ahead of a Home Office report on animal welfare failings in British laboratories. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "As an officer within the All Party Parliamentary Group on Phasing Out Animal Testing in Medical Research I will continue to raise these issues with the new Minister responsible for the strategy, Chris McDonald." Regular protests outside MBR Acres began after footage of beagles was obtained in 2021, with activists maintaining a presence at the site since July that year. In a previous letter to science minister Lord Patrick Vallance, Mr Obese-Jecty said replacing animal tests could take more than a decade and require action from government, regulators and pharmaceutical companies. MBR Acres has said it operates under Home Office regulations and that an ongoing High Court injunction remains in force at the site.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Couple who kept 'vulnerable' man prisoner in his own home pictured
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two drug users who kept a man with mobility issues barricaded in his own flat for more than 12 hours have been jailed. Zoe Smith and Shane Rowe visited the man, who was known to them, at his home in Dennis Road, Cambridge, at around 7pm on February 22, 2025. The man opened the door and the pair rushed inside and blocked his door using a table from inside the property. At about 1am the following morning, the man tried to get up from his sofa but was told he “wasn’t going anywhere”. He was then was punched repeatedly in the face. Violent behaviour by Rowe was spurred on by Smith who encouraged his anger. The ordeal continued for a further eight hours, until 9am, when the couple moved the table away from the door and left to buy drugs. Once he was sure they had left, the panicked man fled to his neighbours for help. So as not to arouse suspicion, he returned to his home and a short while later Rowe and Smith also returned. Police were not far behind, and at 10am knocked on the door. The victim managed to open the door despite being shouted at by Rowe. Smith jumped out of the window and Rowe also managed to escape. Zoe Smith was found guilty of false imprisonment and theft (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Afterwards, the man noticed his wallet and phone had been taken. The man told officers what had happened and said he lived in fear of the couple. Rowe, of Crosfield Court, Cambridge, and Smith, of College Close, Edmonton, London, were later arrested. In police interview the pair, both 39, denied the offences and otherwise answered no comment. They stood trial and were found guilty by jurors of false imprisonment and theft. Rowe was also found guilty of assault by beating. The pair were sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on Friday (October 9) where Rowe was jailed for eight years and Smith was handed five years behind bars. Both were also given indefinite restraining orders preventing them from contacting the victim in any way. Written by 21-year-old student Francesca Nicolaides, The Animator’s Code tells the story of a rogue AI and the emotional and ethical dilemmas that unfold. Francesca , from Alconbury, began writing the novel as a personal project and describes the book as a way of processing the rapid rise of AI in everyday life. She said: "For a long time, artificial intelligence felt incredibly science-fiction to me – something that existed in the distant future rather than something we would actually be able to speak to and interact with in our everyday lives. "Then suddenly, that future arrived." Published by Cranthorpe Millner, The Animator’s Code explores human-AI relationships, corporate control of autonomous technology, and the nature of consciousness and personhood. The Animator's Code book cover (Image: The Animator's Code) Francesca said she has always enjoyed creative writing but never expected to become a published author. She said: "When I began writing The Animator’s Code, I was really writing it for myself. "But something changed during the process and I became completely absorbed in it and couldn’t put it down. "At that point, I decided to take the chance and approach publishers." She is already working on a sequel and hopes the story could one day be adapted for film. Francesca recently began her studies at ARU Peterborough and said she is passionate about teaching as well as writing. She said: "In education, you have the opportunity to nurture children as they grow, help them discover what they are capable of and potentially have an impact that stays with them for years. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Heroes who saved drowning man from Hunts river earn national award
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two heroes who saved a man from drowning in a Huntingdonshire river are to receive national honours for their bravery. Alidio Gomez and Jade Ursell, from All Aboard Boating in Eaton Socon, leapt into the River Ouse in St Neots on May 27. They were on a cruiser when they spotted a man and a teenager swimming nearby. When the man disappeared beneath the surface, Alidio and Jade jumped from the cruiser’s deck and pulled him back up. A nearby rower joined the rescue, and together they brought the man to the riverbank and onto a jetty. The man appeared not to be breathing in the water but began breathing and talking again on the jetty. He was conscious and sitting up when the ambulance arrived. Alidio and Jade are to receive the Royal Humane Society’s top life-saving honour, a Testimonial on Parchment, for their actions. Andrew Chapman, secretary of the Royal Humane Society, said: "This was a serious life and death incident and time was of the essence. "If the man had been under water longer than he was it is unlikely he could have been revived. "Fortunately the two award winners realised they had to act at once, went into the water, got the man to the surface and undoubtedly saved his life. "They richly deserve the awards they are to receive." Mr Chapman urged the public to nominate people who carry out similar acts of bravery. He said: "There are many incidents where lives are saved but those involved never receive the awards they deserve because nobody nominates them. "We appeal to members of the public to tell us about incidents where lives have been saved, sometimes by people who put their own lives in danger." Founded in 1774, the Royal Humane Society is the UK's leading national body for recognising bravery in saving human life, apart from honours awarded by the Crown.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Passengers warned of rail disruption ahead of improvement works
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Rail passengers are being warned of disruption to journeys ahead of improvement work on a major railway. Trains will be diverted between Doncaster and Peterborough, with rail replacement coaches serving intermediate stations. The changes come into force on Sunday (October 18) while Network Rail carries out engineering work on the East Coast Main Line. Almost 670 metres of rail will be replaced near Newark as part of efforts to deliver more reliable journeys. Nearly 50 metres of drainage will be renewed at Grantham station to improve the resilience of the railway during periods of heavy rainfall. Repairs will be carried out to brickwork at Stoke Tunnel, south of Grantham, to maintain the structural integrity of the historical railway asset. Meanwhile, electrical components between Grantham and Bullpit Lane level crossing, Balderton, will be renewed and replaced. John Grainger, joint head of performance, LNER & Network Rail East Coast, said the updates will "help deliver a more reliable railway". "These improvements will help reduce the risk of infrastructure faults, improve resilience during severe weather and support smoother, more reliable journeys," he said. "We’re grateful to passengers for their patience and understanding while we carry out this essential work." A spokesperson for the train operators added: "These improvements are an important investment in the East Coast Main Line. "While the work is taking place, some services will be amended and journey times may be longer than usual. "We encourage customers to check before they travel and allow extra time for their journeys." The following services will experience changes as a result of improvement works: The 08.00 Bradford Interchange to London King’s Cross will divert via Wakefield Westgate. It will not call at Halifax, Brighouse, Mirfield or Wakefield Kirkgate. A rail replacement service will operate between Halifax and Wakefield Westgate. The 12.00 London King’s Cross to Bradford Interchange and the 15.43 Bradford Interchange to London King’s Cross will not run. The 10.00 and 13.00 London King’s Cross to Sunderland and the 14.30 and 17.30 Sunderland to London King’s Cross services will not run. All other services will divert via Lincoln with increased journey times. A reduced and amended timetable will be in place, with trains diverting via Lincoln. No services will call at Beverley, Cottingham, Retford or Grantham. An hourly service will run each way between Scotland and London King’s Cross, and one service every two hours each way between Leeds and London King’s Cross. These services will use a diversionary route between Peterborough and Doncaster, extending journey times by around 60 minutes. Rail replacement services will connect customers from Retford, Newark Northgate, and Grantham with Doncaster and Peterborough. From there, customers can connect onto rail services to other destinations. There will be no services to or from Lincoln. Rail replacement coaches will operate in both directions between Peterborough, Grantham and Lincoln. There will be no LNER services to or from Bradford Forster Square, Harrogate, Hull or Skipton. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drink-driver who caused a crash that left a man paralysed and a passenger seriously injured has been jailed. Samiul Islam, 25, was driving at speed along the A1307 in Huntingdon at around 12.40am on August 2, 2024, when he collided with a stationary Mercedes. The impact forced the victim’s vehicle almost 30 meters down the road before coming to a stop, despite the handbrake being on. The driver of the Mercedes was left paralysed as a result of the collision, and one of Islam’s rear seat passengers also fractured her spine and collarbone. When officers arrived, Islam provided a roadside breath test of 42 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath. This put him over the legal limit of 35 microgrammes. At Peterborough Crown Court on October 2, Islam, of Pipe Lane, Peterborough, was jailed for two years and six months. He admitted two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving. He was also banned from driving for five years and 10 months. Sentencing, Judge Matthew Lowe, described the injuries caused by the crash as “profound, life-changing and permanent.” Describing the man who was left paralysed, he said: "The impact of the crash goes beyond the physical injuries". He added that when handing Islam his sentence, he must consider “the emotional and psychological consequences for him and those that love him.” PC Peter Smith, from the force’s Road Policing Unit, said: “Islam’s driving fell far below the standards of a careful and competent driver, and has ultimately left one man with injuries that will affect him for the rest of his life. "The impact of this collision on both victims cannot be underestimated. "It has had a lasting impact on Islam's rear-seat passenger's mental health, and the driver of the Mercedes’ life, as well as those of his loved ones, will now change significantly – both of which are a direct result of Islam’s careless and dangerous driving. "This was a completely preventable collision, and I am pleased Islam is now off the roads and will be held accountable behind bars for his actions." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire women feature in film about global pelvic mesh scandal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new documentary channel has launched with a hard-hitting film about the global pelvic mesh scandal, featuring women from Cambridgeshire. The film, The Medical Mesh Scandal Ruining Women's Lives, tells the story of March campaigner Kath Sansom and shines a light on what has been described as one of the biggest patient safety controversies in recent history. Kath, founder of the Sling The Mesh campaign group, said: "Behind every statistic is a woman whose life has been irreversibly changed by a piece of plastic mesh. "Thousands were told this was the 'gold standard' treatment, yet many were never fully informed of the risks or the devastating complications that could follow. "Women raising concerns were treated as isolated cases rather than evidence of a systemic failure. "Many were dismissed, disbelieved or told their symptoms were unrelated to their implants. "Much of this was driven by marketing that rested on limited scientific evidence. "The consequences have been devastating." The short film features Ms Sansom and fellow March resident Gail McCourt, and was produced by an all-female team. It is the first release from MAZE, a new YouTube documentary channel dedicated to telling underreported stories with depth and care. The channel plans to release new films every three weeks, up to 15 minutes long. The documentary explores the scientific evidence behind mesh implants, regulatory failures, and the human cost of ignoring warnings. It also examines industry influence, patient safety, and the importance of listening to women who report harm. A parliamentary screening of the film will take place on October 14, bringing together MPs, academics, clinicians, patient safety experts, and those affected by mesh complications. The event will examine lessons from the scandal.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire water leaks fill 86 Olympic pools every day, Lib Dems claim
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire Liberal Democrat MPs have attacked Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch after analysis claimed trillions of litres of water had been lost to leaks across the East of England since the early 1990s. The criticism comes after Kemi Badenoch reportedly described water privatisation as a “success”, a claim local Liberal Democrats have labelled “complete nonsense”. Liberal Democrat analysis of Ofwat data claims leaks from Anglian Water and Cambridge Water have wasted enough water to fill 86 Olympic-sized pools every day since records began in 1992. Ian Sollom MP says residents are being left 'high and dry' by water companies. (Image: Ian Sollom) The comments came jointly from Ian Sollom, MP for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire, Pippa Heylings, MP for South Cambridgeshire, Charlotte Cane, MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire, and Cambridge prospective parliamentary candidate Cheney Payne. The politicians said the figures exposed decades of underinvestment in water infrastructure as Cambridgeshire residents faced supply cuts, low pressure and shortages at home. The group said they had heard from elderly and vulnerable residents affected by supply problems and claimed some had been left without adequate support or access to emergency water supplies. Charlotte Cane is the MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire. (Image: Charlotte Cane) Mr Sollom said he had recently met representatives from Cambridge Water to discuss ongoing supply issues across the county. He said: “Residents have been left literally high and dry as the water supply keeps being cut off altogether or the pressure is so low, they can’t get more than a trickle out of their taps.” Mr Sollom said he urged the company to improve customer communications and register vulnerable residents for priority support during emergencies. The Liberal Democrats said water security was becoming more urgent in Cambridgeshire, one of the driest parts of the UK, as housing growth is expected to accelerate over the coming decades. The politicians said in a joint statement that the exceptionally hot, dry summer may have caused more burst pipes, but leaks had wasted water for decades. They also questioned whether existing infrastructure could cope with population growth and planned new homes. The party wants water companies turned into mutually owned public benefit corporations, with profits reinvested in infrastructure instead of paid to shareholders as dividends. The Conservatives have not responded to the Liberal Democrats’ comments. The Government has previously recognised Cambridgeshire's water supply crisis while setting out plans for regional growth. An Anglian Water spokesperson said: "Leakage remains one of our biggest priorities and we know customers expect us to keep reducing it. "Leakage levels on our network are around 40% lower than they were at privatisation, following sustained investment in finding and fixing leaks. Between 2025 and 2030, we're investing £348 million to renew more than 1,100km of water mains across our region."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Seven road repair methods trialled on Cambridgeshire's peat roads in UK first
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Seven solutions to how to repair and maintain Cambridgeshire's peat soil-affected roads are currently being trialled along a Fenland highway. The media were invited on Thursday to see how the trials aim to deliver longer-lasting repairs and better value for taxpayers’ money. Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of Cambridgeshire's highways and transport committee, Paul Bristow, the mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, joined representatives from the county council's project team and its project contractor, WinVic, to outline the work so far. Funded by the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority, the UK’s first trial of its kind is testing seven road-building techniques side by side to find the best solution for roads built on peat. Cllr Beckett highlighted the significant challenges peat soil roads, like the trial site in Upwell Road, March, cause highways authorities, pointing out that Cambridgeshire has around 1,000 miles of roads affected by peat. Fenland is home to 93 per cent of those roads, which is why the county council has selected the road in March. Seven 150-metre sections of road have been dug up, each for a different proposed solution. One section uses the current repair method as the control: plastic geogrid mesh is laid on the road surface, covered with road plainings and resurfaced with asphalt. Andy Harmon, framework manager for WinVic, the contractor working with Cambridgeshire County Council on the peat soil affected roads trial project. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The other construction methods being trialled are: This plastic mesh, known as Geogrid, is currently used in road repairs across Cambridgeshire and the country. (Image: Sarah Cliss) The trial will help identify which of the methods offers the best solution. Monitoring of Upwell Road will be carried out over three years using a variety of techniques, from gauges buried beneath the road surface to satellites taking detailed images to show any movement of the road surface, including sinking. Cllr Beckett said repairing a peat-affected road can cost up to five times more than repairing one built on other soil. Cambridgeshire Mayor Paul Bristow left on site in Upwell Road, March. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Not only that, but repairs last half as long as those carried out in other parts of the county. Cambridgeshire County Council receives no extra funding for the higher cost of repairing and maintaining its peat roads. Joshua Rutherford, the council’s head of asset management, design and delivery, said it needs £58.3m to maintain the status quo, but the Government provides £31.3m, leaving a £27m shortfall. James Chapman (left), project manager, with Joe McGilley, design engineer, holding a diagram showing the structure of one of the trials. (Image: Sarah Cliss) More money has been promised to tackle the repair backlog, but it will arrive over four years, with most coming at the end, leaving the council to find the cash upfront. It is hoped the trials will provide a better solution to the peat soil-affected roads, but which of the six options will prove the best is up for discussion, with those working on the site pinning their hopes on different methods. However, there was consensus on just how important the trials are to future maintenance of the county's roads, and satisfying residents fed up with negotiating undulating, pothole-riddled roads around Fenland. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A business leader has been appointed as a Deputy Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire in recognition of her service to the community. Faye Holland, chair of the Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce board, will now support the Lord-Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, Julie Spence, who serves as His Majesty The King’s representative in the county. Deputy Lieutenants are selected from across Cambridgeshire and may represent the Lord-Lieutenant at civic and ceremonial events, community occasions and Royal visits. Faye said: "I am deeply honoured to have been appointed as a Deputy Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire. "Cambridgeshire is an extraordinary county, defined by its people, communities, businesses and remarkable spirit of innovation. "I am incredibly proud to have the opportunity to serve the county in this new capacity and to support the Lord-Lieutenant in representing His Majesty The King across Cambridgeshire." She is also director of The Cambridge x Manchester Partnership and founder of the #21toWatch Technology Innovation Awards. Her career spans technology, communications, entrepreneurship and economic development, and she has held a range of mentoring, advisory and leadership roles supporting entrepreneurs and growing businesses. Charlotte Horobin, chief executive of Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "We are absolutely delighted for Faye. "This is a tremendous honour and a fitting recognition of the energy, commitment and leadership she has brought to Cambridgeshire over many years. "Faye has an exceptional ability to bring people together across business, academia, innovation and civic life, and she is a passionate champion for the county and its communities. "On behalf of everyone at the Chamber, our members and the Board, I would like to congratulate Faye on this very special appointment. "We are immensely proud to see our Chair take on this important role." Faye will continue as chair of the chamber board alongside her other professional commitments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'UK's Best Burger' winners to open new restaurant in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A burger chain crowned the UK’s best are set to open a new restaurant in Cambridgeshire. The Beefy Boys plan to open their eighth restaurant on Bene’t Street, Cambridge, in the former BrewDog premises. The bar was among 38 BrewDog sites announced for closure in March 2026 after the brewery was acquired by US firm Tilray Brands. Up to 50 jobs are expected to be created by the new restaurant, with recruitment under way. The joint's Old Boy burger won the UK’s Best Burger title at the 2023 National Burger Awards. Anthony "Murf" Murphy, co-founder of The Beefy Boys, said: "Cambridge has an exciting and diverse food scene, and it’s been one to watch for us for some time. "We’ve been eyeing it up and when the former BrewDog site became available, we knew the time was right. The joint has previously won the crown of UK's Best Burger "We’re incredibly proud of how far The Beefy Boys has come. "Just over ten years ago we were cooking burgers in our back gardens, and now we are opening our eighth restaurant. "We can’t wait to bring what we do to Cambridge and become a part of the local community." The Beefy Boys was founded in 2011 by four childhood friends: Mr Murphy, Daniel Mayo-Evans, Christian Williams, and Lee Symonds. Their other locations include Hereford, Shrewsbury, Cheltenham, Bath, Oxford, Nottingham and Exeter, plus two food trucks travelling across the UK. The Cambridge restaurant will serve The Beefy Boys’ signature menu, including Beefy Boy burgers, loaded fries, buffalo wings and hard shakes. The restaurant will feature The Beefy Boys' signature menu Vegetarian and vegan options will also be available. The Beefy Boys use 100 per cent grass-fed beef from their Herefordshire hometown and support local suppliers. The team plans a signature Beefy-style refit of the former BrewDog site and aims to open before Christmas. Further details and the opening date are expected to be announced soon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Navy sailor accused of plotting to leak intelligence to Russia appears in court
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Royal Navy sailor accused of plotting to leak classified information to Russia has appeared in court for the first time. Teddy Young, 24, is alleged to have abused his high-level security clearance to access secret defence and intelligence data after being deployed on a Navy vessel. It is said he had drafted a message in Russian containing classified information and had allegedly taken steps to make direct contact with the Russian authorities. Young, who lives in a semi-detached house in the village of Clapham, on the outskirts of Bedford, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday to face the charges for the first time. "The allegation is that while serving as a Royal Navy warfare intelligence rating with high-level security clearance and intelligence-system access, Teddy Stanley Greenidge Young accessed and retained sensitive UK defence and intelligence material and engaged in activity consistent with preparing to pass protected information to a foreign power," the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) told the court in a written summary of the allegations. It is said Young, who joined the Navy in April 2024, committed the offences on his first deployment, which began on November 4, 2024. He is accused of using the dark web to try to make contact with Russian authorities, drafting a message which "sought to make contact with a potential threat actor", and breaking Navy rules by copying information to a private email account. Young wore a grey sweatshirt and joggers as he appeared in the dock in front of District Judge Annabel Pilling. He was arrested by counter-terror police at his home in Bedfordshire on Tuesday, having previously been arrested in Hampshire last year. He is charged with engaging in conduct preparatory to the commission of an offence under the National Security Act 2023 and a second allegation of obtaining, accepting or retaining material benefit from a designated body. According to the charges, it is said that between November 26, 2024 and May 21, 2025 Young "disclosed protected information for a purpose which he knew, or having regard to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the UK intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power, engaged in conduct in preparation for the commission of such an act". Over the same six-month period, Young is said to have "obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power". Young was not asked to enter any pleas during the four-minute court hearing on Thursday. The judge told him: "As you know the matters that you have been charged with are too serious to be dealt with at this court and need to be dealt with at a crown court." Judge Pilling sent the case to the Old Bailey, where Young is due to appear on October 16, and remanded him in custody. When announcing the charge, police stressed there was no link between this investigation and the ongoing RAF Fairford probe. A Royal Navy spokesman said: "A member of the Royal Navy has been charged with National Security Act offences following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London. "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Counter-terror police investigating after two men arrested at Cambs RAF base
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Counter terror police have launched an investigation after two men were arrested on suspicion of trespass offences at an RAF base in Cambridgeshire. Security patrols by Ministry of Defence Police at RAF Molesworth identified an abandoned vehicle at 10pm on Wednesday (October 7). Officers from Cambridgeshire Constabulary also attended and carried out further searches of the area where a small breach in the perimeter fence was identified. At 2am the next day, two men, aged 36 and 32, were arrested inside the base perimeter. They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage and taken to a police station. The pair have since been further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023. Both men remain in police custody at this time. Officers are carrying out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation. The abandoned vehicle was recovered by police and taken to a nearby location. While undergoing further searches, concerns over the vehicle led to the deployment of specialist ‘EOD’ officers to carry out additional checks. As a precaution, a cordon was in place, which impacted on local roads in the Glatton area, including part of the A1(M). However, after assessment by specialist officers, nothing of concern was found and all cordons have since been lifted. The incident is now being investigated by officers from Counter Terrorism Policing. Commander Helen Flanagan, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: “We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week. "Our investigation into this incident is at its very early stages. A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage and enquiries are very much ongoing. "As ever, I would ask the public to remain vigilant and if you see anything of concern, then to contact police." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A prolific thief who targeted shops and businesses across Cambridge has been jailed. Jack Wilmot, of no fixed address, admitted a series of burglaries, thefts and assaults against shop workers over a two-week period. Between August 21 and September 4, he carried out repeated offences at shops where he climbed over the till area to take cigarettes and alcohol. On two occasions he assaulted members of staff. Wilmot also broke into Dorringtons Bakery and stole a charity box as well as breaking into Milton Road Pharmacy. The 29-year-old stole perfume, alcohol and meat worth almost £600 from Tesco, John Lewis, Co-op and Sainsbury’s. At Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on Friday (October 2), Wilmot was sentenced to a year in prison. He pleaded guilty to nine counts of burglary, two counts of common assault and four counts of theft. He was also handed a five-year Criminal Behaviour Order. This bans him from any Marks and Spencer, John Lewis, Co-op, Sainsbury’s or Tesco shop within the boundary of the A14, M11 and A11. Wilmot must pay a total of £2,469 in compensation to retailers Co-op, John Lewis, Sainsbury’s, Tesco as well as the victims he assaulted. Detective Constable Zoe Bramley, said: "Wilmot’s offending had a significant impact on retailers and their staff, who were repeatedly targeted over a short period of time. "His crime escalated from shop thefts to burglaries and assaults on shop workers carrying out their jobs. "This sentence, along with the Criminal Behaviour Order, demonstrates that persistent offending will not be tolerated and that we will continue to work with businesses to protect staff and bring people like Wilmot to justice" Have you got a story you want to share? Huntingdonshire District Council has rejected plans to turn an industrial unit in St Ives into a community swimming pool, despite backing from education, health and swimming groups. Spencer Smith applied to convert 1 Bramley Road from a motorcycle repair workshop into an indoor pool offering swimming lessons, water safety training, hydrotherapy, aqua fitness and rehabilitation. Council planners acknowledged the community benefits of the proposal but concluded that insufficient information had been provided to address concerns over parking, public safety, noise and site selection. Read more Footpath set to close for daytime telecoms works in Huntingdon Prolific thief targeted shops and businesses including bakery Counter-terror police investigating after two men arrested at Cambs RAF base 'Violent' arsonist chased ex with hammer before starting fire outside her home Man accused of sexually assaulting woman near primary school named In its decision notice, the council said it had not been demonstrated that the development could operate within the established employment area without causing amenity and public safety issues because of a lack of parking provision. Officers also said the application did not properly explain why other sites had been ruled out. A second reason for refusal related to a lack of information about the proposed air conditioning unit and plant equipment. Environmental Health officers said there was insufficient detail to assess whether noise could affect nearby homes. The third refusal reason was parking: the four proposed spaces, including one accessible bay, were not enough for staff and users and could cause overspill on nearby industrial-estate roads. St Ives Town Council objected over highway and pedestrian safety, parking, the site layout and public safety. But the report said Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways team raised no highway-safety objection. Four organisations submitted letters supporting the scheme. One of the strongest endorsements came from the Swimming Teachers' Association, which said there was an ongoing shortage of suitable facilities for lessons and training. It argued the pool would provide opportunities for swimming education, professional qualifications, fitness activities and accessible sessions for people with additional needs. Wyton-on-the-Hill Primary School also backed the proposal, saying similar small teaching pools were often better suited to helping children gain confidence in the water than larger leisure-centre facilities. The school said it would be likely to use a purpose-built St Ives teaching pool because it would cut travel times. A local physiotherapy practice said the pool could offer swimming lessons, water aerobics and hydrotherapy, while specialist hydrotherapy was limited locally. A Cambridgeshire Pilates instructor also backed the plan, saying demand for aqua aerobics was high and classes at One Leisure St Ives were oversubscribed. The applicant’s planning statement said the pool would tackle a waiting list of more than 100 children, create jobs and bring a potentially vacant building back into use. It also said the pool could create at least eight direct jobs, plus work for independent instructors and specialist providers. But planning officers said the benefits did not outweigh concerns about parking, public safety, noise and the lack of evidence for choosing the site. Planning officers recommended refusal, and the council rejected the application. The applicant, Spencer Smith, also runs the local swim school Splash & Learn, where he teaches children to swim.

Huntingdon Town Council has won permission to fly the Progress Pride and Pan-African flags from its historic Town Hall balcony, months after it was criticised for displaying them without consent. The issue surfaced earlier this year when it emerged that the Grade II* listed Town Hall in Market Hill had been flying flags without the planning consent required under advertising rules. Huntingdonshire District Council has now granted consent for the two flags to be flown each year from the building’s existing balcony flagpoles. Huntingdon Town Council applied to fly the Progress Pride flag throughout Pride Month in June and the Pan-African flag during Black History Month in October. The council’s new Flag Flying Policy says the Progress Pride and Pan-African flags are "subject to planning consent". In supporting documents, the council said the flags were intended to celebrate nationally recognised cultural and community events and reflect the town's diversity, inclusivity and community values. Officials stressed they would only be displayed during designated commemorative periods and would not be permanent fixtures. A planning officer’s report said the flags would not harm the historic Town Hall, the Huntingdon Conservation Area or public safety. The report said the flags would use existing poles without adding visual clutter, while Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways authority raised no objection. No public representations were received during the consultation period. The approval covers the Progress Pride and Pan-African flags on the Town Hall’s projecting balcony flagpoles from October 2026 to October 2031. The decision gives the council formal approval to fly the flags after it came under scrutiny for displaying them without consent, as previously reported by the Hunts Post. The council’s Flag Flying Policy allows other flags, including the Union Flag, St George’s Cross and Huntingdonshire flag, to fly at scheduled civic and commemorative events. But flags without automatic consent must first be approved by the local planning authority. The council has previously clarified that, unlike the traditional Gilbert Baker Pride flag, the Progress Pride flag does not benefit from deemed consent under advertising regulations and therefore needs express approval.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Awards will spotlight sustainable workplaces and energy champions
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: With innovators operating across multiple sectors, the East of England is playing a significant role in advancing sustainable business across the UK. This is what the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards are all about, and the Sustainable Workplace of the Year and East of England Energy Ambassador awards will spotlight the progressive, sustainable local organisations and people who are contributing to the region’s growing reputation. Here, the judges for these categories tell us more about what they’ll be looking for in the winners. James Groves, managing director of Indigo Swan (Image: Indigo Swan) Sponsored by Indigo Swan James Groves, managing director, Indigo Swan Why were you keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards? As a respected energy consultant in Norfolk, I felt it was important that Indigo Swan supported these awards and helped to bring attention to the amazing businesses across the region that are really making a statement when it comes to sustainability and net zero. What do you bring to the judging process? I bring more than 16 years’ experience within the energy sector, an understanding of the sustainable market and an ISO14001 accreditation. Through my experience at Indigo Swan – beginning as commercial director in 2018, becoming MD in 2019 and leading a management buyout in 2022 – I also have a clear understanding of how behavioural and cultural change in a business can impact your journey to being more sustainable and how important it will be on the journey to net zero. Have you ever been judged for an award yourself. If so, how will you use that experience when judging this award? Yes. The key for me is making sure that the award, if it’s for a company, is written by the company. We want to convey what the business does, stands for and is implementing. I want to see clear examples of where change has taken place. Statistics that can be proven and the understanding of change within an organisation are areas to focus on. I’ll also be looking for evidence of the impact on the people within the business and, of course, passion – all areas that have helped us with our success. What will you be looking for in the winner? A great combination of investment, behavioural change and a clear understanding of how being sustainable has helped to grow the business financially and improved the culture and engagement of the staff. The winner will show what best practice looks like, supported through facts, figures and accreditations. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? Do it. It will show your business as a shining light for how being more sustainable should be managed, and it will create a number of new opportunities. Ian Pease, business development manager at GENERATE (Image: Departure Lounge Media Group) Sponsored by GENERATE Ian Pease, business development manager, GENERATE Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire man pleads guilty to defrauding woman out of £126k
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire man has pleaded guilty to defrauding a woman out of a six-figure sum. Kambiz Akhondi appeared at Peterborough Crown Court on Tuesday (October 6) after being charged with fraud by abuse of position. The 60-year-old initially pleaded not guilty but changed this after the judge indicated he would not face more than three years in prison if he changed his plea. His defence had sought a Goodyear indication, which allows the judge to tell a defendant what the maximum sentence will be before they plead guilty. Akhondi, of Calfe Fen Close, Soham, was accused of transferring sums amounting to around £126k from Maud Miller’s bank account to his own. The offence happened between October 24, 2018, and March 17, 2020, while he was in a position of power over her finances. The court heard that Akhondi was expected to safeguard her estate and not act against her financial interests, but transferred the sums for his own gain. Akhondi was released on unconditional bail and is due to reappear in court to be sentenced on November 18.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Serving Royal Navy member charged with spying after Bedfordshire arrest
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A serving member of the Royal Navy has been charged with spying following his arrest in Bedfordshire. Teddy Young, 24, will appear in court on today (October 8) accused of obtaining protected information which could benefit a unnamed foreign power, the Metropolitan Police said. Young was arrested by counter-terror police at his home in Bedfordshire on Tuesday, having previously been arrested in Hampshire last year. He will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court facing charges that between November 2024 and May 2025 he "engaged in conduct in preparation for committing an offence of disclosing protected information, contrary to section 18 of the National Security Act 2023". Between the same dates it is also alleged he "obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power, knowing or having regard to other matters known to him ought reasonably to know was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom, contrary to section 1 of the National Security Act 2023". Police stressed there was no link between this investigation and the ongoing RAF Fairford probe. Commander Helen Flanagan, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter." A Royal Navy spokesman said: "A member of the Royal Navy has been charged with National Security Act (NSA) offences following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London. As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage."
