summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Awesome' Roman cremation urn and ploughshare found at Cambridgeshire dig
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An 'awesome' cremation urn was the big find at an archaeological dig in Cambridgeshire, which was a new attempt to locate a Roman villa. Run by DigVentures, the two-week excavation was crowdfunded, with some of those donating working alongside professional archaeologists to find out more about the site, located in the countryside close to Sacrewell, on the outskirts of Peterborough. In the 1970s, archaeologists found remains of a winged Roman villa, including furnaces, painted plaster and tiled floors, but never uncovered the villa itself. The ploughshare was found alongside the glass cremation urn.. (Image: Jacob Reader) Fifty years on Nat Jackson, site director, and his team from DigVentures set about unearthing more of the villa's story, and that of the people who lived there, and also to make a fresh attempt to locate it. In two weeks, they excavated three trenches and found pottery, coins, roof tiles, underfloor-heating tiles, snail and oyster shells and, most excitingly, the cremation burial. The excavators found a blue glass urn in the remains of a wooden box, alongside an iron ploughshare - the cutting or leading edge of a plough. Reporter Sarah Cliss joined the DigVentures team for the last day of the dig. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Nat believes it could have belonged to someone who lived in the villa and perhaps farmed the land. "It is possible the person thought, 'I am a farmer; I want to be buried with farming tools', that's so cool, and it's a really awesome thing to find. I have never found anything like it before," he said. It was Nat's job to draw up the specifics for the dig, researching as much as he could about the site and determining where the exploration trenches should go. Geophysical surveys have been carried out of the site to help locate the site of the Roman villa and the best place to dig exploration trenches. (Image: Jacob Reader) Geophysical surveys of the site also helped with that, and there were high hopes of finding a furnace in one of the trenches, which had shown a large iron deposit, but digging showed it was a false alarm when a large iron horseshoe was discovered. “It was massive, probably from a shire horse or something like that dating to the 18th century or 19th century, but it was not what we were hoping to find,” said Nat. Harriet Tatton, senior project officer for project development at DigVentures, was equally excited by the burial find. Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) She said the urn's hexagonal shape had helped to date it to around the 2nd century AD - so 1,800 years ago, give or take 100 years - so around the Antonine period or possibly to the time of the Emperor Flavian. The urn’s contents will be excavated carefully off-site in the hope of revealing more about the person buried inside. It is easy to make assumptions that it was a man because the person was buried with a ploughshare, but it could be a female and if we are lucky, we might be able to discover which. Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Harriet said it was common for people to be buried with objects that meant something to the people in life, but it should be remembered that the choices would most likely have been made by their family, not by the person themselves. Some of the volunteers were sponsored to join the dig through the online adult learning App Nibble, which also allowed me to join the fun for the day. Like the many other volunteers working alongside the professionals, I was given a trowel, a brush and bucket and set to work cleaning the stones of earth in one of the excavation ditches. Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Read more Investigation launched after boy found on railway tracks closed Reform councillor arrested over alleged false statements in election papers Cambridgeshire roadwork overruns fall 42% after £424,000 fines and charges The best places in Cambridgeshire for pizza, according to local diners Five new family hubs open across Cambridgeshire to support parents and children The aim was to reveal the natural geology of the area and to show the ditches that had been dug by the Roman occupiers of the site, ready for detailed work off-site. The other volunteers came from across the country; some had donated to the crowdfunding appeal, while others had received the dig as a gift. One man, who was a huge fan of Channel 4's Time Team hosted by Tony Robinson, had always dreamed of joining a dig and had been given the chance as a 60th birthday present from his wife. Volunteers and professionals worked side by side to unearth the secrets buried at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Another had received it as a retirement gift. Both thoroughly enjoyed getting stuck in and were excited when they unearthed a piece of roof tile. One woman from Leicestershire was delighted that she had been given a chance to help unearth the urn. “I can't believe I got to work on something so precious. I told my family not to tell the team just how clumsy I can be, as I didn't want to miss out; it was so special,” she said. Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Another man from Kent said it had reawakened an old passion, and that it was wonderful to pull a piece of history out of the ground and hold it in his hand. Harriet said all the finds would be cleaned, examined and catalogued. The urn, ploughshare and coins could go to a museum, while less significant items may be reburied. Nat and his team are planning to return next September when they hope to excavate in an adjoining field, where they hope to finally discover the location of the villa. "We can't wait to come back, and hopefully find ourselves a Roman villa," he said, "that would be the dream."on site, Site director Nat Jackson carefully handles the iron ploughshare unearthed at the site. (Image: Jacob Reader) Site director Nat Jackson talks to the volunteers about the one of the trenches. (Image: Jacob Reader) Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Site director Nat Jackson leads a tour of the site. (Image: Jacob Reader) Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) The finds will be carefully cleaned, examined and catalogued. (Image: Jacob Reader) Volunteers worked alongside professional archaeologists at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) Volunteers and professionals worked side by side to unearth the secrets buried at the site near Sacrewell. (Image: Jacob Reader) A team from the adult online learning App Nibble were also on site having sponsored some people to join the dig. They had travelled from Ukraine to join the excavation. (Image: Jacob Reader) The site forms part of the Nene Valley, a major Roman centre of production, transport and trade that included villa estates, pottery kilns and ironworking facilities.

Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service visited Longsands Academy, in St Neots, at the end of September, it has been revealed. In a letter seen by The Hunts Post, the inspection was organised to assess concerns raised about the safety of the premises. Fire safety officers unearthed several deficiencies under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005. It comes after two sources approached this newspaper to raise concerns about fire safety at Longsands, which is run by the Astrea Academy Trust. The school has since confirmed it is working to resolve the issues, which include a defective fire alarm sounder and a damaged set of fire doors. Inspectors raised concerns about a set of fire safety doors in N Block (Image: Supplied) In a letter to parents, the school said the site is "considered to be safe and complies overwhelmingly" with required fire safety standards. It added: "The inspection highlighted one or two minor deficiencies which our site team is now working on to resolve. "The fire safety inspectors found that the fire alarm sounder in H Block is faulty, due to a defect on the fire panel, and that some emergency lighting is not working properly. "They also said that two fire-resisting doors in N Block needed to be repaired, after some damage was caused. "However, the inspectors are satisfied that we are working to put these issues right and do not feel the need to re-inspect the school." Longsands Academy revealed the fire doors had been damaged (Image: Supplied) It continues: "I would like to take this opportunity to remind parents and carers of the important role families play in supporting Longsands’ approach to appropriate student behaviour. "In recent weeks, some damage has been caused to school property by students and we would ask you to reinforce at home the expectations we have around respect and responsibility." A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service confirmed officers "arranged for a further visit at the end of September." They added: "A minor deficiencies notice was issued to the Responsible Person, which was focussed on routine maintenance issues. "The Responsible Person has been fully engaged in the process and proactive in addressing the highlighted deficiencies." Have you got a story you want to share? Additional charges included four counts of causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, three counts of making an indecent image of children, and one count of possessing prohibited images of children. He was also accused of possessing extreme pornographic images. Ray is no longer a serving councillor following elections at Peterborough City Council in May 2026.

Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones visited the PCC’s Victim and Witness Hub and Peterborough Women’s Aid services on September 30, to meet survivors and see the impact of the specialist support services. Ms Davies-Jones said: "Meeting victim-survivors today and hearing first-hand about their experiences has been incredibly powerful. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire residents asked to shape council spending priorities through survey

The survey asks residents to share their views on where the council should prioritise spending and savings in the years ahead. Lucy Nethsingha, leader of Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "Every year, the council has to set our business plan and a balanced budget, which is increasingly challenging as demand for services grows and costs continue to rise. "Despite these challenges, over recent years the council has provided much-needed stability in an increasingly uncertain world, and we remain in a stronger financial position than many councils across the country. "We are not immune to the significant cost and demand pressures faced by local government and must make careful decisions about how we use the finite resources available to us. "It is so important that residents have their say so that we can better understand what matters most to people and the priorities they believe are important for the Council. "Your feedback will help inform our business planning and budget-setting process, as councillors consider how best to plan and fund our services for the years ahead. "We hope as many residents as possible will take part in the survey, making their voices heard and informing future decisions about the council’s services across Cambridgeshire." The majority of day-to-day spending is required to support children's and adult social care, education and SEND, with the remainder used to maintain the highways network and deliver community-based services, including libraries and registration services. The engagement survey will be in two phases, with Phase 1 closing on 15 November 2026. To take part, visit Your Voice on the Cambridgeshire County Council website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Mayor warns devolved power over water services ‘a bit bonkers’
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Andy Burnham’s plan to give regional leaders more power over water utilities “frankly, is a bit bonkers”, a mayor has warned. Paul Bristow claimed mayoral devolution in England was a “success story” for his party, the Conservatives, but warned it was “not going to solve all our problems”. Devolution has been a central plank of Mr Burnham’s governing agenda since he became Labour leader and Prime Minister earlier this year. During his first week in Downing Street, the former Greater Manchester mayor hosted regional leaders – including mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Mr Bristow – at his new No 10 North in Manchester. Asked whether cross-party efforts to work on mayoral devolution could continue, Mr Bristow told the Press Association that the Government’s “message is good”. He said: “We want that responsibility, that accountability, but we need the resources that come with it.” The Prime Minister last week promised mayors “will have new powers to hold water companies to account, with tougher consequences for those which repeatedly fail”, as part of a bid to “strengthen public control” over the sector. Mr Burnham more widely pledged “more power and control over the basics”, which he said would be “in the hands of people and places to set their own ambitions”. Attending the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham, Mr Bristow said: “The idea that I’m going to become responsible for a water company or Anglian Water, I think, frankly, is a bit bonkers.” He added devolution was “about the market, and it’s about Government, and it’s about institutions like the universities working together” on regional priorities. He also said: “I think the water companies want to be responsible to their shareholders, don’t they? They’re a private organisation. “So, it’s about having the right devolution in the right places.” Mr Bristow said: “Devolution is just not a means for growth itself. “You can’t just say devolution is going to solve all our problems. “It’s not going to solve the problems associated with defence, it’s not going to solve the problems associated with welfare – the fact we’re paying more on welfare than we raise in income tax. “It’s not going to solve some of these big fundamental state-led issues, but what it can do is deliver growth in targeted areas.” Asked about the Conservatives’ approach towards devolution, Mr Bristow said he wanted to see his party “back what works”. He added: “Kemi Badenoch, I’m sure, will understand that English devolution is a Conservative success story.” Several regional mayoralties were set up under the Conservative government, including Cambridgeshire and Peterborough in 2017. In the same year, Mr Burnham became the first mayor of Greater Manchester, a role he held for just over nine years. In the English Devolution White Paper, published during former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership, the Government set out its ambition for everywhere in the country to have a strategic authority, such as a mayor-led body.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: More than 60 babies remembered in St Ives memorial ribbon display
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A town councillor has organised St Ives’ first baby loss memorial ribbon display. The event is being held to support families and break the silence around pregnancy and baby loss. Laura Thompson, who has experienced miscarriage herself, launched the memorial in St Ives after hearing from local mothers who wanted a way to remember their babies closer to home. St Ives Town Bridge will be illuminated pink and blue (Image: St Ives Town Council) She said: "Until 2024, our town had nothing to commemorate Baby Loss Awareness Week, and as a mother who has miscarried a child myself, and having surveyed local mums who said they can't drive miles to another town for baby loss week, I felt I just had to do something to remember our beautiful babies." "This will be the third year running, and like the last two years, local businesses all come together and do a lovely pink and blue display in their shop windows in support too, so the whole high street has scattered pink and blue, with some shops and pubs lighting up their own buildings pink and blue too." The memorial aims to support families affected by baby loss. (Image: St Ives Town Council) A ribbon memorial will be displayed outside St Ives Methodist Church from October 9 to 15, with more than 60 babies already named in previous years, some dating as far back as 1975. Ribbons and markers will be available for visitors to write messages in memory of their babies. Donations are welcome for Sands Baby Loss Charity, though not required. Laura Thompson (Image: St Ives Town Council) Laura said: "Having lost a baby myself, its the recognition that really counts, it says that you are seen, that it is a real loss, not 'just one of those things,' and officiates it." The St Ives Town Bridge will also be illuminated in pink and blue throughout the week, a gesture that last year sparked conversations and raised awareness across the community. All are welcome to visit the display, regardless of age, gender, religion, or the length of time since their loss.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Teens who left man with fractured skull in unprovoked attack avoid jail
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two teenagers who left a man with a fractured skull in an unprovoked attack in Cambridgeshire have been sentenced. The 20-year-old victim was approached by two teenage girls in Market Square, in Cambridge, on August 12, 2024, and asked to buy them alcohol. When he refused, the girls became aggressive, with one repeatedly hitting him with her slipper. As the situation escalated, more teenagers gathered around the victim, leaving him cornered against a spiked metal fence near St Mary’s Church. During the attack, Xavier Matelot launched a flying kick to the side of the victim’s head, causing it to strike the metal fence. Zein Gibril then repeatedly punched him before the group dispersed. The victim was taken to Addenbrooke’s Hospital, where he was treated for a skull fracture and a bleed on the brain. Sentencing the pair at Cambridge Crown Court on September 25, the Judge described the group that surrounded and attacked the victim as behaving like ‘a pack of wolves’. Gibril, 18, of Cavendish Avenue, Cambridge, was handed an 18 month Youth Rehabilitation Order after admitting causing grievous bodily harm without intent and possession of cannabis. He must also complete 100 hours of unpaid work. Matelot, 19, of Briar Way, Peterborough, was sentenced to 21 months imprisonment, suspended for two years, after admitting inflicting grievous bodily harm without intent. He must complete 120 hours of unpaid work. Detective Constable Luca Bellomo, who investigated, said: “This was a shocking and entirely unprovoked attack on a young man in broad daylight. "The victim suffered serious injuries and as a result has been left with potentially life changing injuries. "Violence of this nature has no place in our communities." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire farmer warns environmental progress at risk after £150k funding loss
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire farmer has warned that environmental progress could be lost after missing out on vital funding. Peter Hatley, NFU Cambridge branch chair and a third-generation farmer from Landbeach, was unable to secure support through the Government’s Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI) scheme. The scheme, which encourages environmentally friendly farming practices, closed just six hours after opening on September 22, leaving many farmers without access to funding. Mr Hatley said: "All the work that has been done to support wildlife and the environment here will need to be ripped up. "We are left with no choice but to farm intensively as a business so I can look after my family and look after my business." He and his adviser encountered technical problems with the application portal and by the time they reached the Rural Payments Agency for support, the funds had already been exhausted. Mr Hatley said: "We were hoping for £150,000 over three years, which is a monumental amount of money for us to lose. "I don’t know what we’re going to do now. "I don’t want to have to rip everything up, and if we had any clarity about when SFI 27 is going to open it would make decision making much easier." His family has farmed the land for nearly 100 years, and they have taken part in environmental schemes for two decades. He said: "Without this funding, nature won’t pay the bills and we will be left with no choice but to undo much of what we’ve spent so long working to achieve." The NFU has repeatedly called on the government to expand the SFI budget. By 4pm the government confirmed that the 2026 SFI scheme was closed for applications, with the entire budget allocated.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Five new family hubs open across Cambridgeshire to support parents and children
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new network of family hubs has opened to support parents and children in Cambridgeshire. Cambridgeshire County Council launched the five Best Start Family Hubs on September 28 in Cambourne, Cambridge, Ely, Huntingdon and Wisbech. The hubs aim to offer joined-up support in one place, covering health, childcare, housing and financial wellbeing. Edna Murphy, chairwoman of Cambridgeshire County Council’s Children and Young People’s Committee, said: "Our new Best Start Family Hubs will make it easier for families to access the support they need. "It shows our commitment to giving children and young people the best support possible. "While parenting can be incredibly rewarding, it can also be challenging at times. "Family Hubs offer free, friendly and accessible support, helping families feel connected, informed and confident." The new hubs replace existing Child and Family Centres in each location, but will continue to provide support for families from pregnancy through to age five. This includes stay and play sessions, health advice, infant feeding support, early learning opportunities and parenting guidance. Over time, the service will expand to support families with children up to age 19, or 25 for those with special educational needs or disabilities (SEND). The scheme is part of a national programme. Existing Child and Family Centres across Cambridgeshire will become Best Start network sites, helping to strengthen the family hub offer while continuing to serve their communities. The hubs are free to use and open to all families. They are designed to reduce inequalities and help every child reach their potential. Edna encouraged families to explore the support available. She said: "Whether you’re looking for advice, activities for your child, or support with everyday family life, our Family Hubs, network sites and online resources are here to help. "I’d encourage families to visit their local hub, where they can expect a warm welcome and a wide range of support."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs women urged to attend breast screenings as 141 cancers detected last year
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A breast care team is urging women in Cambridgeshire to attend their screening appointments during Breast Cancer Awareness Month. North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust is taking the opportunity to remind women aged 50 to 70 to prioritise their breast screening appointments. The NHS offers free screenings every three years to help detect cancers early and improve survival rates. Kaylie Harvey, breast service manager at the trust, said: "Raising awareness of breast cancer – in women and men – is important, particularly during Breast Cancer Awareness Month. Women are being urged to attend their breast screening appointments (Image: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust) "We would urge anyone who has been invited to attend breast screening to keep their appointment. "As part of their regular breast care routine, we would like to remind women about the importance of checking their breasts on a monthly basis. "Women with any concerns or changes should contact their GP in the first instance and they will refer to your local breast unit if required." Breast cancer is the most common cancer in the UK, with one in seven women affected in their lifetime. Around 55,000 women and 400 men are diagnosed with the disease each year. Last year, the trust invited more than 19,000 women for screening, with 14,100 attending. A total of 141 cancers were detected through the programme. Screening can save approximately one life for every 200 women screened – an estimated 1,300 lives each year across the UK. Breast Cancer Awareness Month takes place throughout October (Image: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust) The trust is also raising awareness through information stands at Peterborough City Hospital from October 1 to 29, and at Hinchingbrooke Hospital in Huntingdon from October 5 to 9 and October 26 to 29. Breast screening services are available at hospital sites as well as through mobile units, which regularly visit Stamford and Rutland Hospital and other community locations. Further information about appointments is available at nwangliaft.nhs.uk.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire roadwork overruns fall 42% after £424,000 fines and charges
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Tougher enforcement has helped slash roadwork overruns by nearly half in Cambridgeshire. Cambridgeshire County Council recorded a 42 per cent drop in overrun days during 2025/26, following a clampdown that included issuing more than £424,000 in fines and charges to utility companies and other organisations. Councillor Alex Beckett, chair of the highways and transport committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "We know how frustrating roadworks can be for all of us travelling around Cambridgeshire. "Utility companies have a legal right to work on our roads. "Our role is to make sure works on the highway are properly managed and that unnecessary disruption is kept to a minimum." The total number of days works overran fell from 1,191 in 2024/25 to 692 in 2025/26. This reduction indicates that stricter enforcement and financial penalties are encouraging organisations to complete roadworks on time. The council issued 1,443 fixed penalty notices, totalling £196,286, for offences such as working without a permit or failing to comply with permit conditions. An additional £228,350 was recovered through overrun charges. Cllr Beckett said: "It is particularly encouraging to see the number of days that roadworks overran falling by almost 42% in a single year. "This suggests that our approach to enforcement is helping to improve compliance and reduce disruption." He added that higher penalties introduced in January have created a stronger financial incentive for companies to follow the rules and complete works on schedule. The county council issued 36,685 permits in 2025/26, regulating the timing and management of works across the road network. In Cambridgeshire, 51 utility companies are authorised to carry out work on public roads. The council said it will continue to use its enforcement powers to hold organisations accountable and minimise disruption for residents.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire firefighter retires after 30 years of service
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A long-serving firefighter has retired after 30 years of service in Cambridgeshire. Tony said: "I have been fortunate to serve in the fire service for 30 years and I have enjoyed my last day as much as my first. "I would wholeheartedly recommend it as a career. "I don’t have a specific favourite memory but collectively I have 30 years of happy memories and being surrounded by people that have been a part of that. "I have had the privilege of working with some wonderful, incredibly talented people. "The fire service is all about the team, and we are only ever as good as those around us. "I have often needed support and guidance, and people have always been willing to give it." Tony began his career at Cambridge Fire Station and later served at Dogsthorpe in Peterborough before rising through the ranks. He eventually managed Ely and Soham stations before taking charge of the service’s training centre in Huntingdon. Matthew Warren, chief fire officer, said: "Tony will be greatly missed by everyone at Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. "He is highly regarded by colleagues across the Service and has never had a negative word to say about anyone. "As his career progressed over the years, Tony showed a genuine desire to learn and develop, which he was keen to pass onto colleagues, whether they were in the operational world or in a support role. "Everyone wishes Tony all the best for in his well-earned retirement" Tony also thanked his family for their support. He said: "I want to thank my wife, Hannah, and my children, Billy, Florence and Albert. "The fire service is not always a job you can switch off from, and there were times when, although I was at home, my mind was elsewhere."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Former Cambridgeshire County Council Green Group leader resigns from party
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The former leader of the Green Group on Cambridgeshire County Council has resigned from the Green Party. Cllr Elliot Tong, who is also a Cambridge City councillor, said he no longer feels the party will allow him to stand up for what’s right. He led the group on the county council until May of this year, after first being elected to represent Abbey Ward in 2025. He has also represented Abbey on the city council since 2023 and was previously the Green Group’s deputy leader on the city council. Cllr Tong confirmed he will continue to sit as an independent councillor on both councils. He said he had become increasingly disillusioned with the party, who he said had pushed back against building council housing and his support for Palestine. In a statement released on Friday (October 2), he said: “Today, I’ve resigned from The Green Party, as well as the Green Group on both the city and county council. “I entered politics because I wanted to stand up for what’s right. I no longer feel that the Cambridge and South Cambridgeshire Green Party will allow me to do this. “Locally, my Green colleagues have pushed back against council housing in their own wards. “I have been threatened for standing up for Palestinians and told that doing so is unimportant. “Behind the scenes, I have been mocked for my neurodivergence. My loyalty will always be towards doing what’s right, not what’s convenient. “I am excited to continue standing up for regular people across Cambridge.” The two Green Group leaders on the city council, Cllr Sefira Davison and county council, Cllr Darren Green, issued a joint statement in response to the resignation which they said came as a “disappointment and a shock”. They said: “As we’re currently away at party conference at present, we don’t have all the facts on the ground. “Our feeling at present is that in our time in politics, we have come to know Elliot as a campaigner, a colleague, and a friend. “To hear from Elliot that he no longer felt able to stand as a Green was a disappointment and a shock. “We want to go on record first as saying that any form of harassment or discrimination is not acceptable to us, nor compatible with Green values. It should not be acceptable to anyone. “Elliot has been a steadfast colleague and a tireless councillor. His energy, enthusiasm, and support will be missed, and we hope to continue working together for the good of residents on both councils.

Coogan told The Hunts Post he has "worked and will continue to work with the police as part of the investigation". It comes after the force revealed it had launched an investigation into the alleged false statements shortly after the May election. A spokesperson said the inquiry relates to Coogan and the most recent election, though it has not disclosed the nature of the alleged statements. At the time, a spokesperson for Huntingdonshire District Council said: "We are aware of a police referral in relation to the recent district council elections. "As this matter is a live investigation, it would not be appropriate for the council or the returning officer to comment further at this stage." Coogan previously ran as Reform UK's candidate in the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough mayoral election, coming second last year. He was among the party's first representatives on the district council, winning his seat along with two other Reform candidates to represent the Ramsey ward. According to the Electoral Commission the penalties for a false statement on a nomination paper in England and Wales include an unlimited fine or up to one year in prison. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts families urged to check benefits and bills as living costs rise
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: As we head into autumn, many households are once again feeling the pressure from rising living costs, higher energy bills and stretched budgets. For some, it can feel like no matter how carefully they manage their money, it simply doesn't go as far as it used to. While we can't always increase our income overnight, there are often steps people can take to make their money stretch further. We regularly see clients who are missing out on financial support, paying more than they need to for essential services, or simply aren't aware of the help available. Even a small increase in income or reduction in household bills can make a real difference over the course of a year. Could you be missing out on benefits? One of the most effective ways to improve your financial situation is to check whether you're receiving all the benefits and support you're entitled to. Many people assume they won't qualify because they work, own their home or have some savings. In reality, entitlement isn't always straightforward and it's often worth checking, especially if your circumstances have changed. A benefits check could identify support such as: • Universal Credit • Pension Credit • Personal Independence Payment (PIP) • Attendance Allowance • Carer's Allowance • Council Tax Reduction We regularly speak to people who are surprised to discover they qualify for support they never thought they could claim. It's also worth remembering that some benefits can act as a gateway to additional help, including Free School Meals, Healthy Start Vouchers, help with NHS prescriptions and hospital travel costs. Free School Meals Since September 2026, all children in England living in households that receive Universal Credit can qualify for Free School Meals, regardless of household income. The support isn't yet applied automatically, so families should check with their local authority and make sure they've submitted an application. Look at ways to reduce essential costs Making your money go further isn't just about increasing income. Reducing regular household costs can be just as effective. It's worth checking: • Whether you're eligible for social tariffs on broadband, phone or water bills. • If you're on the most suitable energy tariff. • Whether you're eligible for any council tax discounts or reductions. • Insurance policies that may automatically renew at higher prices. • Local discount schemes and community support available in your area. Many households can save money simply by reviewing bills they haven't looked at for some time. Keep track of where your money goes It's often the smaller, everyday expenses that add up without us noticing. Taking some time to review bank statements, use a budgeting app or keep a spending diary can help build a clearer picture of where your money is going. Once you know where you're spending, it's easier to identify opportunities to cut back without affecting the things that matter most. Don't wait until a crisis Financial difficulties can affect anyone. Ill-health, redundancy, reduced working hours, relationship breakdown or rising household costs can quickly put pressure on a budget. The earlier people seek advice, the more options are usually available. Too often we see people struggling on alone for months before reaching out for support. There is absolutely no shame in asking for help. Many people are facing similar challenges, and advice services are there to help find practical solutions and make sure people receive the support they're entitled to. Help is available If you're worried about your finances, now is a good time to take stock. A benefits check, a review of household bills or some simple budgeting changes could leave you better off. And for those facing severe financial hardship, additional support may be available through food banks, local welfare schemes, crisis grants and other community organisations. Sometimes a conversation and a quick check can put hundreds, or even thousands, of pounds back into a household budget. That's why it's always worth asking. You can contact Citizens Advice on Freephone 0808 278 7807: 9.30am-3.30pm Monday, Thursday, and Friday, and from 9.30am-7pm Tuesday and Wednesday, or head to our website https://www.citizensadviceruralcambs.org.uk/ for more information.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Steam train with 'remarkable history' coming to Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A legendary steam locomotive with a "remarkable history" is coming to Cambridgeshire this winter. The Nene Valley Railway in Peterborough will welcome No. 4079 Pendennis Castle—a celebrated Castle Class engine built in 1924—as part of its 2026 Christmas programme. The historic steam train, visiting with the cooperation of Didcot Railway Centre, will remain at the railway into early 2027 for a series of special events. A spokesperson for the Nene Valley Railway said: "We're incredibly excited to welcome Pendennis Castle to the Nene Valley Railway. The famous steam train will remain at the Nene Valley Railway for December and January (Image: Didcot Railway Centre) "This is a locomotive with a remarkable history, from the famous trials against Flying Scotsman to more than two decades spent in Australia, and it will be a privilege to see it operating here. "Christmas is already one of the most special times of the year at the Nene Valley Railway, and having Pendennis Castle hauling selected Santa Specials will make some of those journeys even more memorable. "We're also delighted that visitors now have several opportunities to experience Pendennis Castle after Christmas. "Whether that's getting behind the controls on one of our Driving Experiences, enjoying an evening Fish and Chip train or simply travelling behind this magnificent locomotive on our Winter Warmer service, we're looking forward to starting 2027 in style." In December, Pendennis Castle will haul selected Santa Specials, giving families festive journeys behind one of Britain’s best-known steam locomotives. The historic locomotive was famously trialled against the Flying Scotsman (Image: Didcot Railway Centre) Built at Swindon Works and completed in February 1924, No. 4079 Pendennis Castle was the seventh of 171 Castle Class locomotives made by the Great Western Railway. It shot to national fame in 1925 after trials against the LNER’s new Pacific engines, including Flying Scotsman, on the East Coast Main Line. The locomotive left Britain for Australia in May 1977, where it hauled excursion trains through the Chichester Ranges. After more than 23 years away, Pendennis Castle returned to Britain in July 2000 and is now part of Didcot Railway Centre’s collection.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Live facial recognition to identify wanted people rolled out in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Live facial recognition technology is being rolled out for use in another area of Cambridgeshire. Following a series of successful deployments in Peterborough, the equipment, which allows officers to identify wanted people, was rolled out in Cambridge city centre on Friday (October 2). LFR works by comparing faces captured by a live camera feed against a police-generated watchlist. It converts key facial features into a mathematical template to identify potential matches in real time. The watchlist includes people wanted for offences, those with outstanding warrants and high-risk offenders subject to court notification requirements. An officer checks every potential match before deciding whether to act. The technology analyses key facial features ad converts them into mathematical representation Images triggering an alert are deleted immediately or within 24 hours, while the images and biometric data of people who do not trigger one are deleted automatically. Deleted images and data cannot be retrieved. Sergeant Luke Charlton from the Cambridge neighbourhood team said: "Live facial recognition is another valuable tool that helps us protect the public by identifying wanted offenders and those who may pose a risk to our communities. "Following successful deployments in Peterborough, we’re now bringing this technology to Cambridge. "It allows us to locate people who are sought by the courts or wanted in connection with offences, helping us bring them to justice more quickly. "We understand people may have questions about how the technology works, which is why officers will be on hand throughout the deployment to speak with members of the public and provide information. "Transparency is really important to us, and we want people to understand the safeguards that are in place." For more information about live facial recognition in Cambridgeshire, visit the force website.

The consultation will help decide the scope and detail of the Environmental Statement submitted with any application. After the consultation, the Planning Inspectorate will issue a scoping opinion listing the environmental issues the application must address. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hundreds march in protest against Cambridgeshire puppy breeding facility
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 200 people have marched in protest against the breeding of dogs for laboratory testing at a Cambridgeshire facility. Organised by Save The Dogs UK, the five-mile march began at Huntingdon railway station at 1pm on September 26 and attracted supporters from Cambridgeshire, across the UK and Europe. Event organiser Sarah Gard welcomed the crowd before organisers read out a code of conduct urging a peaceful, lawful demonstration. The march passed through Huntingdon town centre, where Save The Dogs UK media lead Hazel Williams addressed protesters outside the town hall. The five-mile march began at Huntingdon railway station and continued to MBR Acres (Image: Vegan Photographs) Ms Williams said: "We have been completely blown away by the support and engagement from the local people of Huntingdon. "This isn’t just a national issue; it’s a local one." She raised concerns about using beagles in research and said many residents did not know dogs were being bred nearby for it. Ms Williams called for non-animal research and pointed to Cambridgeshire’s scientific expertise. Ms Williams claimed many residents did not know dogs were being bred nearby for that purpose (Image: Vegan Photographs) The march continued along the B1090 towards the MBR Acres facility, with demonstrators carrying placards and chanting in support of the beagles. Organisers said passing motorists sounded their horns as the group approached the site. The protest was organised by Save the Dogs UK (Image: Vegan Photographs) At the march’s end, protesters left dog collars and messages of kindness outside MBR Acres for the animals inside. Hundreds of protesters turned out for the event (Image: Vegan Photographs) The protest was livestreamed on social media (Image: Vegan Photographs) Ms Gard said she was "super proud of the peaceful and lawful event" and thanked the marshals, first aider, safety-vehicle driver and photographers who helped organise it. The event was livestreamed on TikTok and Instagram and reached supporters in Australia and Malaysia, according to Save The Dogs UK social lead Natalie Beach. Ms Beach called the atmosphere "incredible" and said the march united familiar faces with new supporters. Marshals, first aiders, photographers and a safety-vehicle driver took part (Image: Vegan Photographs) A spokesperson for MBR Acres said: "While animal research is a sensitive topic, the development of new human and veterinary medicines is strictly governed by UK and international regulatory frameworks, which legally require animal safety testing. "Our lawful role is to breed and supply healthy dogs for regulated scientific research—a lawful critical component of the UK medical development process. "Disrupting this vital work only risks delaying essential research and, ultimately, the treatments that patients and families are waiting for. "Every medicine used by families and their pets today relies on this critical work. "Under UK and international regulatory frameworks, safety testing remains a strict requirement to prove that new treatments are safe before they can ever progress to human clinical trials or veterinary use. The protest took place on September 26 (Image: Vegan Photographs) "We are fully committed to the development of non-animal alternatives and strongly support the advancement of New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). "However, while these technologies are maturing, they cannot yet fully replicate the complex biological systems of a living human or animal. "Until new alternatives are fully capable of ensuring absolute safety, these studies remain an irreplaceable step in protecting loved ones. The demonstration was intended to be peaceful and lawful (Image: Vegan Photographs) "Those calling for the closure of our facilities are not considering the severe consequences that this would have on research and development in the UK. "We will not tolerate unlawful behaviour, or the intimidation of our dedicated team, our absolute priority remains the compliance, safety and security of the animals in our care."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts Philharmonic marks 50 years with six-concert season across Huntingdonshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A music society is marking 50 years of music-making with a season of concerts across Huntingdonshire. Huntingdonshire Philharmonic, known locally as Hunts Phil, will perform six concerts in Huntingdon, Godmanchester, and St Ives between October and June 2027. The group was formed in 1977 through the merger of Huntingdon Choral Society and Huntingdon Orchestral Society. Bronwen Rayner, chair of Hunts Phil, said: "Fifty years is a long time for any organisation, but the reason people come hasn't changed at all. "They want to make music with other people on a Tuesday or a Thursday evening. "That was true in 1939 and it's true now." The society now includes around 100 players and singers. Peter Downes, aged 88, joined in 1986 and still rehearses twice a week in the viola section. Mr Downes said: "I have no illusions about being a talented musician, but for two hours on a Tuesday and a Thursday I forget everything else. "I watch the Proms now and think, oh yes, I played that once." Kay Coope, a choir member since the first season in 1977, said: "It doesn't feel like fifty years, but I've definitely become one of the 'nodding grey heads' I used to joke about as a young choir member. "Belonging to a choir gives you a good sing. "It's uplifting, it blows the cobwebs away, and you make new friends." The 50th-anniversary season opens on Saturday, October 17, at St Ives Free Church with a programme of Berlioz, Tchaikovsky, and Dvorak, featuring cellist Joely Koos. Anniversary concerts will also be held on Friday, March 12, and Saturday, June 26, at Hinchingbrooke Performing Arts Centre. Hunts Phil rehearses on Tuesdays and Thursdays in Godmanchester and welcomes new members without audition. Tickets are available at huntsphil.org.uk.

Plans have been submitted for five new homes on land near a Grade II listed farm in a Huntingdonshire village. Sue and Dominic Rice have lodged an application with Huntingdonshire District Council for five dwellings to be built on land at Christs College Farm, Green Lane, Upton, near Huntingdon. The plans would demolish a barn and stables and add three detached homes, two semi-detached homes, gardens, an adapted drive and biodiversity areas. The site is located roughly in the centre of Upton, which has a population of around 200, with Green Lane to the north and Upton Hill to the east. The dwellings would be built on grassy land on the farm and would be two storey, with a small area at one and a half storey on one house. The plans seek to provide mixed accommodation of two to four bedroom houses and would be "respectful of the listed dwellings in their vicinity". According to the heritage statement, the existing barn and stables are not historic structures associated with Christs College Farm and instead date from the 1980s. However, the barn is located 30 metres from Grade II listed Christs College Farm and 48 metres from Grade II* listed St Margaret's Church. The heritage statement reads: "Overall it is respectfully submitted that the setting of these assets would at least be preserved and may be considered enhanced through the removal of the barn and stables." If approved, all five homes would have sizeable private rear gardens. The Design & Access Statement says: "The houses are scaled to be of a reasonable height, which, given the benefit of the downward slope of the site, enables generously scaled houses, without them becoming overly imposing on the sensitive surroundings." No decision has yet been made on the plans. Full details are available on the Huntingdonshire District Council planning portal under reference 26/01761/FUL.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Lawyers welcome Bedford rail crash findings as compensation efforts continue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Lawyers representing victims of the Bedford rail crash welcomed the Rail Accident Investigation Branch's (RAIB) interim report, saying it offers early answers about the collision. Published today, the report examines the crash near Elstow and identifies factors that may have contributed to it. The wider investigation continues. Des Collins, senior partner at Collins Solicitors, represents several passengers affected by the crash. Mr Collins said clients would be pleased that the RAIB had produced "a relatively swift interim report" and that his firm would now be advising victims on their legal options. Read more Initial report into fatal Elstow train crash reveals driver passed red signal Stevenage runner wins individual bronze as England take trail race team gold Letchworth family firm Norton Industrial Fasteners celebrates 50 years of trade Fairlands Valley Spartans celebrate busy race weekend and raise £753 for charity Teenager charged with theft of moped found abandoned in Codicote He highlighted the report's findings regarding a signal passed at danger (SPAD) and the apparent absence of a Train Protection Warning System (TPWS) on the stretch of railway where the collision occurred. Mr Collins said: "It is already clear from today's report that the fact of a signal passed at danger (SPAD) was compounded by a lack of a Train Protection Warning System (TPWS) on that stretch of railway. "This system is specifically designed to automatically bring a train to a safe stop, which would have prevented this accident." He also questioned previous assessments that the location was considered low risk and suggested lessons from previous rail disasters had not been fully implemented. The solicitor said his firm had invited both East Midlands Railway and Network Rail to accept liability in principle, with discussions ongoing. He said an early admission of liability could help passengers access interim payments to cover lost earnings and other immediate financial pressures while longer-term compensation claims are assessed. Mr Collins added that the full value of any claims would depend on the final investigation findings and the extent of individual injuries and losses. Stephanie Clarke, a personal injury partner at Stewarts, also welcomed the interim report but stressed that it does not determine blame. She said the role of the RAIB is to investigate technical and operational issues and identify measures that could prevent similar incidents from happening again. Ms Clarke said the report pointed to a possible problem with the train's Automatic Warning System (AWS) and likely human error in the crash. "These are important findings for the rail companies and network providers at the centre of the Bedford incident," she said. "They also help personal injury lawyers like myself representing victims as we seek to learn the reasons for their injuries." She said understanding the crash could help injured passengers and bereaved families come to terms with what happened. Ms Clarke said her team represents a family involved in the collision and is advising them on the investigation, rehabilitation and possible claims. She said many victims face long recoveries, with some suffering serious physical injuries and others psychological trauma, anxiety or post-traumatic stress. The lawyer stressed that today's report is only interim and that investigations by the British Transport Police and Office of Rail and Road continue. "Nevertheless today's report is very valuable and an important milestone," she said. The RAIB's final report is expected to explain the collision in more detail and recommend ways to improve rail safety. The crash killed driver Shaun Burton, 60, and injured more than 160 of the approximately 257 people on board; 102 passengers were taken to hospital. RAIB said the Corby-to-London St Pancras train acknowledged a red signal but continued accelerating, reaching 76mph, before emergency braking was applied about 200 metres from the stationary train. The stationary train had stopped unexpectedly after a fault with its Automatic Warning System equipment caused its brakes to apply, which turned the signal behind it red.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 325 young people supported to help prevent serious violence in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Early intervention is helping to prevent crime before it happens, according to Cambridgeshire’s police and crime commissioner. Darryl Preston told members of the Police and Crime Panel in Peterborough that early intervention schemes were reducing offending and protecting vulnerable people, including women and girls. He said: "I have always been clear that prevention is better than cure and intervening earlier is better than responding after harm has occurred. "By addressing the underlying root causes that contribute to offending behaviour and by providing support at the earliest opportunity, we can help prevent crime, reduce future victimisation, and build safer communities." In his update, Mr Preston highlighted the Respect Programme, which supports families experiencing child-to-parent abuse, and the Drive programme, which targets domestic abuse and stalking perpetrators. He also pointed to the Safer Corridors Toolkit, developed with schools to identify and challenge harmful behaviours. Between April and June, 325 young people under the age of 24 received support through the Serious Violence Reduction Programme to help prevent involvement in serious violence. Mr Preston said: "While crime prevention remains a core part of policing, it cannot be delivered by police alone. "Success requires strong partnership working across all agencies within the local criminal justice system." Other recent initiatives include the selection of Cambridge Crown Court as an Intensive Supervision Court pilot site, and the delivery of trusted adult schemes, detached youth work, and diversionary activities funded through the Serious Violence Duty. Efforts to tackle serious and organised crime include the SOC Fusion knowledge events, which bring together agencies to identify threats and strengthen joint responses. Mr Preston said: "I cannot stress enough the importance of strong partnerships, targeted investment, and a shared focus on reducing harm before it occurs." Full reports and updates from the Police and Crime Panel meeting are available on the commissioner’s website.

We visited the restaurant on the village's High Street and were impressed from the moment we walked through the door. The clean, modern interior is surprisingly spacious while retaining a cosy feel, giving diners room to eat in comfort. The starter of chicken and king prawns was beautifully presented. (Image: Sarah Cliss) We were welcomed by the restaurant's proud owner, Kosur Miah, who proudly showed off all that the restaurant has already achieved, including the fact that it is a past winner of the 'Champions of Champions' national award in the Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA). It is currently in the running as an East of England regional finalist in the awards dubbed the 'Oscars of the Curry Industry ', due to be held in London on October 12. Kosur is especially proud because customers nominated the restaurant for another chance to be crowned the nation’s top curry house. The Curry Palace in Cottenham offers diners plenty of space to enjoy their meal. (Image: Sarah Cliss) It is easy to see why customers are taking the time and trouble to nominate as the quality of the food, service and atmosphere is everything you would want from a restaurant. The near-capacity Wednesday-night crowd enjoying the extensive menu was proof of its appeal. Kosur chose our food for the evening, starting with papadams and chutneys. The mango was rich and sweet, the lime tangy and tongue-tingling, while the red sauce was tasty, and the onion salad fresh and crisp. Curry Palace in Cottenham has been named a regional finalist in the ARTA awards 2026. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) Next came a beautifully presented chicken and king prawn starter. The huge prawns were delicately spiced and breadcrumb-coated, while the chicken was melt-in-the-mouth, served with refreshing salad and a tongue-tingling sauce. On to the main, and once again Kosur's choice did not disappoint. Two types of rice - onion and mushroom - both fluffy and light, were served with chicken tawa shashlik karahi - a house speciality - one of the best lamb curries we have ever tried - lamb sagwala. The lamb was tender, beautifully spiced and utterly delicious. The third was a king prawn bhuna, and once again it did not disappoint. The sauce was delicious, and the prawns were perfectly prepared. The accompanying mixed niramish (mixed vegetables) were cooked to perfection, and the garlic naan was sizzling hot and tasty. Unfortunately, the starters and mains were so delicious that there was no room for dessert, but the restaurant offers an extensive choice guaranteed to satisfy all tastes. All in all the experience was a 10/10 - the staff were friendly, efficient and helpful, the food was extraordinarily good, and the ambience was excellent. The Curry Palace thoroughly deserves its nomination, so fingers crossed it repeats its success of 2018 to take the 'Champion of Champions' title on the 12th. Curry Palace was established 26 years ago by Kosur and has built a fantastic reputation for top quality food. More than 1,250 restaurants and takeaways were nominated for this year’s ARTA awards by diners and food enthusiasts.

Cromwell Vets team (Image: Cromwell Vets) Mental health is a significant concern in the veterinary profession, with vets reportedly four times more likely to die by suicide than the general public. Additionally, nearly 70 per cent of veterinarians have lost a colleague to suicide.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Broadcaster and Childline founder Dame Esther Rantzen has died aged 86
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen has died aged 86. Dame Esther had previously shared that she was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in May 2023. In a statement, her family said: “Our adored mother Dame Esther Rantzen died today. “Her legacy of compassion and understanding will live on in her charities Childline and the Silverline, and through those of us who were lucky enough to love and be loved by her. “We are grateful she is finally at rest with her beloved husband, Desmond Wilcox, but we will miss her immeasurably. She was our sunshine. “We will always remember her endless capacity for joy, her ability to comfort every heartache, her beautiful way with words and her expert guidance in all things." Dame Esther became a household name in the UK during her time on the BBC; she was best known for presenting That’s Life! – a programme featuring a mix of investigations, topical issues and entertainment – from 1973 to 1994. Alongside her successful career as a journalist and broadcaster, she also set up children’s charity Childline in 1986. Dame Esther created Childline to help offer counselling and support for children and young people in the UK up until the age of 19, in 2006 the charity became part of The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC). The late broadcaster also set up The Silver Line in 2013, a charity which supports elderly people in the UK who are battling loneliness. In 2015, Dame Esther was made a DBE by the late Queen Elizabeth II for services to children and older people due to her charity work. During her lung cancer diagnosis, Dame Esther had been very open with her thoughts on death and in December 2023 she shared she had joined the assisted dying organisation, Dignitas. Dame Esther had also called for a free vote on assisted dying, sharing: “I think it’s important that the law catches up with what the country wants.” Dame Esther Rantzen is survived by her three children, Rebecca, Miriam and Joshua Wilcox.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Woman arrested after 'burglary' at Cambs puppy breeding facility
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A woman has been arrested following a break-in at a beagle breeding facility in Cambridgeshire. Police were called to MBR Acres in Wyton, near Huntingdon, at 11.10pm on September 29, after reports of a burglary. A spokesperson for the force confirmed that a 43-year-old woman from Inverness was arrested on suspicion of burglary. She remains in custody. The incident is believed to be linked to an "open rescue" at the site, where beagles are bred for use in laboratory testing. Campaign group Camp Beagle, the UK's longest-running permanent animal rights protest camp, has maintained a continuous presence outside the facility since the summer of 2021. The organisation demands that the facility close and end the use of beagles for research purposes. MBR Acres previously told The Hunts Post: "Our operations are entirely legal and carried out under strict UK Home Office regulatory oversight. "We remain committed to meeting all required welfare and operational standards." Footage shared with Camp Beagle appears to show people entering the facility and reaching sheds where the dogs are kept. Police did not confirm what was taken during the burglary.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: NINE areas of Cambs where crime rise is 'concerning'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nine areas of Cambridgeshire have been highlighted after a ‘concerning’ rise in crime was reported. South Cambridgeshire District Council has reported ‘concerning trends’ after a rise in rural crime in a number of areas. The council’s cabinet has approved a new plan to combat shoplifting with a focus on specific wards. A report said the focus should be on areas which “are flagging on multiple crime and activity types” or where “professional concern indicates a need for a focus”. These include Cambourne, Histon and Impington with a focus on Orchard Park, Northstowe, Milton and Waterbeach, Fen Ditton and Fulbourn and any other areas where “the data shows spikes or concerning trends”. It will allow the South Cambridgeshire Community Partnership – a joint effort between the council and emergency services and voluntary groups – to work to address the problem. Cllr Dr Lisa Redrup, lead cabinet member for healthy communities, said there were “several new priorities” for the partnership this year. The Liberal Democrat councillor said this included looking at rural shoplifting as “rates have been rising” and it is a “really difficult problem”. She said the partnership would help to find different ways to tackle it. It also said that there was a “concerning” and “large increase” in drug offences over the last year, but this may have been down to how they were recorded. Cllr Bridget Smith, leader of the council, said she was “very pleased” that tackling rural shoplifting was made a priority as she has witnessed it herself. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “The gall with which it is carried out is quite mind boggling actually. “It makes shop workers feel incredibly vulnerable and actually makes other people going to shops where this is happening in such a laden fashion feel very very vulnerable as well.” She said small supermarkets were particularly at risk as they sell “some quite high value goods” and asked if advice could be given to them. She said: “Now that food prices are so very high, stealing a steak is actually quite an expensive thing to nick really. If there’s any more that could be done that would be really helpful.” The cabinet approved the new operational and communications plan for the community safety partnership for 2026/27. A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire Constabulary said: “We’re aware shoplifting can have a huge impact on those involved in the business community as well as local residents, and this is one of the reasons why it is a key issue for officers across the county. “We work closely with retailers concerning shoplifting and seeking prosecutions where possible. For repeat offenders, we are applying for Criminal Behaviour Orders preventing them from entering areas where they have previously committed crime. “We have a Spree Offender Team who proactively arrest and seek to charge prolific shoplifters. “The force would also encourage businesses to reporting shoplifting to us as it helps our officers build a bigger picture of what is happening across the county. “This can be done online (https://www.cambs.police.uk/ro/report/ocr/af/how-to-report-a-crime/), calling 101 or 999 in an emergency.” They also said that drug-dealing “remains a priority” for their teams and said the rise in offences could be due to “two factors – proactive policing work and a change in recording practices.” They said police across the country have been carrying out “proactive stop-searches in hotspot areas”, but also that all reports from border forces of drugs intercepted coming into the country are now recorded as crimes rather than intelligence items.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Sheep rescued from St Ives river after becoming trapped in the water
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A sheep stuck in a river sparked a rescue operation in St Ives. Firefighters from Huntingdon and Cambridge were called to Meadow Lane after the animal became trapped in the water. Crews used a sled to reach the sheep and safely brought it back to dry land. Sheep rescue (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service) A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service said: "Whilst these types of incidents can't always be avoided, we would like to urge those that have animals to please ensure fences and gates are secure to reduce the chances of animals becoming stuck in places like rivers. "We train to be able to help animals who have found themselves stuck in a variety of scenarios so that we can free them safely. "If you spot an animal stuck in water, do not attempt to rescue them yourselves. "Dial 999 and ask for the fire service."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Aerial photos show scale of new David Lloyd health club in Huntingdonshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Aerial photos show the scale of a new premium health and wellness club in Huntingdonshire ahead of its grand opening. The new David Lloyd club will officially launch on October 6, bringing fitness, swimming, racquet sports and spa facilities to St Neots. The club will have more than 100 workout stations, heated indoor and outdoor pools, and racquet sports areas. Its courts will include cushioned acrylic tennis courts and padel courts. Aerial photos by Maciek Platek at St Neots Gallery show the scale of the new club, which is located on Nuffield Road in Wintringham. The new club will feature workout stations, indoor and outdoor pools and racquet sports areas Children will get fun, safe coaching through the Swim Stars and Tennis Stars programmes. Facilities in the club's spa retreat will include a Himalayan salt sauna, crystal steam room, cold plunge pools and a swim-in, swim-out hydro pool. The retreat will also feature heated beds and a spa garden. Mr Borer said: "I’m so excited to be joining David Lloyd St Neots as the Club General Manager. "There’s already a great deal of excitement surrounding the new Club and I’m really looking forward to welcoming members through the doors later this year. The new David Lloyd club in St Neots will open on October 6 "Throughout my 16 year career with David Lloyd Clubs, I’ve had the opportunity to work across several fantastic Clubs and I can’t wait to bring my passion for delivering a great member experience to St Neots. "I’m looking forward to meeting members and becoming part of the St Neots community." The opening is expected to create local jobs in hospitality, fitness and spa services. Membership prices to David Lloyd clubs vary between locations but can be up to £100 a month, whilst standard day passes can be around £20.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs paedophile who sent explicit images to decoy account jailed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire paedophile who believed he was talking to a 13-year-old girl online has been jailed after being caught by a decoy account. David Clark, 52, from Akeman Street in Cambridge, shared explicit messages and images with an account he believed to belong to a 13-year-old girl. He had contacted the account on Snapchat in September 2025, not realising it was operated by an online child abuse activist group. Clark continued to engage in sexual conversations despite being told multiple times that the girl was only 13. He asked about her sexual experiences, described sex acts and sent an explicit picture of himself. He also asked her to send indecent images and sent a picture of two adults having sex. Clark was arrested in November 2025. David Clark was jailed for three years and two months (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Officers seized several devices and found Clark had tried to delete the chat history. He pleaded guilty to attempting to engage in sexual communication with a child, causing a child to look at an image of sexual activity, and attempting to cause or incite a girl to engage in sexual activity. Clark was jailed for three years and two months at Huntingdon Law Courts on Friday, September 25. Detective Constable Bethany Reynolds, from the Online Child Abuse Safeguarding Team (OCAST), said: "Clark is clearly a risk to children. "He advised the 'child' in this case to delete the messages in case her parents found them, proving he knew what he was doing was wrong. "Although thankfully a decoy account, Clark still attempted to prey on and groom what he believed was a child. "Protecting young people from harm is one of our top priorities and we will do all we can to bring offenders to justice." For more on child abuse, including how to report it and spot the signs, visit the dedicated pages on the Cambridgeshire Police website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Police release sketch of man wanted in connection with serious sexual assault

The suspect is described as a white man with a pale complexion and very dark short hair. He is believed to have been wearing a black T-shirt, black shorts, and white trainers at the time of the assault. Anyone who recognises the man is urged to come forward after the force released an artist’s impression. The suspect is described as a white man with a pale complexion and very dark, short hair (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Detective Constable James Howard, the investigating officer, said: "The victim has shown considerable courage in assisting our investigation and has worked with a forensic artist to produce this image. "I am asking the public to carefully look at the drawing and consider whether they recognise the person depicted. "Even if you think the information you hold may be insignificant, I encourage you to come forward. "Small details can often make a significant difference in helping us identify a suspect. Officers also want to hear from anyone who saw a dark Tesla near Mill Lane around the time of the incident. As of September 30, no arrests have been made and the investigation remains ongoing.
