summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Young advocate wins Centrepoint Award for her work to change the care system
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A 22-year-old advocate from Kent will be recognised for her work to improve the housing system for care leavers at a London awards ceremony this month. Hayleigh went into care when she was 10 years old and since then has navigated a number of challenges. “Growing up, the situation at home wasn’t working so my grandma stepped in and gave up her job as a nurse of 18 years to look after us,” explains Hayleigh. Hayleigh remembers that it was hard to trust adults trying to provide help as there was a lack of consistency in the system: “When I was younger, there were a lot of social workers involved at different times.  I struggled to connect with them as I thought they were all just doing it because it was their job -not because they wanted to help me.  For me, that was a big struggle.” There is currently inadequate support for young care leavers looking to secure affordable and stable housing, and Hayleigh struggled with this huge turning point in her life. But over the past decade, The Young Lives Foundation in Kent – a valued partner of Centrepoint’s - have consistently supported Hayleigh with independence and helped her to find her voice as she worked towards securing her own home. Through the charity’s programmes, the support she received helped her to identify that she lacked confidence in her own abilities and often judged herself harshly.  As she started to find her voice, she began to see that her natural empathy and warmth towards others were two of her greatest skills, and wanted to put these to good use advocating for other young people from similar backgrounds. Hayleigh is now an active member of the Children in Care Council and both officials and councillors defer to her to be the voice of care experienced young people. She is also continuing to work with The Young Lives Foundation, becoming an inspiration for the charity’s younger members. Describing Hayleigh, her Leaving Care Mentor Amy said: “I met Hayleigh four years ago and was immediately impressed.  Seeing her talk so passionately about other young people and wanting to support them is so admirable.  I look up to her – I’m just really proud.” Hayleigh was nominated for Centrepoint’s ‘Partner’ award by her Young Lives Foundation team. She is looking forward to attending the awards with one of her biggest supporters – her grandma. Hayleigh said: “When I found out that I won an award, I was speechless.  It’s really rewarding as it shows you are doing something right.  When I was younger, it was hard for me to express myself but now people are recognising me.  It’s not just for me, but for other young people as well.” (Image: Centerpoint) A new Housing Benefit rule comes into effect this month, making it easier for young people in supported housing to start and stay in work. It follows campaigning from youth homelessness charity, Centrepoint, to end a long-standing benefit trap which was preventing young people in supported housing from entering the workforce. The flaw in the system meant that these young people were actually left worse off when taking on more hours of work. Centrepoint estimated this was limiting opportunities for over 30,000 young people in supported housing. However, this October the government introduces a new earned income disregard in Housing Benefit for claimants in supported housing and temporary accommodation. It means that more of a young person's earnings will be ignored when their Housing Benefit is calculated, allowing them to keep more of what they earn. This will remove the quirk in the system that disincentivises work, and reduce the financial cliff edge when moving into, or progressing in, employment. Lisa Doyle, Head of Policy and Public Affairs at Centrepoint, said: “This is a significant victory for those trying to escape homelessness, particularly young people at the start of their careers, who have so far found their ambitions blocked by the system." She added, “This would not have been possible without our partners and campaigners, particularly those who have joined our calls for the government to make work pay. “We are incredibly grateful to them and would like to thank each of them on behalf of the young people we support.” Last year, over 118,000 young people faced homelessness. That’s one young person every four minutes. At a time of life when most of their peers are trying new things and taking their first steps into adulthood, these young people found themselves alone and afraid, and unsure where to turn. It doesn’t have to be like this, with the right support at the right time, these young people can escape homelessness or avoid it altogether. At Centrepoint, provide more than a bed for the night. We provide a safe place to rebuild, support into education and work, and the confidence to believe in a better future. Youth homelessness is not inevitable. With the right help at the right time, it can be prevented and it can be ended. Our mission is to end youth homelessness – and you can help us. Whether it’s running a marathon or holding a sleep out, you, your friends, family and co-workers can join our movement to end youth homelessness and give vulnerable young people a brighter future. To find out more, donate or get involved, please visit our website http://www.centrepoint.org.uk/newspaper (Image: Centerpoint) Centreprise - an innovative programme, designed to inspire a new generation of business leaders - has been launched by the youth homelessness charity, Centrepoint. 16 young people from London and Bradford were given the opportunity to develop entrepreneurial skills, build confidence and develop business ideas that could one day grow to become the UK’s next big company. It culminated in a Dragon's Den-style final, during which participants pitched their ideas to a panel of respected business leaders and entrepreneurs including; Centrepoint donor Alison Fortescue; founder of Amber Labs, James Bennet; and Co-founder of Little Moons, Vivien Wong. Sadie Odeogberin, Head of Centrepoint Works, said: “All young people want to work but there are some who aren’t given the support or opportunities to do so. Centreprise is changing that. "The past few weeks have been amazing, and I’m incredibly proud of what the young people have achieved.” The initiative was made possible thanks to the extraordinary generosity of Alison Fortescue, whose late husband Alex Fortescue left a £1 million legacy gift. The money will fund Centreprise for the next five years and this year was put towards equipment, software and professional services which judges allocated at the end of the day to help young people build their businesses. They will also have access to weekly 1-to-1 mentoring sessions, plus check-in calls with their mentors for three months. Alison Fortescue said: “I was so impressed by the enthusiasm of the young people participating in Centreprise, their commitment and ambitions are truly inspiring.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New local media planning tool Raid launches today
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The local news media sector's new audience measurement platform Regional Audience Intelligence Data (Raid) has officially launched today, enabling media planners to see local more clearly. The new Raid platform, the only place to find UK local news media’s total brand audience, offers a host of new benefits including more immediate and accurate audience data, a reduction in modelled readership data, and a new bespoke user interface. News Media Association chief executive Theo Bamber said: “Local news media presents a unique and compelling proposition for advertisers. Local titles are highly trusted environments with deep connections to the communities and people they serve. “Raid gives planners a clear and dynamic view of this market, allowing them to see the scope and scale of local media and connect brands with the right audiences. It's an important innovation at a time when the advertising model is evolving, and will deliver significant benefits to publishers and agencies alike.” (Image: Raid) Developed by the international research agency RAM Penetrace on behalf of local publishers, Raid launches today with an advertising campaign across the media trade press and local news media sector. Over the past month, more than 100 local publishers and media planners have been introduced to Raid through a series of webinar training sessions. The system offers users readership insights right down to the postcode level. Tags deployed by the RAM Platform across local news websites capture the reach, frequency and demographics of the sector’s digital audiences, with additional readership surveys used to capture print readership data, powering Raid’s total brand audience data. CEO RAM Penetrace UK Ltd Dianne Newman said: “Raid has been designed with the flexibility to adapt quickly as the local news sector evolves while offering media agencies the rigour required to plan with complete confidence. "We look forward to continuing our work with publishers, agencies and advertisers as the rollout of this exciting new tool progresses over the coming weeks and months.” Raid replaces JICREG, which will continue to be available as a legacy system for the time being.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Curious guinea pig rescued from poor conditions seeks new home in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "curious little guinea pig" is searching for a new home in Cambridgeshire after being rescued from poor living conditions. Jarek, a one-year-old guinea pig, is currently being cared for at the RSPCA Block Fen Animal Centre. He was removed from a multi-animal household and is now looking for a loving forever home. A spokesperson for the centre said: "Jarek is a very curious little guinea pig with a lovely personality and a big appetite. "He loves mealtimes and is always keen to see what tasty treats are on offer. "He is becoming a confident boy. "He is still learning that everyone can be trusted and will benefit from patient owners who are willing to continue building his confidence through gentle, regular handling." Jarek is looking to be rehomed with a single female or a group of females. He has not yet been neutered, so temporary separate accommodation will be required until this is complete. Last year, 419 guinea pigs were taken into RSPCA national centres in England and Wales (Image: RSPCA) The RSPCA recommends a minimum space of 10 square feet for a pair of guinea pigs and will ask to see photos of the enclosure as part of the rehoming process. The adoption fee is set at £25. Anyone interested in rehoming Jarek is encouraged to complete the centre’s online application form. The RSPCA has reported a rise in guinea pigs being surrendered, citing overbreeding, the cost-of-living crisis, and a general lack of owner knowledge as contributing factors. Last year, 419 guinea pigs were taken into RSPCA national centres in England and Wales—an increase of 181 from the previous year. Guinea pigs typically live five to six years and are active for up to 20 hours a day. They are social animals that require companionship and should never be kept alone.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs man charged with firearms offences after dawn raids targeting crime gang
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire man has been charged with firearms offences following a major police operation targeting a suspected organised crime group. Andreas Nicolas, 64, of Duxford, was charged with possession of a firearm (a revolver) and possession of a weapon to discharge a noxious thing, namely electricity. He was remanded in custody and will appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on October 1. Mr Nicolas was arrested in the early hours of Tuesday as part of a wider operation that saw 17 people arrested during raids at 24 properties across Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire, London, Essex and Suffolk. More than 800 Met officers took part in the arrest operations. Mr Nicholas was initially bailed on Tuesday evening but was re-arrested on Wednesday after officers discovered weapons during property searches that were suspected of belonging to him. He is the fourth person to be charged in connection with the operation. Charles Charalambous, 56, from Cockfosters, was charged with wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm to resist arrest, relating to an incident in which a police officer was stabbed while executing a warrant. Carl Robinson, 49, from Essex, was charged with possession of offensive weapons in a private place, namely three knives. Bradley Byford, 37, from Bishop’s Stortford, was charged with possession of a weapon to discharge a noxious thing, namely electricity. All three men appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, September 30. Mr Charalambous was remanded in custody to appear at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday, October 29. Mr Byford was bailed to appear at the same court on the same date. Mr Robinson’s case was adjourned for discussion of a legal matter, and he was bailed to appear again at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Thursday, October 1. All four men remain under investigation as part of the wider operation and have been bailed for those offences, along with the other 14 individuals arrested on Tuesday.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New order tackles anti-social behaviour, street drinking and vandalism in Huntingdon
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new Public Spaces Protection Order is now in force in Huntingdon to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour. Huntingdon District Council introduced the order with Cambridgeshire Constabulary on October 1 after residents and businesses raised concerns about rising anti-social behaviour. The order gives council officers and police powers to tackle disruptive behaviour in public spaces. Neighbourhood PCSO Jim Gardner with senior community safety officer Georgia Patterson from Huntingdonshire District Council (Image: Police) Colin Norden, neighbourhood inspector for Huntingdonshire, said: "This PSPO gives us the tools we need to address persistent issues, such as anti-social behaviour including street drinking, public urination and defecation, vandalism and other activities that disrupt public spaces. "With this order in place, we can respond more effectively to the concerns of residents and businesses, working together to create an environment and a space that are enjoyable and accessible for all." The order covers Huntingdon town centre and the area inside the ring road. The order will last three years and be reviewed every year. Debbie Mickelburgh, executive councillor for communities, health and leisure, said: "This Public Spaces Protection Order demonstrates our commitment to working in partnership with Cambridgeshire Constabulary and the local community to tackle anti-social behaviour. "Residents and businesses have been clear that action is needed, and this order provides additional tools to help address behaviours that impact people’s enjoyment of Huntingdon town centre. "Together, we can help ensure Huntingdon remains a safe and welcoming place for all."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Inquest opens into death of Cambs motorcyclist, 19, who died in crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An inquest has been opened into the death of a 19-year-old who died in a crash between two motorbikes in Cambridgeshire. Rolas Saskovas, of Lawson Avenue, Peterborough, was injured in the crash on August 31 and later died in hospital. Police were called to the head-on collision on the A605 Stanham Way, near Cardea, at around 5.20pm. Mr Saskovas was riding a blue Yamaha MT-03 which collided with a black BMW S100. The BMW rider, a 32-year-old man from London, sustained serious but not life-threatening injuries. He was taken to hospital after the crash. Area Coroner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Simon Milburn opened Mr Saskovas' inquest on October 1 at Vantage House in Huntingdon. The brief hearing heard how Mr Saskovas was the rider of a motorcycle that was involved in a collision, and as a result he suffered a number of injuries. The provisional cause of death was given as 1A multiple severe traumatic injuries with the toxicology results pending. Mr Milburn adjourned the hearing for an inquest on March 11, 2027, at Vantage House.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts man charged with dangerous driving after police pursuit ends in crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdon man has been charged with dangerous driving after a police pursuit ended in a crash. A compliant stop was attempted but the driver refused to stop and sped off. The driver crashed into a parked car before fleeing on foot. Police confirmed on October 1 that Mr Burns had been charged with dangerous driving, criminal damage and failing to stop. He is due to appear at Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on October 22. The incident was part of ‘Operation Chambers’ in Sawtry – a multi-agency day of action aimed at disrupting criminality on Huntingdonshire's rural road networks. During the day, the force conducted multiple stops to check for overweight vehicles and potentially stolen machinery.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire arsonist jailed after setting fire to his own home
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An arsonist who set fire to his own Cambridgeshire home has been jailed for two years. Police officers and firefighters were called to a property on Cheviot Avenue, Gunthorpe, Peterborough belonging to Robert Hill, 46, on May 9. Smoke and flames were seen coming from the property. Hill was inside with a family member when he started the fire, and officers found two lighters on him. Hill admitted arson at Cambridge Crown Court on September 29 and was jailed for two years. Detective Constable Nat Cook, who investigated the case, said: “The consequences of Hill’s reckless actions could have been catastrophic, and he is seriously lucky no-one was harmed in the blaze. “The fire was deliberate and put himself and a family member in serious danger, so I am pleased the sentence reflects the damage and distress he caused.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Initial report into fatal Elstow train crash reveals driver passed red signal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The driver of a passenger train that crashed into another service near Bedford passed a red signal while accelerating, according to an interim investigation report. The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) has published its latest findings on the fatal collision between two East Midlands Railway trains near Elstow, Bedfordshire, on June 19. The crash happened at around 5.13pm when a Corby to London St Pancras service struck the rear of a stationary Nottingham to London St Pancras train on the Midland Main Line about 2.5 miles south of Bedford station. An image showing the impact of the two trains. The driver of the Corby service suffered fatal injuries and more than 160 people were injured. Investigators estimate that 257 passengers and staff were aboard the two trains when the collision occurred. Both trains derailed and suffered significant damage. The report confirms that the Nottingham to London train had come to an unexpected stop after an automatic emergency brake application. The scene just south of the Elstow interchange between the A421 and the A6 in Bedford South after two East Midlands Railway (EMR) trains were involved in a collision around 5.15pm on Friday, June 19. (Image: Chris Radburn/PA Wire) Signal WH154, the signal protecting the stationary train, was displaying a red danger aspect. Forward-facing CCTV footage from the Corby train showed the signal was correctly displaying red as the train approached. Investigators found the train was travelling at about 58mph and accelerating when it passed the signal. An image showing the impact of the two trains. Data recovered from the train's on-board recorder showed the driver first applied the brakes around 10 seconds before impact while travelling at approximately 76mph. The train's speed had reduced to around 50mph at the point of collision. RAIB said its investigation remains focused on understanding why the Corby service passed the red signal. The report also exposes problems with the Nottingham train before the crash. Investigators found it received an Automatic Warning System (AWS) warning indication despite approaching a signal showing green. Read more WATCH: Shocking footage of scene after head-on crash seriously injures two people Latest court results for North Herts and Stevenage Hertfordshire woman avoids jail after abusing and killing dog Hertfordshire wedding venue could lose licence over noise concerns McDonald's submits plans for new restaurant in Arlesey The warning was not acknowledged within the required time, triggering an emergency brake application and bringing the train to a stand. The train's driver subsequently reported an AWS fault to the signaller. Witness evidence suggests neither the driver nor an instructor travelling in the cab recognised a continuous alarm as an AWS warning indication. Investigators also found a second incident on July 9, when another train wrongly received an AWS warning at the same green signal. Further checks found part of the AWS equipment was outside the required tolerance. The point of impact between the two trains. (Image: RAIB) The report notes there had been no previous recorded incidents of trains passing signal WH154 while it was displaying red since records began in 1985. Analysis by the Rail Safety and Standards Board indicated no train had encountered a red aspect at the signal before the accident in 2026. RAIB stressed that its job is to improve railway safety, not assign blame or liability. The scene just south of the Elstow interchange between the A421 and the A6 in Bedford South after two East Midlands Railway (EMR) trains were involved in a collision. (Image: Jamie Lashmar/PA Wire) The investigation will examine the actions of those involved, why the Corby train passed the signal at danger, the braking and warning systems, why the Nottingham service stopped, signal WH154’s status and visibility, the trains’ crashworthiness and the emergency response.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham announces plans to end pension triple lock to fund social care service
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
The state pension triple lock is being drawn into the debate over how the Government could fund a national care service, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham putting care as a key priority. The triple lock ensures the state pension rises each year by whichever is highest out of inflation, average wage growth or 2.5 per cent. But changing the policy could free up money for other Government priorities at a time when ministers are considering how to tackle the long-running pressures facing social care. Burnham is calling for an “honest conversation” about some of the difficult choices facing the country. In his first conference speech as Prime Minister, he said that the triple lock will be honoured for the rest of this term, but added: "From there, in April 2030, we will adjust it. The state pension will continue to rise every year, at least by prices, or 2.5 per cent, and it will hold its value relative to earnings over time, so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation." Today's Poll: Would you support scrapping State Pension triple lock (amount its guaranteed to rise by) to pay for universal social care?
    
    NB. This is a vibe question. There are many other routes, options & things money could go to. Yet given a straight choice what's your view? — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) September 28, 2026 The link between pensions and social care is emerging as ministers consider how a national care service could be funded. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) estimates that the triple lock currently adds around £16 billion a year to state pension spending compared with uprating pensions in line with average earnings. That does not mean £16 billion could simply be transferred to social care if the triple lock were changed. The eventual saving would depend on what replaced the existing system, how pension increases were calculated and the wider impact on Government finances. But the size of the figure illustrates why the triple lock is being discussed as ministers look at competing demands on public spending. The debate comes against a backdrop of substantial increases in state pension payments since the guarantee was introduced. Press Association analysis of DWP data found that the average annual state pension increase between 2012/13 and 2026/27 was 4.1 per cent. That compares with an average of 3.5 per cent during the previous 15 years, from 1997/98 to 2011/12. The IFS estimates that if flat-rate state pensions had risen in line with average earnings since 2010 rather than under the triple lock, they would now be around 12 per cent lower - equivalent to approximately £1,500 a year less. The think tank says the triple lock has therefore played an important role in increasing pensioner incomes, although it is not the only factor. State pension spending is now around £154 billion a year, according to the IFS. That is equivalent to around 4.9 per cent of national income, compared with 4.3 per cent in 2010 and 3.6 per cent in 2006/07. The IFS estimates the triple lock itself accounts for around £16 billion of additional annual spending compared with an earnings-linked alternative. The triple lock will remain until 2030. The Budget on 28 October will provide a key opportunity for the Government to set out more of its spending plans. For pensioners, the crucial question will be whether they are better off with the triple lock, or with a fully funded social care service.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Pensioners given major tax promise as Andy Burnham reveals new care plan
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Pensioners living mainly on the state pension have been given a fresh tax promise by Andy Burnham as he set out plans for a national care service. The Prime Minister said low-income pensioners will not be “dragged into paying income tax” during this Parliament, as he linked the pledge to his wider offer of a rising state pension and no care charges. Under the current rules, the standard Personal Allowance is £12,570 – the amount of income an individual can receive before they normally start paying Income Tax. The allowance is currently frozen at that level. Burnham told Labour conference: “Some may not realize it, but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen. “I can also confirm today our commitment to ensure that the low-income pensioners won't be dragged into paying income tax in this Parliament. “So this is the deal: a state pension that rises every year, no care charges, and a high-quality national care service to give peace of mind in later life. Conference, I am going to go out and argue for that-a good deal for our pensioners and for older people in the 21st century” The Personal Allowance is the amount of income people can normally receive each tax year before Income Tax becomes due. For 2026/27, it stands at £12,570 and is due to remain at that level for 2027/28 under existing legislation. Someone whose total annual income is below their Personal Allowance will not normally pay Income Tax. This includes pension income. The full new state pension is currently below the Personal Allowance, meaning someone receiving only the full new state pension would not normally have an Income Tax bill on that pension alone. However, people with other taxable income can have a tax liability once their total income exceeds their available allowance. The issue is particularly significant because the state pension is increasing while the Personal Allowance has remained frozen. Burnham's pledge means the Government is committing to ensuring that low-income pensioners are not pulled into Income Tax during this Parliament. The precise mechanism for achieving that commitment was not set out in the speech. The Personal Allowance is currently £12,570, while the full new state pension is £241.30 a week, or around £12,548 a year when paid for 52 weeks. That leaves only a small gap between the full new state pension and the current tax-free allowance. Burnham presented the tax pledge as one part of a broader package for older people. He said his plan would combine a state pension that continues to rise each year with no care charges and a national care service. His comments come as the Government faces a major debate over how such a service would be funded. Burnham has also put the future of the state pension triple lock into the wider conversation, although the Government has said the existing commitment will remain during this Parliament. The triple lock currently guarantees that the state pension rises each year by whichever is highest of inflation, average wage growth or 2.5 per cent. If someone's taxable income is above £12,570, Income Tax can be due on the amount above the allowance, depending on their circumstances and tax bands. For 2026/27, the basic Income Tax rate in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is 20 per cent on taxable income within the basic-rate band. This means pensioners with a state pension plus private or workplace pension income, earnings or other taxable income may have to pay tax even if their state pension itself is below the Personal Allowance. Burnham's conference pledge puts the Personal Allowance alongside the state pension and social care at the heart of his offer to older people.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Southoe church launches community hub after £245,082 heritage grant
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A church in Southoe has officially launched its new community hub. The celebrations on September 12 took place at St Leonard’s Church, marking the opening of a flexible space for year-round events. The community and church members have worked on the project since 2021. Major repairs and interior reordering began in November 2026. The project, supported by 15 grant-making bodies, includes two new toilet cubicles, a new bell-ringing floor and staircase, a refurbished floor, and a ramp into the south porch. The National Lottery Heritage Fund contributed £245,082, while Hunts District Council provided £20,082 for new solar panels. The community gathered at St Leonard’s Church for the celebrations (Image: St Leonard’s Church) Upgraded water, sewerage, and power supplies were also required. About 150 people attended the celebrations, with local MP Ben Obese-Jecty cutting a ribbon to announce the opening. The project team has secured funding for a new electric green energy heating scheme, complementing the solar panels, from the Church of England Net Zero Boiler Replacement Fund (£38,804) and the National Lottery Community Fund (£19,464). This installation should be completed by early November. The space is already in use, with the local community choir rehearsing, along with a coffee morning and a weekend quiz night.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 24 fined after waste dumped beside Cambourne charity bring banks
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Twenty-four people have been fined for fly-tipping in Cambourne, where waste was dumped next to charity bring banks. South Cambridgeshire District Council issued the fines after repeated incidents at the recycling area in the Morrisons car park, outside Home Bargains. A range of items, including vacuum cleaners, TVs, mattresses, furniture, and child seats, were left at the site, prompting the removal of the bring banks. Laurence Damary-Homan, lead cabinet member for environment at South Cambridgeshire District Council, said: "We know people in Cambourne were frustrated by rubbish being left beside these bring banks and it is an issue nationally. "Most residents use them responsibly, they provide income for good causes, and they’re a convenient recycling option. Residents are being urged not to leave waste beside bring banks (Image: South Cambridgeshire District Council) "But leaving items next to full bring banks or dumping unwanted goods is fly-tipping and is simply not acceptable. "If there is no room in a container, please take your items home and return another day or use a Household Recycling Centre. "If they get misused, they’ll be removed as we’ve seen in Cambourne. "Our officers investigate to identify those responsible wherever possible, and we will continue to issue fines and pursue prosecutions where we can." Over the past two years, the council’s envirocrimes officers issued 14 Fixed Penalty Notices for fly-tipping, eight for littering, and sent seven warning letters. Six prosecutions have been brought forward, with two Duty of Care Fixed Penalty Notices issued and 11 further cases under investigation. The council is taking action against fly-tipping in South Cambridgeshire. (Image: South Cambridgeshire District Council) The envirocrimes team is now visiting recycling and charity bank sites across South Cambridgeshire to offer advice, identify problems, and work with site operators to prevent further dumping. Leaving waste beside bring banks can attract more fly-tipping, vermin, and creates a burden for those maintaining the sites. Residents are asked to check for space before depositing items and to use Household Recycling Centres if banks are full.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Officer stabbed as police arrest 17 during dawn raids targeting crime gang
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Seventeen people have been arrested after dawn raids targeting an organised crime group across five areas, including Hertfordshire and Cambridgeshire. The arrests were made this morning (September 29), during raids at 24 properties across Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire, London, Essex and Suffolk. More than 800 Met officers took part in the arrest operations. A Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "These arrests mark a significant point in this investigation. "Those arrested are suspected of leading or being involved at a senior level in serious and organised crime and related financial offending." The operation follows a months-long investigation by specialist Met detectives working with HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Officers from both agencies helped search the properties. The FCA has also disrupted seven firms and is pursuing a further 30 as part of the wider operation. A spokesperson for the FCA said: "Tackling financial crime requires the type of partnership shown by today’s joint action and the many months of close cooperation leading to it. "We’ll continue to work with the police and others to identify and disrupt organised crime groups who abuse our financial system to launder dirty money." Those arrested included a 65-year-old man suspected of taking part in an organised crime group, conspiracy to commit grievous bodily harm, money laundering and tax evasion. A 31-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of conspiring to commit GBH and taking part in an organised crime group. A 56-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of GBH over the stabbing of a police officer, as well as taking part in an organised crime group, money laundering, tax evasion, false accounting and failing to report suspected money laundering. Others were arrested on suspicion of money laundering, cheating the public revenue, false accounting and breaching anti-money-laundering rules. A spokesperson for HMRC said: "Today’s action highlights the importance of close collaboration between HMRC and other law enforcement partners in tackling serious and organised crime, including suspected money laundering and other criminal activity." An officer was stabbed in the leg while executing a warrant at a property in Cockfosters, Barnet, during the raids. Colleagues and paramedics treated him at the scene before he was taken to hospital with injuries that were not life-changing. The Met said: "We will ensure he gets all the support he needs." The force also warned that organised crime harms whole communities. A spokesperson said: "We know the impact of serious and organised crime stretches well beyond those at senior levels of the organisations involved. "Lines can often be drawn from the top, all the way to those involved in the criminality that blights communities, including serious violence and exploitation." Organised crime investigations are among the Met’s most complex operations, demanding time, resources and expertise from police and partner agencies. The spokesperson said: "We hope these arrests show how determined we are to ensure organised crime groups cannot operate freely in London. "We will work tirelessly to identify them, to gather evidence and to take action." Searches are continuing at several properties, with police warning of a visible presence in affected areas for days. Met, HMRC and FCA officers are continuing to gather evidence and build cases against those arrested.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire first in UK to pilot AI-powered crime reporting tool
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire has become the first place in the UK to pilot AI-powered crime reporting technology. Cambridgeshire Constabulary is trialling Citizen Assist, an artificial intelligence system that guides users through reporting non-urgent crimes via a conversational, text-based tool on the force’s website. The pilot launched on September 24 as part of a national scheme led by the National Police Chiefs' Council to improve digital public contact. Simon Megicks, chief constable of Cambridgeshire Constabulary, said: "This scheme is ultimately about utilising new technology to improve the service we can provide to the public, by developing and enhancing the reporting options already available to them. "As we move through an increasingly digital world, as a constabulary, we recognise the importance of embracing AI in a way that means we’re able to provide another, convenient way to report crime digitally." Citizen Assist is designed specifically for policing and supports the entire reporting process. It gathers information, builds a structured crime report, and submits it directly into police systems. Simon said: "Citizen Assist is a great opportunity to harness modern technology to help ensure crime reports reach us with accurate, high-quality information from the outset, benefiting both the public and the force. "Whilst the AI technology will help to collect and collate relevant information and turn it into a crime report, all decisions about the report will remain firmly with police staff and officers, just as it does with existing online crime reports." He emphasised that the technology is intended to supplement, not replace, existing reporting channels. Members of the public can now use Citizen Assist to report non-urgent crimes through the ‘report a crime’ section of the force’s website. Further details about the system and its use in Cambridgeshire are available on the Cambridgeshire Constabulary website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham announces VAT cut on energy bills 'from this Thursday' in keynote speech
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Andy Burnham has announced VAT will be removed from domestic energy bills from 'this Thursday', October 2026. The move, worth £850 million, is expected to save the average household around £45 a year, giving families extra help as colder weather approaches, and the energy price cap increases. At his first party conference speech since becoming Prime Minister, Mr Burnham said the Government wanted to provide immediate support for households facing ongoing cost-of-living pressures. From this Thursday, October 1 2026, VAT on domestic electricity bills will fall from 5% to 0%. The Government says energy suppliers are expected to pass the saving directly on to customers, including those on fixed tariffs. Officials estimate the measure will help millions of households from this week: While the exact saving will depend on individual energy use, the announcement is expected to provide welcome relief for millions of families heading into winter. The Government explained the moves in July, saying the measure will be funded by cancelling the previous digital ID programme and reprioritising existing departmental budgets, allowing households to benefit without introducing new taxes. Chancellor John Healey said this summer the announcement would provide reassurance for families while helping to tackle the cost of living: "For too long, too many people have struggled with the cost of living. "Today's energy tax cut will give families some breathing room on bills and provide reassurance this winter."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: East Anglia Clean & Green Awards judges reveal what makes a winning entry
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Businesses that are championing greener ways of working will be put in the spotlight at the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027. The Project of the Year and Sustainability Strategy Award categories will focus on the specific, measurable schemes that have made a substantial impact on the environment. Here, the judges for these categories tell us more about what they bring to the process. Paul Ager, divisional port manager, East Anglia at Associated British Ports, which sponsors the Project of the Year award (Image: ABP) Sponsored by Associated British Ports Sponsor judge: Paul Ager, divisional port manager, East Anglia, Associated British Ports Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? I joined ABP (Associated British Ports) in June 2016, having previously spent more than 14 years in leadership positions in logistics, supply chain and the construction sector. In June 2022, I joined the Suffolk Chamber of Commerce Board and I sit on the Suffolk Business Board, which allows me to contribute to the development of the region. Why were you keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards? As someone who was born and raised in Suffolk, I am passionate about supporting businesses that are investing in the region, creating opportunities and driving positive change. What do you bring to the judging process? My experience allows me to assess projects from both a strategic and practical perspective. I understand the challenges involved in taking a project from concept to completion, managing stakeholders and delivering measurable outcomes. Through ABP’s recent delivery of the Lowestoft Eastern Energy Facility, we’ve seen first-hand what it takes to deliver a complex infrastructure project that creates long-term value for both industry and the wider community. What will you be looking for in the winner? I will be looking for a project that has delivered clear and lasting benefits, whether that is for the environment, the economy, the community or a particular industry. The winner should be able to show how their project has made a meaningful difference and created value beyond its immediate objectives. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? Don’t underestimate the value of sharing your story. Many organisations deliver impressive projects but are often too modest about their achievements. Focus on clearly explaining the challenge you set out to address, what made your approach unique and the results you achieved. Why should those entering be able to demonstrate community and/or industry involvement? The most successful projects rarely happen in isolation. Strong projects create benefits that extend beyond a single organisation and often rely on effective collaboration with customers, suppliers, local communities, industry partners or public bodies. Demonstrating this shows that a project has generated wider value, built meaningful partnerships and delivered outcomes that others can learn from. Those qualities are often what turn a good project into a truly outstanding one. Johnathan Reynolds, managing director of Opergy Group, which sponsors the Sustainability Strategy Award (Image: Opergy) Sponsored by Opergy Group Sponsor judge: Johnathan Reynolds, managing director, Opergy Group Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? I have spent much of my career working across sustainable development, energy, infrastructure, innovation and skills. I advise businesses, public bodies and major projects on turning complex evidence and ambition into practical strategies, investment and delivery. Why were you keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards? East Anglia has a strong community of organisations doing serious, practical work on sustainability. I wanted to support an award that recognises that effort, shares good practice and gives businesses and organisations of different sizes a platform to demonstrate what they are achieving and learning. Have you ever been judged for an award yourself? Yes. I have experienced multiple awards processes from both entrant and judging perspectives, so I understand the work that sits behind a strong submission and the importance of a process that is rigorous, fair and focused on evidence rather than presentation alone. How will you use that experience when judging this award? I will focus on what sits behind the polished submission: the evidence, decisions, delivery and outcomes. Having experienced award processes myself, I know entrants often invest considerable effort in telling their story, so I will approach each submission carefully, consistently and with respect for what has actually been achieved. What will you be looking for in the winner? A clear, credible strategy that has moved into delivery and produced evidence of real change. I will be looking for strong leadership, measurable outcomes, collaboration and a willingness to tackle difficult trade-offs rather than simply present a perfect story. Why is it important for entrants to demonstrate the scalability of their strategy? Scalability shows that a strategy can create value beyond a single pilot, site or short-term initiative. That does not always mean becoming bigger; it can mean being repeatable, adaptable or capable of influencing others. We want to understand whether the approach can sustain momentum and deliver greater impact over time. The deadline for entries to the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards is Sunday, November 8 at midnight. For more information or to enter, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Red Arrows flying over Cambridgeshire this week — here's when and where to see them
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The famous Red Arrows are set to fly over Cambridgeshire this week — here's when and where you can see them. The jets will be appearing in the skies over the county on Friday (October 2), as they make a short 18-minute flight from RAF Waddington to RAF Mildenhall. They will take off from Lincolnshire at 1.47pm, fly south and enter Cambridgeshire around 1.56pm, north-west of Wisbech. The Red Arrows will fly south-west before turning south-east over Thorney, near Peterborough, at 1.58pm. A minute later, at 1.59pm, the seven jets will roar directly over Chatteris. They will fly over Mepal, Wilburton and Stretham around 2.01pm before heading east to RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk. The timings and route could change before Friday afternoon’s flight. It has been a turbulent year for the Red Arrows, after the RAF confirmed in May that their famous nine-jet formation would be cut to seven. The change was blamed on shortages of parts and engines for the ageing BAE Systems Hawk T1 jets, which have been used by the team since 1980 and are due to retire in 2030. The team was also stranded in Canada during July and August after displaying in the US for the country’s 250th anniversary celebrations. Prolonged bad weather prevented its return to the UK. All Hawk aircraft, including those used by the Red Arrows, were grounded last week after a training jet crashed in Wales. The RAF has now cleared them to fly again. Friday's flight will be one of the last chances to see the Red Arrows this year, with the jets displaying at IWM Duxford's Flying Finale on Saturday (October 3) as the UK airshow season wraps up for another year.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans have been submitted to turn a historic outbuilding beside a Grade I listed building into a five-bedroom home. Mick Hilless has applied to Huntingdonshire District Council to turn a barn and office building linked to Bodsey House into a home on Bodsey Toll Road, Ramsey. Bodsey House is Grade I listed, meaning it is of exceptional interest. The property was once a 13th-century hermitage belonging to Ramsey Abbey but has since been altered and turned into a family home. The plans would turn the barn and office building at the rear of the site into one five-bedroom home. The historic barn is curtilage listed, which means it is legally protected as it sits within the grounds of a listed building. Documents by Scroxton Architects say the barn and office building are dilapidated and no longer suitable for modern agricultural or commercial use. The plans would demolish the modern open-sided portal barn at the rear and replace it with a two-storey extension forming a five-bedroom home. The site is about 1.8km north-east of Ramsey and covers 0.2 hectares. The planning documents state: "The demolition of the unsightly, open-sided concrete portal barn and its replacement with the sensitive and subservient timber-clad proposal would significantly enhance the immediate setting, helping to restore the model-farm character of the historic farmstead. "By removing the non-historic modern portal barn and replacing it with a subservient, high-quality extension, the development secures the long-term visual preservation of the historic barn while significantly enhancing the setting of the Grade I listed Bodsey House." The plans also include three parking spaces, secure storage for five bicycles and new biodiversity-friendly landscaping. Access would remain through the existing entrance on Bodsey Toll Road. The applicant says in a heritage statement that the development would secure the historic buildings’ future while preserving the setting of the neighbouring listed property. Full details are available on the Huntingdonshire Planning Portal under reference 26/01763/FUL.

Mr Bristow said he had "lost faith" in the council and was seeking alternative providers if no deal could be reached. Huntingdonshire District Council strongly denied blocking the scheme. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs police officer dismissed and barred after gross misconduct
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire police officer has been dismissed without notice for dishonesty amounting to gross misconduct. The officer, referred to as PC A, was dismissed from Cambridgeshire Constabulary following an accelerated misconduct hearing held at Lysander House in Bedfordshire on September 21. PC A resigned on September 16 but was still a serving officer when the hearing took place. She denied all the allegations. The hearing centred on PC A’s links to Person B, her former partner, and his brother, Person C. Person C had previously been jailed for a serious offence. After becoming a police officer, PC A told Northamptonshire Police she had suffered domestic abuse and that Person B had forced her to hide the clothes Person C wore during the offence. In 2024, PC A told the chief constable she had ended all contact with Person B in 2019, apart from unwanted contact he initiated. She also denied ever having contact with Person C. However, phone records and evidence from Person B indicated that she had been in touch with both individuals. In his written decision, Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: "I find that she would have been aware that the Chief Constable would rely upon her truthfulness in retaining her in the Constabulary. "This included the importance of her providing a full and accurate account of contact with Persons B and C. "This was essential, given her knowledge as a police officer of the seriousness of Person C's criminal behaviour. "I find that she was aware that the accounts provided were not accurate. "In my view, this was not misremembering, as alleged by her, but the deliberate misleading of a senior police officer in a formal hearing. "I then applied the standards of ordinary decent members of the public, who in my view, would consider such conduct by PC A to be dishonest." The panel found that PC A had repeatedly misled the chief constable and the Professional Standards Department. The panel found that PC A’s actions amounted to gross misconduct and breached the honesty standards expected of officers. Aggravating factors included repeated dishonesty, conduct during formal investigations, and the personal gain involved in attempting to remain employed as a police officer. Limited weight was given to personal mitigation, despite PC A’s reported history of domestic abuse. Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: "In my view there was no mitigation for the misconduct. "Having carefully considered the difficult personal life and the impact on PC A, I am still minded to place limited reliance, in determining the appropriate sanction, on personal mitigation. "However it is my view such misconduct is at the upper end of seriousness, causing significant harm to confidence in the Constabulary." As well as dismissal without notice, PC A will be placed on the College of Policing’s public barred list. Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: “PC A deliberately misled investigators and senior officers during formal proceedings about her associations and contact with individuals linked to a serious crime matter. “Honesty is fundamental to policing. "When an officer fails to uphold those standards, it risks undermining public confidence in the police service. "The outcome reflects the seriousness with which we treat such conduct.”

It revisits a site first uncovered in the 1970s during water pipeline work, which revealed a Roman villa and evidence of industrial activity, including furnaces, tiled floors, painted walls, and metalworking. Participant with find (Image: Nene Valley) Harriet Tatton, Senior Project Officer for Project Development at DigVentures, said: "This area has such a rich history of industry and trade, and we’re excited to investigate this villa site to see what fresh discoveries we can uncover about Roman life here. The 1970s excavation did not reveal the full extent of the villa complex, leaving many questions about its residents and role in the wider Nene Valley. Pottery (Image: Nene Valley) The region was a major centre of Roman production, transport, and trade, with sites like Durobrivae (near modern-day Water Newton) forming part of an extensive network of villa estates, pottery kilns, and ironworking facilities. DigVentures will conduct a two-week excavation to help uncover more of the site’s layout, including the villa itself, nearby buildings, and other areas of activity. Councillor Edna Murphy, chair of Cambridgeshire County Council’s children and young people’s committee, said: "Every child deserves the security, love and sense of belonging that comes from having a permanent family. "Unfortunately, there are still too many children waiting for adoptive families, and every extra day they wait is a day without the stability they need." The Every Day is Everything campaign highlights the need for more adoptive families and stresses that children need love, stability and commitment. Over the past year, children placed for adoption through the service were aged two years and six months on average and waited 17 months for a family. Cllr Murphy said: "We want people who may have considered adoption in the past to know that they do not need to have a perfect home, perfect finances, or all the answers. "What matters most is your ability to offer a child love, stability, and a lifelong commitment." The adoption service supports families from their first enquiry through approval, matching, placement and beyond. Throughout September, the service will share adoption information and adoptive families’ experiences on social media. People interested in adoption can email adoptionenquiries@cambridgeshire.gov.uk, call 0300 123 1093 or visit www.cpadoption.co.uk.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire hospitals to introduce shared electronic patient record system
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridge University Hospitals (CUH) and Royal Papworth Hospital are joining forces to introduce a shared electronic patient record (EPR) system. The system will improve care across the Cambridge Biomedical Campus and beyond by helping the two NHS trusts share information and avoid duplication. Harvey McEnroe, Royal Papworth Hospital’s chief operating officer and senior responsible officer for the EPR programme, said: "This is a huge step forward for our organisations and the patients we serve. The partnership aims to support more joined-up patient care (Image: Royal Papworth Hospital) "We are grateful to NHS England, our integrated care board and all our partners for their support and collaboration in helping make our ambitions to create a shared electronic patient record a reality." The EPR will use CUH’s Epic system, which has been in place since 2014, through the Epic Connect model. The model has already been used elsewhere in the UK to link neighbouring hospitals more closely. The rollout is expected to take just over a year and will involve both trusts and Epic Systems Corporation. Royal Papworth Hospital (Image: Royal Papworth Hospital) Harvey said: "This clinically led decision will transform the way we deliver care, strengthen collaboration between our hospitals, and enhance our research capabilities, benefiting patients and staff for years to come." Patients will get more joined-up care, with clinical teams able to see their complete information in one place. It should mean patients repeat themselves less and move more smoothly between services. Royal Papworth Hospital and Cambridge University Hospitals are working together (Image: Royal Papworth Hospital) Dr Sue Broster, chief medical officer at Cambridge University Hospitals, said: "This important development will improve the experience of patients receiving care across our two hospitals. "By bringing information together securely in one place, it will support smoother transitions, reduce duplication and help us achieve our aim of patients only having to tell their story once. "It will also help ensure that care remains consistent and is delivered at the right time." The partnership comes as GSK plans a £400 million global research and development centre on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, with around 1,000 scientists expected at the site by 2029.

The nursery encourages visitors to walk, cycle, or take the bus to the event due to limited parking. The community plant nursery is powered almost entirely by volunteers and has established itself as an integral part of the Godmanchester community, not only as a plant nursery but also as a place people can visit for free to enjoy nature. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A deaf rescue dog is capturing hearts at Block Fen Animal Centre in Cambridgeshire. Six-year-old Eddie, a bull breed, was rescued by RSPCA officers and police from unsuitable living conditions having been left behind in a property, in County Durham, when his owners moved out. He was taken in by the RSPCA’s Block Fen Animal Centre earlier this summer, where staff soon discovered he was deaf. Tiffany Fowler, kennel supervisor at Block Fen, said: "We believe Eddie was born deaf and he copes very well without his hearing. "In fact, we often forget that he’s deaf. "We all chat away to him and if he’s looking at us he’ll wag his tail and get excited; it’s like he can lip-read and knows we’re speaking to him." Deaf dog Eddie (Image: RSPCA) Staff believe Eddie could learn sign language and respond well to visual commands. Despite his hearing loss, Eddie has settled comfortably into kennel life. Ms Fowler said: "When we arrive in the mornings and go to say ‘good morning’ to all of the dogs, who are all barking and wagging their tails at their doors, Eddie is usually fast asleep, snoring in his bed. "He doesn’t get stressed by the noise and the other dogs, and this can be tough for some dogs. "We go into his kennel and give him a gentle stroke to wake him up and let him know that we’re there, so we don’t startle him and make him jump." Eddie has been enjoying spending time with the reception team at the animal centre, welcoming visitors to Block Fen. Ms Fowler said: "Eddie is one of those dogs who has a gift for making people smile. "He is incredibly friendly, affectionate and adores being around people." The RSPCA hopes to find Eddie a patient and caring home with someone who can continue his training and help him adjust to a new life.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council has revealed why a crematorium in Cambridgeshire was evacuated just weeks after it first opened to the public. Firefighters from Ely and March were called to Lake View Bereavement Centre on Chatteris Road, in Mepal, at 9.52am on Friday (September 25). Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service confirmed crews arrived "to find smoke issuing from a building". "They cleared the smoke using a positive pressure ventilation fan and left the building with the site management team," a spokesperson said. East Cambridgeshire District Council has since confirmed the electric cremator is undergoing a "period of testing during the commissioning process". The spokesperson added: "On Friday morning, one of these tests caused an increased level of smoke to be emitted," the local authority said in a statement. "Two fire crews attended as a precaution. "There was no fire or any damage caused, and the matter was resolved within an hour with no further actions to be taken." They added: "We would like to assure residents that no public services were impacted during this testing process, and other services will continue as normal." The county's newest crematorium opened its doors with a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by nearly 200 guests on September 10. The £13million facility stands on the former Mepal Outdoor Centre, which lay derelict for years. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fast food chain given permission to extend opening hours
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A popular fast food chain has been given permission to extend its opening hours despite fears it may increase littering. KFC in St Neots applied to increase its closing time from 2am until 5am and to open an hour earlier from 9am instead of 10am. A resident objected to the longer opening hours for the chicken shop on Great North Road as they were “fearful that this may lead to a rise in anti-social behaviour”. They also raised concerns about littering which they said was “often quite evident” along the road heading into Eaton Socon. They said customers “may not bother taking their rubbish home with them and either dump it on the path, or, worse, simply dispose of it into people’s properties”. KFC had agreed to pick up litter within a 100m radius of the fast food shop but the objector said this “may not be enough” and asked for it to be extended further up the road. Huntingdonshire District Council’s licensing officer said that KFC didn’t consider this to be “reasonable or proportionate” and could lead to safety risks. They said patrols during the late evening and early morning “would require staff to leave the immediate vicinity” of the store and raise “welfare and safety considerations”. The officer added that there “is a limit to the level of control that any business can reasonably exercise over customers once they have left the premises”. The council’s licensing sub-committee granted KFC the extended licence with conditions to prevent noise and disturbance to neighbours. Customers won’t be allowed to use the outside seating areas after 11pm and four bins will be provided in the car park and regularly emptied.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Lorry driver killed 'loving family man' in horror motorway crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A lorry driver who killed a "loving family man" after ploughing into the back of his van on a busy Cambridgeshire motorway has been jailed. Misroslaw Muszynski, 69, failed to notice Gary Porritt, 43, had slowed for traffic in his Ford Transit Van. The horror crash occurred on the southbound carriageway of the M11, near junction 10 for Duxford, at about 12.15pm on June 12. Muszynski's HGV pushed the van into the back of another HGV, causing fatal injuries to Mr Porritt. Mr Porritt, of Exchange Square, Stockton-On-Tees, Teesside, who had been driving to a fishing trip with friends, was pronounced dead at the scene. Muszynski remained at the scene and passed breath, drugs, field impairment, and eyesight tests before being arrested. On Tuesday (September 22), at Huntingdon Law Courts, Muszynski, of Priory Road, Dartford, Kent, was jailed for three years and four months. He pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving. He was also banned from driving for six years and eight months. In a tribute, Gary's family described him as a "loving family man" (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) DC Kevin Drury said: "Gary Porritt should have been enjoying a fishing trip, but Musyznski's driving meant his life was tragically cut short. "The sentence reflects the seriousness of the offence and the devastating impact it has had on those who knew and loved Gary. "No prison sentence can undo the harm that has been caused, but we hope the outcome of these proceedings provides some measure of closure for his family. "We would urge all drivers, particularly those operating large vehicles, to recognise the immense responsibility they bear every time they get behind the wheel. "Preventable collisions continue to cost lives and cause lasting heartbreak." In a tribute, Mr Porritt’s family said: "Gary was a loving family man, a devoted partner to Claire and a great friend to many. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Millions of pensioners could be owed money after HMRC mistake
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of pensioners are set to receive tax refunds after an HMRC calculation error left them paying too much tax on their state pension. Around 3.2 million pensioners are affected, with repayments expected to total around £19.3 million. That works out at roughly £6 per person on average, although the amount each pensioner receives will vary. The error relates to the way HMRC calculated annual state pension income when working out how much tax was due. Tax specialist Andy Wood from Tax Barrister UK said the mistake could have been difficult for pensioners to spot - and warned that those affected need clear information about exactly which years have been checked. The problem concerns the pension income figure used in HMRC's tax calculations. Normally, where the state pension increases during the tax year, the annual figure should include one week at the previous pension rate and 51 weeks at the increased rate. However, some calculations instead used the higher pension rate for all 52 weeks. This meant the annual pension income figure was overstated, potentially resulting in too much tax being collected. Andy Wood said: “An error like this can be difficult for someone to spot because the pension figure used in their tax calculation may look perfectly plausible. “The difference between the two calculations might appear small, but accuracy matters. Pensioners should be able to trust that the income figure used to work out their tax is correct.” The HMRC correction exercise covers affected cases from the 2020/21 tax year onwards. Pensioners do not generally need to apply for the correction. Repayments will be dealt with automatically through PAYE adjustments, Self Assessment credits or other payment methods, where appropriate. Andy said automatic corrections should make the process easier for people who had no reason to realise something had gone wrong. He said: “Automatic corrections are welcome because they reduce the burden on people who may have had no reason to suspect an error. “However, the explanation accompanying a correction is just as important. People need to understand which tax years have been reviewed, how their repayment was calculated and whether anything remains outstanding. “The headline total should also be put into context. This is a correction of tax overpaid, so individuals should not assume they are all entitled to the same amount.” One important point is that the automatic correction does not cover tax years before 2020/21. HMRC does not hold sufficient data to correct those cases automatically. However, people who believe they may have been affected in an earlier year can request an individual review and provide supporting evidence. That means pensioners should not necessarily assume that an automatic repayment means every possible overpayment has been dealt with. Andy said: “The position for earlier years deserves particular clarity. Someone receiving an automatic correction could reasonably assume that every affected year has been addressed. “HMRC needs to make the boundaries of this exercise clear, including what evidence it would consider for an earlier period. That would help pensioners understand what has been resolved and where further questions may remain.”

Nicholas Lyes, director of policy and standards at IAM RoadSmart, said: "Ignoring a red X sign on a smart motorway is dangerous because it risks a serious collision and, for this reason, we welcome police forces clamping down on those who break the law. "The majority of drivers have serious reservations about the safety of smart motorways where the hard shoulder has been removed, and these figures are unlikely to persuade them they are safe." National Highways staff activate the red X signs when a stopped vehicle is detected in a live lane, to prevent collisions and protect emergency responders. Mr Lyes added: "We know that no new all-lane running smart motorways will be built but it does beg the question of what we do with the existing stretches that are in operation? "This is something the new Government needs to give some serious thought to." A spokesperson for National Highways said: "A Red X signal is there to increase the safety of everyone using the road by highlighting an issue ahead. "Above 90% of drivers observe Red X signals, but ignoring Red X signals is an offence and puts themselves and others at risk." Speed cameras work using radar or road markings to monitor a vehicle’s speed and capture evidence of any offence. While older cameras used film, most modern devices are fully digital and can even track your average speed over many miles. These digital systems record: In some cases, they even capture a clear image of the driver and passenger. Contrary to common belief, there’s no universal “10% + 2mph” rule baked into law. Experts from BigWantsYourCar.com explained: ““The idea that you’re safe doing 35mph in a 30 zone is one of the biggest myths we hear. “Technically, you’re liable for a fine the moment you go even 1mph over the limit.” While the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) does recommend a “10% plus 2” margin to allow for officer discretion, this is not a legal threshold and can vary depending on the enforcement area or the officer reviewing the case. RAC advice adds: “The law states that you are liable for a speeding fine as soon as you exceed the limit, so if you’re doing 31mph in a 30 limit or 71mph on a motorway, you’re breaking the law and could receive a fine. “It is well worth remembering this is totally dependent on the officer who catches the speeder, and it is up to that officer whether to fine the offender or not. “The best advice is to not speed full stop.” Here are some other common speed camera myths: No. There are no laws about visibility, so nothing is stopping an officer from operating in the dark. But they don't often choose to do this and maintain that being visible acts as a deterrent in its own right. Go Safe Casualty Reduction Officer, Gareth Thomas said: "Legally, we don't have to be visible. I could camouflage myself if I wanted to - but it's all about being fair, education and preventing an accident. Even if I parked my van and went for a walk somewhere, it would deter people from speeding right away." If drivers choose to flash to warn others about a speed van, they could be in breach of the law. Under section 89 of the Police Act 1997 it is an offence to "wilfully obstruct a constable in the execution of his/her duty". However, Gareth says while it is an offence, it is very difficult to prove. He said: "It doesn't bother me that people flash to warn them of the speed van - I just want to educate people and the van to act as a speed deterrent." It all comes down to the circumstances within which you were caught speeding, and how much you were more than the limit. The minimum penalty for being caught speeding on the UK's roads is a £100 fine. But Gareth explained in some circumstances, police can offer the option of attending a speed awareness course - an alternative to a fine and penalty points. Gareth, said: "An accredited course is far more likely to improve driver behaviour and consequently make our roads safer. So for example, anyone travelling over 86mph on a motorway would not be offered the awareness course. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New dig to start at Cambridgeshire Bronze Age site with £700,000 of funding
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Archaeologists will begin a new dig at one of Britain’s most important Bronze Age sites in Cambridgeshire next year. The dig, at Flag Fen near Peterborough, must begin before information preserved in peat is lost as the ground dries out amid climate change. The timber causeway at the site was 1.1 km long, about 20 metres wide, and had about 22,000 posts, Mark Knight of Cambridge Archaeological Unit said. It was thought to have played a role in communication and trade, connecting two pieces of dry land over an area that got wet around 3,300 years ago, he said. Mr Knight, who will be excavation director on the new dig, said information was preserved in wet peat without oxygen for thousands of years but the hotter climate is drying the peat out. He said that a section of the causeway that was “a bit closer to the surface” is “drying out a little bit quicker”. “If we don’t excavate it in the next couple of years it will be gone forever so we will lose all of that information,” he said. Jacqui Mooney, general manager at Flag Fen Archaeology Park, said she was also concerned by a peatland fire that broke out at Holme Fen, around 11 miles from Flag Fen, during drought conditions last month. A blaze broke out at Holme Fen this summer (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue) “We’re on the peat, peat will burn and it will take a lot to put the peat out,” she said. “We absolutely don’t want that to happen here on such a significant landscape.” The area of destruction at Holme Fen covered 60 football pitches in total (Image: Emily Stevens) The six-month dig at Flag Fen, to begin next year, has received £700,000 in grant funding through the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service, Defra’s partnership with Historic England. Mr Knight said the excavation would be the “biggest area that’s ever been opened over the monument”. “We’re doing that because we want to gain pattern, we want to see it for what it is,” he said. “There’s been 40 years of investigation on this site but it tends to be keyhole, it tends to be small holes looking at small parts. “We think the way to really understand it is to see it on a scale that’s commensurate with the feature itself.” He said past interpretations of the causeway included that it was a “ritual monument, a place where you go and deposit metalwork or the dead”. “It’s also about communication, about trade, movement of people and animals, and it’s about a route that was once there back in the day before water levels rose and now, with water levels rising, they’ve been cut off so it’s about re-establishing that,” he said. “What’s really impressive is that our monument has at least 400 years of different iterations or different repairs and builds. “It’s got duration and longevity.” Flag Fen has been on Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register since 2012. Few Bronze Age platform structures survive anywhere in the world, and Flag Fen’s scale, complexity and completeness make it nationally significant. Farming Minister Stephen Morgan said: “Flag Fen has survived for thousands of years and it really demonstrates an extraordinary window into Bronze Age Britain. “We’re so pleased to be investing in this important community project.” The excavation project will offer volunteering opportunities, with volunteers being given training to become supervisors and tour leaders.
