A council has approved plans for new homes despite fears from residents of increased sewage spills in a village already suffering from the worst spills in the area. Huntingdonshire District Council’s development management committee met to decide an outline plan for up to 70 homes on land south of Blenheim Grove in Offord D’Arcy. Offord Cluny and Offord Darcy Parish Council had objected to the plans as they said wastewater treatment plants were already suffering from “capacity problems”. Simon Young, a parish councillor, said figures from the Environment Agency show that Buckden has an average of 116 raw sewage discharges per year. He said this is 66 per cent higher than the second on the list – Kimbolton at 70 – and four times higher than the average across Huntingdonshire. He said the villages have “long-been a supporter” of “appropriate developments” but that Anglian Water’s infrastructure is “not fit for purpose”. Anglian Water originally objected to the application in 2025, but this was because the applicant had not identified a suitable connection point to their network. After two connection points were suggested, they removed their objection. They had always said there was “sufficient capacity” at the nearby Buckden Water Recycling Centre to accommodate the new homes after assessing dry weather flow. Cllr Young said: “The Buckden Works was discharging raw sewage on August 13, when we all know there’d been no rain for weeks. And the ten hours of discharges in June came after recent light rain – or almost no rain for days. As far as I’m aware, Buckden and the Offords do not have their own microclimate such that it rains more here.” Cllr Julie Kerr, of St Ives West, said she was “very concerned” by the “high numbers of spillages”. The independent councillor said: “There really shouldn’t have been any and you have a very poor network by the sounds of it in a village that’s already struggling.” Council officers advised that it would be “very difficult” to go against the advice of Anglian Water as they do not have the “technical expertise” to be able to defend their decision on appeal. Cllr Tom Sanderson, of The Stukeleys, said they would not be able to use their decision to “deal with an existing issue”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “Particularly as Anglian Water haven’t raised an objection now, they withdrew the objection they did have, I think it would be very difficult for us to object on that basis.” Cllr Lara Davenport-Ray said she felt the benefits of the scheme did not outweigh the harms. The Green councillor said: “If Anglian Water is saying that they have capacity and that there is no problem, then there is no condition that we can word to mitigate a problem that on paper doesn’t exist. Our officers cannot identify harm because they haven’t been shown that there is any harm that’s been created because their experts have failed to do so, but we can.” The committee first reached an impasse with five votes for and against the application and three abstentions – but it was approved on the second attempt with six for, four against and three abstentions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs Chamber of Commerce urges Chancellor to tackle barriers to business growth
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Connor Butler, engagement manager for the Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, writes his first column Across the region, businesses are not short of ambition. They want to recruit, invest, innovate, expand and trade. But too often, that ambition is being held back by things outside their control: infrastructure constraints, skills shortages, rising employment costs and an increasingly difficult investment environment. That is the message we have taken to the Chancellor ahead of the Autumn Budget. Our region has an extraordinary economic opportunity. We sit between the science and innovation strengths of the Oxford-Cambridge corridor and the manufacturing, energy, agri-food, logistics and international trade strengths of the wider East of England. But potential alone does not deliver growth. We need action. That means progressing Ely-Haughley and the transport links that connect businesses to people and markets. It means ensuring skills funding responds to what employers actually need. It means securing the water, power and wider infrastructure required for businesses to invest and expand. And it means recognising that higher National Insurance, energy bills and business rates all influence decisions about recruitment and investment. We also need to make Britain a place where entrepreneurs want to start, scale and keep their businesses, and where more SMEs have the confidence and support to trade internationally. This is not about asking Government to create growth itself. It is about making targeted decisions that unlock far greater private investment. The question I hope the Chancellor asks of every Budget measure is simple: will this make it easier for businesses to employ, invest, scale and trade?

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire fire service warns damaged or propped-open doors put lives at risk
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Damaged or propped-open fire doors could put lives at risk, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service has warned. The service is urging businesses and building managers across Cambridgeshire to check their fire doors during Fire Door Safety Week and ensure they are correctly installed, maintained and used. Station Commander Vinnie Crook, one of the service’s fire protection managers, said: "Having effective fire doors and checking them regularly are vital for business premises. "The difference it can make in an emergency cannot be underestimated. "Yet we often find that they are neglected and not maintained properly, putting premises and staff at risk." Fire door breaches remain one of the most common reasons for fines under the Fire Safety Order, with problems including wedged-open, missing or damaged doors and non-fire doors installed in their place. The fire service has launched an animated video showing building users what to check and how to record it. Mr Crook said: "Our new animation gives business owners a short guide to what to check and how to record it, as these records will be requested during a fire safety audit." He stressed that fire doors compartmentalise buildings and slow the spread of fire and smoke, giving people more time to escape and firefighters more time to act. The service recommends checking for certification labels, gaps of less than 4mm, damaged seals or hinges, and a door that closes properly onto the latch. Anyone who notices a damaged fire door, or a flat entrance door that hasn’t been checked for fire performance, is advised to report it to the building manager or landlord immediately. More guidance and resources are available from Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New St Neots feature uses stone believed to be from original Priory Abbey
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Saint Anselm feature has been installed in St Neots. Designed to resemble a well, it recalls a miracle attributed to Saint Neot involving fish and a well. The capstone bears an image of Saint Anselm, the former Archbishop of Canterbury who was born in Aosta, Italy. The saint is shown with enlarged hands, a Greek tradition intended to convey symbolic meaning when few people could read. His right hand represents benediction, while the book in his left signifies scholasticism and piety. The capstone is made from Welsh granite, similar to stone used in early medieval churches in the Fawton area of Cornwall and at Glastonbury Abbey, where Neot served as sacristan. The artwork is located where there was once a river inlet to the Priory of Saint Neot (Image: Priory of Saint Neot) The circular well is clad in Barnack Ragstone, quarried near Peterborough. The ragstone cladding, believed to have been part of the original Priory Abbey of Saint Neot, was retrieved from an archaeological dig in St Neots. The feature stands on a green where a river inlet and boathouse may once have stood in the Priory grounds. Saint Anselm’s endorsement helped establish St Neots as a major centre of pilgrimage and royal patronage for the next 500 years. An archaeological evaluation beneath the Priory Centre found medieval pottery and charcoal suggesting the site may have been an open ditch or watercourse, alongside evidence of human activity possibly associated with the priory.

A spokesman for the Food Standards Agency warned: “The presence of salmonella in the products listed above. “Symptoms caused by salmonella usually include fever, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps. Thursday 24 September. World of Sweets recalls Alyan Dubai Style Crunchy Knafeh and Alyan Dubai Style Chocolate Truffles due to Salmonella #FoodAlert https://t.co/33mYrJ39WO pic.twitter.com/tMepY2BHD5 — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) September 24, 2026 “If you are experiencing these symptoms, you should stay away from work, school or nursery until you have stopped having symptoms for at least 48 hours to avoid passing it on to others. “World of Sweets is recalling the above products. The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. "This anniversary celebration is an opportunity to recognise everyone who has been part of our journey, while looking ahead to the future and the growing need for community support across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough." The charity supports people through three services: Help at Home, RISE (Resilience, Intervention, Support and Empowerment) and Community Support. Its work tackles social isolation, builds confidence and connects people to services and transport. Care Network supported 2,479 people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough in 2025, many facing loneliness, poor mental health or other challenges. The charity’s results show its impact: 90 per cent of clients reported greater independence and 94 per cent felt less isolated. A further 89 per cent said they felt less lonely, while up to 62 per cent said the support helped them avoid NHS services. Referrals to the RISE wellbeing service rose 21 per cent in 2025. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 28 per cent of Year 6 children in Cambridgeshire's poorest areas have obesity
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Obesity rates remain a major health challenge despite ongoing efforts to improve public health across Cambridgeshire. Members of the Adults and Health Committee at Cambridgeshire County Council met on Thursday, September 17, to review progress on reducing obesity and creating healthier environments for residents. Councillor Luis Navarro, vice chair of the committee, said: "Obesity remains one of the most significant public health challenges facing our communities, affecting people's health, wellbeing and quality of life. "While progress is being made, there is still much more to do, particularly to address the inequalities that mean some communities experience poorer health outcomes than others. "By working together through the Strategic Obesity Framework and Obesity Charter, we can help more people eat well, stay active and live independently, supporting our ambition to enable full, healthy lives for all in Cambridgeshire." The committee heard that childhood obesity rates, which rose during the pandemic, have now returned to pre-pandemic levels but remain high and have since stagnated. Data from the 2024/25 National Child Measurement Programme shows that 7.7 per cent of children in Reception and 17.2 per cent of children in Year 6 in Cambridgeshire are living with obesity. Rates are higher in areas of deprivation, with 28 per cent of Year 6 children in the most deprived areas affected compared to just 13.2 per cent in the least deprived. Obesity rates also remain above average in Fenland. The council is delivering its Strategic Obesity Framework in partnership with NHS organisations, schools, district councils and community groups. Efforts focus on improving access to healthy food, increasing physical activity, and addressing broader social and economic factors that contribute to obesity. The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Obesity Charter brings organisations together with a shared goal of making healthy weight the norm across the region.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Jail for uninsured driver who fled Cambs crash scene after killing pedestrian
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A uninsured driver from Cambridgeshire who fled the scene after hitting and killing a pedestrian has been jailed. Marcin Pilarski, 36, struck Sam Pope, 28, as he walked alongside Oil Mills Road, Ramsey Mereside, at just before 11pm on May 11, 2024. The crash was only reported when another driver called 999 after seeing Mr Pope, of Lincoln Road, Peterborough, laying in the road. Emergency services attended but despite their efforts, Mr Pope was declared dead at the scene. In a tribute, his family said: "Sam was a free spirit, who liked to live his life at 100mph and believed that rules were meant to be broken. "We shall miss his smile and crazy sense of humour that would always make you laugh, despite what mood you were in that day. "Sam was a rough diamond with a heart made of gold and will leave a big hole in our lives." Sam Pope was struck as he walked alongside Oil Mills Road (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Less than an hour after the collision, at 11.40pm, police were called by Pilarski’s partner who told them he had returned home in her Vauxhall Astra. She revealed the car was badly damaged, with a smashed windscreen and headlamp, and that there was also blood on the front of the vehicle. The woman said that they lived 15 minutes, about nine and a half miles, from the scene of the fatal crash. Police visited the house where they also noticed the damage to the car, and Pilarski, of Sorrell Avenue, Whittlesey, was arrested in relation to the fatal collision. In a statement, Pilarski’s partner said he had called her at 11pm to tell her he had “hit or killed somebody” who had been in the road, but she had to end the call due to him screaming. She said when he returned home in her damaged car she told him they needed to call the police and he answered, “I know”. In police interview Pilarski answered no comment to most questions. However, he later pleaded guilty to causing death by driving a car without a licence or insurance. He was sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on Thursday (September 17). He was handed one year and three months in prison. He was also disqualified from driving for four years and six months. The car was badly damaged, with a smashed windscreen and headlamp, and had blood on the front (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) In a victim impact statement, Mr Pope’s family said they had been left feeling angry that Pilarski didn’t seem remorseful and hadn’t apologised for his actions. The statement added: “We hope the memory of the night keeps him up at night like it does us. I don’t really know how as a family we will ever come to terms with this.” Detective Inspector Craig Wheeler, who investigated, said: “Pilarski made a conscious decision to drive his partner’s car without a licence or insurance. “He should never have put himself behind the wheel of a car and my thoughts and sympathies remain with the family and friends of Mr Pope, who needlessly lost his life at such a young age. “No sentence will ever ease the pain of their loss, but I hope the case acts as a stark reminder against getting behind the wheel while uninsured or without a licence. Just one journey could end in tragedy.” Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A 16-year-old Cambridgeshire girl died from a head injury after the car she was travelling in crashed into a river, an inquest heard today. Four members of Eden Bunn’s family attended the inquest into the horse-loving teenager’s death at Vantage House, Huntingdon. The inquest heard Eden, from Sutton Bridge, was sitting in the middle of the rear seat of a Volkswagen Polo driven by Declan Berry when it ended up in the River Nene at Wisbech on March 17. Eden Bunn loved her horses. (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Ms Gray heard evidence from a collision report prepared by police accident investigators. The report said Mr Berry, 18, was driving the Polo at about 90mph on North Brink, Wisbech, at around 8.19pm when it hit a pothole, left the road, rolled several times and plunged into the fast-flowing river. Three other teenagers, all aged 18, were in the car with Eden and Mr Berry. Mr Berry also died, and his body was recovered from the river at Wisbech Marian nearly two weeks later. Read more 'Excessive speed' and potholes blamed for fatal Wisbech river crash inquest told Families pay tribute to young girl and 18-year-old man involved in river crash Help wanted to clear debris at town harbour in search for missing Cambs teen 'Excessive speed' and potholes blamed for fatal Wisbech river crash inquest told 'Predator' raped woman in horrific late-night attack near filling station The many floral tributes that were left by the River Nene in Wisbech after the fatal crash that claimed the life of Eden Bunn. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Three of the passengers escaped the submerged car, but Eden did not get out. Her body was recovered the following day. A post-mortem found that Eden’s severe head injury was the primary cause of death. Ms Gray said there was no evidence of water in her lungs. The collision report blamed the car’s speed but said the road’s potholes, crumbling edges, undulating, and uneven surface also played a “less than minimal” part in the crash. Declan Berry had been driving the VW Polo in which Eden was a passenger. (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) The three surviving passengers said Mr Berry was driving fast and that the front-seat passenger told him to slow down moments before the crash after noting he was doing 90mph. A female rear-seat passenger said Eden also shouted “Declan” just before Mr Berry lost control. The witnesses said Mr Berry shouted “oh shit” after the car hit a pothole and left the road. A nearby resident who witnessed the crash said he saw the headlights and rear lights “rotating through the air” but could not tell how they were rotating. He helped pull the survivors from the water, then searched the bank for the two missing occupants before emergency services arrived. Ms Gray said Cambridgeshire Highways had received 127 complaints about the road and that a survey four days before the crash found 98 potholes along North Brink. One near the crash site measured a quarter of the road’s width. The road was due to be repaired within 21 days, but the crash happened first. Highway workers filled the potholes the next day while the road was closed due to the incident. Ms Gray recorded a conclusion that Eden died in a road traffic accident, stating excessive speed was the main cause of the crash, and that the poor road surface had made more than a "minimal contribution" to the crash. She offered her condolences to Eden’s family members who were present: two aunts, an uncle and a cousin. Eden’s parents did not attend. An inquest into Declan Berry's death was heard yesterday.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Family describes horrific reality after teen's tragic death in Cambs river crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The family of a teenage girl killed in a river crash at Wisbech earlier this year have described the “horrific reality” they now face after an inquest into her death. The hearing held today in Huntingdon heard that Eden Bunn, 16 and from Sutton Bridge, died as a result of a severe head injury suffered in the accident which happened on North Brink on March 17. Eden’s father Dean, mother Lisa, brother Jay and sister Shelby released the following statement after the inquest. “Eden was the kindest, most wonderful person and to have her snatched away from us so suddenly has left us heartbroken. "She was a beautiful soul and had such a love of life. No words can describe the devastation we feel and we will never get over losing her. "Nothing will bring Eden back and her death is a horrific reality we will have to live with forever.” Sarah Townsend, a personal injury lawyer at Hodge Jones & Allen who represents the family, said: “Eden’s passing has understandably left her family inconsolable with grief and struggling to cope. "What is most tragic is that it was entirely avoidable and should serve as a warning to young drivers to not drive recklessly and put others at risk. "I hope that now the inquest process has concluded Eden’s family can slowly start to rebuild their lives.” The inquest heard that Eden was a rear seat passenger in a car driven by 18-year-old Declan Berry, from Wisbech, who also died in the accident, which was blamed on excessive speed, with potholes in the road a contributory factor. Another passenger in the car had told police the VW Polo had been going 90mph moments before the crash, which saw the vehicle leave the carriageway, roll down an embankment, before being fully submerged in the River Nene.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Six people complete 24-hour St Neots fitness challenge with 10,000 burpees
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Six people completed a gruelling 24-hour fitness challenge in St Neots. The challenge, set by outdoor fitness group ABSolute Storm Fitness (Abstorm), included 25 back-to-back bootcamp sessions, 10,000 burpees, and a spin bike that ran non-stop for the full 24 hours. The event raised money for Ehlers-Danlos Support UK, Children’s Burns Camps and Parkinson’s UK. Abstorm founder and head coach Abi Black led all 25 sessions and oversaw the 10,000 burpees. Members of ABSolute Storm Fitness (Abstorm) who took part in the charity bootcamp (Image: Andy Clifton) Ms Black said: "We did it. "24 hours of bootcamps. "What a whirlwind of laughter and craziness, and so many memories. "I'm completely broken, but immensely proud. "This was our third year, our biggest year, and seeing six of our members pull off the full 24 hours non-stop is just unbelievable. "Abstorm isn't just a fitness group; we are a family and a core part of this community. "A massive thank you goes out to every single member who turned up to support, every person who jumped into a session, and everyone who has donated so far. "If you haven’t, please help us get to our total." Members of ABSolute Storm Fitness (Abstorm) who took part in the charity bootcamp (Image: Andy Clifton) The six participants, averaging 56, completed the entire challenge. The six were Ursula, 59, a Slimming World consultant; Ian, 57, a driving instructor; Nadine, 46, an environmental health officer; Sarah, 58, a geospatial analyst; Neil, 59, an aerospace and defence project manager; and Shaz, 58, a police force communications centre lead. They are the largest group to complete the full 24-hour challenge since the event began. Abstorm is aiming to raise a record £10,000 for the charities. Members of ABSolute Storm Fitness (Abstorm) who took part in the charity bootcamp (Image: Andy Clifton) The group promotes outdoor fitness in St Neots and nearby areas and welcomes members of all fitness levels. Sessions are held at Priory Park in St Neots and The Green in Brampton. The group's 2025 event raised more than £8,000—well above its £5,000 target—with support from more than 70 people who took part throughout the night.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs paedophile found with hundreds of indecent images claimed he was 'lonely'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A paedophile from Cambridgeshire who messaged people he believed were children and arranged to meet them has been jailed. Timothy Pavitt, 73, was brought to police attention after he uploaded indecent images of children to a Kik account in 2024. Officers were able to trace the IP address of the account, which led them to Pavitt’s home in Boxworth End, Swavesey. He was arrested on February 19, 2025, and claimed in interview to be “lonely” and using chat sites to speak to children and download images. A review of his devices found he had been speaking in a sexual manner with users he believed to be children and arranging to meet up with them. The devices also contained more than 350 indecent images. The identities of the people he was messaging have never been confirmed. Pavitt was jailed for four years and eight months at Peterborough Crown Court on Monday September 21. He had previously admitted to 18 counts, including communicating sexually with children and making indecent images. He was also handed an indefinite sexual harm prevention order (SHPO). Det Sgt Zip Lloyd said: "Pavitt knew what he was doing was wrong but continued to seek out users he believed were children, encourage sexual conversations and make indecent images. "He was also actively sharing those images for others to view, further fuelling the exploitation of children. I am pleased he is now behind bars. "Protecting young people from harm is one of our top priorities and we will continue to work tirelessly to keep children safe." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: REVEALED: Number of Cambs students suspended for physical assault in last five years
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nearly 3000 students were suspended from schools in Cambridgeshire for physically assaulting teachers and other pupils over the last five years, data has revealed. A total of 2,990 pupils faced suspensions or exclusions from state-maintained schools in the county, according to a Freedom of Information Act request. In the 2025/26 academic year there were 635 students suspended or excluded for physical assault against other students or teachers. The majority of these were primary school students at 510, with 118 incidents in secondary schools and six in special educational needs, or SEND, schools. Cambridgeshire County Council said they do not hold data on whether these were cases of physical assault towards other students or towards teachers. They also said they don’t record how many of these incidents were referred to the police or reported severe injuries needing medical attention. The number of suspensions or exclusions peaked at 797 during the 2024/25 academic year including 635 at primary schools, 152 at secondary schools and 11 at SEND schools. It had been steadily increasing from 2021/22 when there were 291 suspensions and exclusions – 223 in primary schools, 68 at secondary schools and none in SEND schools. Physical assault incidents – exclusions: Year Primary Secondary Special 2021/22 223 68 0 2022/23 436 103 4 2023/24 590 134 0 2024/25 635 152 11 2025/26 510 118 6 The council added the data is only what has been reported by the schools themselves and only as accurate as what they have reported to the council. They said that moving forward all schools have agreed that the council’s early years and education system (EYES) will capture this data straight from the school. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: “Our teams work closely with school staff and families to keep pupils in school. “It is always disappointing when pupils are excluded and it is always a last resort. “Schools have to follow statutory guidelines and will always look at potential suspensions and exclusions on a case by case basis. “We work closely with teaching staff and families to help manage challenging and difficult behaviour and keep pupils in school.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Awards will celebrate the sustainability leaders of today and tomorrow
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027 will celebrate the organisations and individuals helping to create a more sustainable future across the region. This week, we spotlight the Net Zero Award and One to Watch Award. The judges for these two categories explain why they are important and the opportunities they provide to recognise success, innovation and environmental progress. Sophie Lewis, commercial director, Hornsea 3 at Ørsted, which sponsors the Net Zero Award (Image: Ørsted) Sponsored by Ørsted Sponsor judge: Sophie Lewis, commercial director, Hornsea 3, Ørsted Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? I have worked in offshore wind for 13 years, eight with Ørsted, having started my career in the industry as a business analyst for Norfolk-based Seajacks. I then continued within the financial and commercial areas of the sector at the UK Green Investment Bank, before moving to Ørsted. Why were you keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards? I spent the first 20 years of my life in Great Yarmouth, and nearly all my family and many of my close friends in the area are now involved in the renewable industry. I’ve witnessed the region transition from oil and gas to becoming a leader in renewables, and I am passionate about championing this continued path. What do you bring to the judging process? Passion for positive change, both for a cleaner environment and stronger local communities, is something I bring to every judging process. Alongside an open-minded and balanced approach, I’ll be looking at how projects deliver environmental outcomes while contributing to long-term community wellbeing, collaboration and inspiration for others. Have you ever been judged for an award yourself? Yes, I have been judged for awards in the past. Having been on the other side, I understand how much effort, pride and sometimes vulnerability goes into an application. I’ll use that experience to approach judging with empathy, fairness and respect. What will you be looking for in the winner? Ideally the winner would deliver a mix of tangible short-term outcomes with measurable results, but at the same time it’s important to see evidence of sustained and scalable improvements. The strongest entries will be those that break new ground, inspire others and bring people together through collaboration, while demonstrating a clear commitment to positive change. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? Don’t just focus on the numbers – also share your passion and purpose behind your drive towards net zero. This is your moment to shine! Why is ‘scalability’ an important consideration for the Net Zero Award? Cutting emissions at the scale needed to meet national or global net zero targets can’t be achieved by isolated organisations or one-off projects. Solutions must be able to spread across industries, regions and communities. Amy Bendall, managing director of Pier, which sponsors the One To Watch Award (Image: Pier Marketing Limited) Sponsored by Pier Sponsor judge: Amy Bendall, managing director, Pier Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? I’ve worked in PR and communications my whole career, across various industries. The golden thread running through everything has been a motivation to do good. At Pier we specialise in renewables and sustainability for exactly that reason – and that’s why Pier has been my home for almost half my career. What do you bring to the judging process? I’ve judged awards before, so this isn’t my first rodeo. The diversity of my 20-year career helps, including delivering campaigns at the fantastic environment charity, Friends of the Earth. I’d like to think I know what good looks like – and I won’t be sucked in by greenwashing. Have you ever been judged for an award yourself? Many times! Pier has been lucky enough to scoop several accolades over the years, including the prestigious PR Consultancy of the Year. We also draft award entries for our clients, so it’s a well-honed skill. How will you use that experience when judging this award? While a well-written entry certainly makes judging easier, ultimately what matters are the hard facts and the drive to do the right thing. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? Just go for it! The Clean & Green Awards are genuinely meaningful – not all awards give such due diligence to judging the entries. It means that even making the final is a well-deserved achievement that can and should be celebrated. What will you be looking for in the winner? I’d love to see passion and long-term thinking for a clean and green future. Why is ‘innovation’ an important judging consideration for this award? Innovation is essential to ensure we remain progressive – but I don’t think entrants should feel constrained by the size of their innovation. The small wins matter just as much as the big ones. The deadline for entries to the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards is Sunday, November 8 at midnight. For more information or to enter, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A solar farm has been approved on farmland next to a small village. Huntingdonshire District Council’s development management committee met to decide on the application for land off Vicarage Lane in Diddington, just west of the A1. Buckden Parish Council and Southoe and Midloe Parish Council had objected to the plans as they said “there should be no more solar farms on greenfield sites until all residential and commercial roof spaces and brownfield sites have been fully utilised”. Edmund Thornhill spoke in favour of the application and said the solar panels, expected to generate 35MW of electricity, are proposed on the “poorest performing” fields. He said: “There needs to be careful consideration around best use of land even if that use is for a finite period – the farm already provides food, housing and space for nature. “We want to support energy production as well over the poorest land. “This scheme would provide diversified income to help fund moving to more regenerative agriculture on the rest of the farm.” Around 45 hectares of land will be covered and the solar farm is expected to operate for 45 years, which Mr Thornhill said would allow the soil fertility to improve. The company behind the plans, Cell Energy Limited, said it has an agreement with Anglian Water to provide the company with energy. An underground cable will be built to their facility at Grafham Water which the planning application said was a “very significant energy user”. Cllr Jon Neish, of Holywell-cum-Needingworth, said he couldn’t see a reason to object to the plans aside from the parish council’s objection. The Conservative councillor said: “Unfortunately they haven’t come to explain a bit more in detail their views so at the moment I would struggle anywhere to say why we shouldn’t agree with it.” Cllr Lara Davenport-Ray, of St Neots East, said renewable energy projects are “really important” as natural gas is still used to generate much of the electricity in the area. The Green councillor said: “If we don’t stop creating carbon emissions then our planet will continue to warm and it will make the growing of any crops impossible. “I am disappointed to see no battery storage included but because of the overall direction that we need to go in I will suggest that we approve this application.” The plans were approved with 12 voting in favour and one against.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Excessive speed' and potholes blamed for fatal Wisbech river crash inquest told
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Wisbech teenager Declan Berry drowned after his car hit a pothole at 90mph and plunged into the River Nene, an inquest heard. The teenage driver was told to slow down moments before his car plunged into the water, killing him and sixteen-year-old rear passenger, Eden Bunn. Mr Berry, 18, was travelling at around 90mph when his Volkswagen Polo hit a pothole on North Brink, Wisbech, and rolled down an embankment into the river, the hearing heard. Declan Berry's family and friends laid tributes and waited for news as searches of the River Nene were carried out for his body. (Image: Sarah Cliss) None of his family was at the hearing at Vantage House in Huntingdon, which was conducted by written statements, and heard that Mr Berry drowned after the March 17 crash; his body was recovered from the river nearly two weeks later at the town’s marina. A police officer called to identify the body confirmed it was Mr Berry due to an unusual tattoo on the back of his neck and his clothing. Police investigator James Mills concluded that speed was the main factor in the crash, while the pothole-riddled road, with crumbling edges and an uneven surface, also contributed. Cambridgeshire area coroner Elizabeth Gray read the evidence from the various witnesses about the crash, which happened at around 8.19pm as Mr Berry drove four teenage friends along North Brink, away from the town centre. The front-seat passenger told police he had looked at the speedometer and that Mr Berry was driving at 90mph moments before the crash and he had asked him to slow down. Mr Berry replied, "It will be all right", before the car hit a pothole and he lost control. The witness said he met Mr Berry at McDonald’s, accepted an invitation to go for a drive and believed Mr Berry had "intended to show off". He escaped through the broken passenger window and described the water around him as dark, telling officers he did not know where the others were as he made his escape. Declan Berry's body was recovered from Wisbech Marina nearly two weeks after the fatal crash. (Image: Alan Berry) A female passenger sitting behind the front passenger, who was not wearing a seat belt, recalled a near miss on the same stretch of road a week earlier. The other unnamed second rear-seat passenger, who was sat behind Mr Berry, heard a thud beneath the car but did not know what it struck before it rolled into the water. She struggled to release her seat belt before escaping through a broken window and being rescued by members of the public. One of the women had also told police that she was used to Mr Berry driving at speed, and it was what she expected. Many floral tributes were left by the River Nene in Wisbech following the horrific crash. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Eden Bunn from Sutton Bridge was sitting in the middle and had reportedly called out "Declan" moments before the crash. Her inquest is due tomorrow. An eyewitness on his driveway at the time of the crash heard a vehicle approach at speed before a loud bang. He saw the headlights and rear lights "rotating through the air", then ran and found the vehicle completely submerged. He asked his partner to call emergency services before helping those involved, who had made it to the bank but needed help out of the water. A Cambridgeshire Search & Rescue team were at the scene for several days. The accident report said speed was the main factor: it left the driver less time to react to potholes before he lost control. At a lower speed, the rollover would have been less severe. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs primary school praised for 'welcoming' environment in Ofsted report
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire primary school has been praised for its "welcoming and nurturing" environment in its latest Ofsted report. Earith Primary School near Huntingdon, part of the Active Learning Trust, was inspected on July 14 and met the expected standard overall, with early years and personal development judged strong. Inspectors said pupils feel safe and well supported in a “welcoming and nurturing” school where they enjoy positive relationships with staff and each other. Ofsted also praised the school for tailoring parts of its curriculum to the local community. Because the school is surrounded by waterways, pupils receive extra water-safety lessons, while older children learn about healthy relationships, artificial intelligence, digital footprints and online misinformation. Duncan Low, Director of Learning at Active Learning Trust, said: “We are very pleased to see Ofsted inspectors recognise the strengths and achievements at Earith Primary School and the positive experience it provides for pupils and their families. Inspectors said pupils build a strong understanding of different cultures, religions and beliefs through the school council, voting and debates about democracy. Every pupil has a responsibility in the school community, helping them build independence and leadership skills. The report also highlighted extra-curricular opportunities including sporting events, educational visits, music activities and residential trips. Inspectors noted that pupils develop a strong understanding of different cultures (Image: Earith Primary School) Pupils particularly value the on-site swimming pool, which inspectors said is important because of the school’s location. Most pupils achieved in line with national expectations, made appropriate progress and were well prepared for the next stage of education. Attendance was above the national average, including among disadvantaged pupils and those with special educational needs and/or disabilities. Headteacher Thomas Abbs said: “I am delighted that this Ofsted report recognises the warm, welcoming and inclusive environment we work so hard to achieve at our village school. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The hardest secondary schools to get into in Cambridgeshire revealed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The hardest secondary schools to get into have been revealed as parents and carers decide where their children will study next year. The window for applications for pupils starting year 7 in September 2027 opened earlier this month and will run until October 31. Last year, 7,050 students found out where they’d be heading with 96.7 per cent securing a place at one of their first, second or third preference schools. The hardest school to get into was Chesterton Community College, with enough places for just 60 per cent of children who put it down as their first preference. Earlier this year, the school was listed as the top performing school in the county – with 83.7 per cent of pupils achieving a Grade 5 or higher in their English and maths GCSEs. In its latest Ofsted report the school was also found to be outstanding in every category, with the inspector finding it has an “extremely high level of ambition for all pupils” which is matched by the pupils’ “own determination to succeed”. St Bede’s Inter-Church School in Cambridge was the second hardest to get into with 190 places for 301 first-place preferences – a success rate of 63 per cent. Soham Village College was ranked third with 78 per cent of pupils successfully admitted to 270 places from 247 first-place preferences. Parents and carers of children about to enter secondary school can submit their applications for places on the county council website. They have until the national closing date of October 31, after which late applications will be considered once all on-time applications are determined. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: “This year in Cambridgeshire 96.6 per cent of children were offered a place at either their first, second or third preference schools, this is above national benchmarks. Notably, both this year and last year, 5 per cent more children in Cambridgeshire received an offer from their first preference school than did nationally. “We’re committed to providing the best possible start in life for young people in our county and access to high quality education close to home is key. With population centres changing over time around our growing county, the council’s Education team work hard, in partnership with schools and with careful reference to pupil forecasting figures, to try and ensure we can offer the right numbers of school places, in the right areas, when they are needed.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire campaign could unlock £2m a year in unclaimed Pension Credit
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A campaign could put up to £2 million a year back in the pockets of older Cambridgeshire residents. More than 700 households across Cambridgeshire will be contacted about unclaimed Pension Credit in a joint council campaign. The campaign is the county’s first targeted campaign to increase residents’ income since approval of the procurement of the Low-Income Family Tracker (LIFT) software platform at a meeting of the County Council’s Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee in February, funded through the UK Government’s Crisis and Resilience Fund via the DWP. Alison Whelan, chair of the Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "This new targeted campaign will boost financial security and quality of life for hundreds of families across our county. "I’m delighted to know that in Cambridgeshire we’re putting money, up to £2M, back in the pockets of the families that are most vulnerable to the cost-of-living pressures facing us nationally. "Please help us to spread the word about this excellent campaign so that families contacted by their district or city council will know they can trust the information they’ve been given – it’s good news!" Eligible residents will be contacted directly by their local council: Cambridge City, East Cambridgeshire, South Cambridgeshire, Huntingdonshire or Fenland. Councils will contact residents by letter, email or phone. Pension Credit comes in two parts: Guarantee Credit and Savings Credit. Some households may be eligible for both. The council estimates the 500 identified households could gain more than £2 million a year if they all claim Guarantee Credit, based on an average award of £4,300. No scams have been reported in connection with the campaign. The campaign follows a 2024 council motion calling for a proactive campaign to ensure eligible pensioners were informed about Pension Credit after changes to winter fuel payments.

Plans to turn a pub into a corner shop have been approved on appeal after an inspector found its loss was “sufficiently justified”. The Bulls Head in St Neots shut in August 2023 before being put on market by brewery Greene King as they failed to find a new landlord. Huntingdonshire District Council refused plans from Noble Trading (UK) Ltd to re-open the Cambridge Street building as a “modern convenience store”. The Campaign for Pubs organisation objected as they said it had been a “popular pub which was well supported until its closure”. A licence application for the proposed shop was granted to allow them to sell alcohol, but planning permission was needed for the conversion to go ahead. The council rejected this as it would result in the loss of a pub and community space and they said there wasn’t enough evidence it had been marketed for continued use as a pub. Inspector David Reed of the Planning Inspectorate said the property was marketed over 15 months with a total of 38 enquiries, 16 viewings and one offer “which was withdrawn after a serious water damage incident occurred”. He said that feedback from the viewings “was poor” with potential buyers saying the kitchen was too small, there was no parking and the building was in “poor condition” with “too much work needed”. After the price was reduced it was bought by the current applicant, Mr Jeyaseelan Thambirajah. Mr Reed said that although there are no other pubs in the surrounding area, there are nine within one kilometre. He said: “These include Ye Old Sun, the Ale Taster, The Hyde Park and The Coach House. “This competition was also a likely contributing factor to the lack of interest in a public house use.” The council had said there was no proof certain websites listed in the marketing report were actually used but the inspector said this was “an unwarranted allegation”. They also said the premises were only actively marketed for eleven months and that “the asking price was unrealistic”. Mr Reed said that a gap while an offer proceeds “is standard practice” and the price was within the range of other “local comparable public houses”. He said: “It can be concluded that reasonable steps were taken to market the public house without success”. Permission was granted for the shop to open between 6.30am and 11pm from Monday to Saturday and 8am to 9pm on Sundays and Bank Holidays.

Baulk added a third eight minutes after the interval, meeting a cross from Furlong with a powerful volley which gave Key no opportunity. Histon responded with attacking substitutions, but the changes failed to alter the pattern of the match. St Neots continued to defend comfortably, with their back line breaking up most attempts before they could develop into clear chances. Barnes struck the post with a header, and Histon’s problems deepened when Jonny Hall was sent off after 68 minutes. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 75 people flocked to a sold-out Huntingdon talk on the dark history of witch trials. The event was part of this year’s Heritage Open Days in Huntingdonshire and was organised by Huntingdon Town Council and The Cromwell Museum. The talk, led by Cromwell Museum curator Stuart Orme, was moved from the Court Room to the larger Assembly Room, but extra tickets quickly sold out. Stuart said: "The Huntingdonshire Witch Trials are one of the most intriguing aspects of our local history, so it has been wonderful to see so many people wanting to learn more about the people and events behind the story. "Whilst Heritage Open Days shines a spotlight on our shared heritage, the Cromwell Museum is free to visit throughout the year, and I would encourage anyone with an interest in Huntingdon's past to come along and discover more of the remarkable stories our town has to tell." Guided Walk at Priory Road Cemetary (Image: Huntingdon Town Council) The talk covered the region’s witch-trial history, including the Witches of Warboys, the infamous Witchfinder General Matthew Hopkins and Huntingdon woman Mary Hicks, who may have been the last person executed for witchcraft in England, although both her existence and that claim are disputed. The witch-trials talk was part of a wider Heritage Open Days programme that included an open day at Priory Road Cemetery and Chapel, where visitors explored burial records and learned about former Huntingdon Burial Board members. The programme will conclude with two fully booked guided tours of Huntingdon Town Hall, giving attendees the chance to explore the town’s civic heritage. The Cromwell Museum and self-guided trails from the Discover Huntingdon Visitor Centre offer residents and visitors year-round ways to explore the town’s history. Huntingdon saw witchcraft trials in 1593, 1646 and 1716, with at least four people hanged at Mill Common after the 1646 proceedings.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Small changes urged as Zero Waste Week highlights how to rethink rubbish
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Cooper, owner of The Refill Shop of Ikigai in St Ives, writes his latest column It's time to rethink our rubbish. Do you know how much waste you produce on a weekly basis? With more bins being rolled out from the council, it’s hard to keep track of just how much we are throwing away, but Zero Waste Week is an opportunity to take notice. Zero Waste Week was held between September 7 and 11 and has become a regular in the calendar of environmental campaigns to help us reduce what we throw away. But why does it matter? Carry reusable items (Image: Martin Cooper) The scale of our waste problem is easy to overlook because most of it disappears the moment the bin lorry pulls away. We generate millions of tonnes of rubbish every year, most of which ends up in landfill rather than being reused or recycled. Landfill sites take up valuable land, can leach pollutants into soil and waterways and represent a huge waste of the energy and resources that went into making the products in the first place. Every takeaway container, unopened food packet or old appliance thrown away is a small loss multiplied by millions of households doing the same thing. Rather than demanding perfection – which we know will never be achieved, Zero Waste Week encourages us to pick one habit and try to improve it for seven days – then keep going until it sticks. And it’s not as hard as you might think: You can audit your bins – during Zero Waste Week, make note of what you throw away most – awareness alone often changes behaviour. Cut your food waste by planning meals, freezing leftovers and using up odds and ends before they spoil – food waste is one of the easiest and most impactful areas to tackle. Choose reusables – swap single-use bags, bottles and cutlery for versions you can use again and again. Repair, don’t replace – Huntingdonshire has a number of repair cafés throughout the year, that can fix clothes, electronics, and furniture that might otherwise be binned, and the Sew, Mend and Repair group, who meet in St Ives, help repair and alter clothes to keep them going. Buy loose and local – reducing packaging by shopping at markets or refill shops will cut your waste before it even reaches your home – and gives you an opportunity to reuse what you already have. Zero Waste Week won’t solve the waste crisis on its own, but small, collective changes add up. This September, it’s worth asking “what’s one thing I could throw away less of?”.

Sling The Mesh has renewed calls for change on World Patient Safety Day, which was marked on September 17. The group is pushing for compensation and greater transparency following the First Do No Harm review, which exposed the harm caused by pelvic mesh and other treatments. Kath Sansom, founder of Sling The Mesh and a campaigner from March, said: "World Patient Safety Day is a moment to reflect on what happens when patients are not listened to, warning signs are ignored and vested interests are allowed to outweigh patient welfare. MP Sharon Hodgson with Kath (Image: Kath Sansom) "The greatest mistake would be to believe that the mesh scandal belongs to history. "It does not. If we fail to deliver accountability and transparency now, we create the conditions for the next patient safety scandal to emerge. "It may already be happening in plain sight." The group wants to see two key recommendations from the First Do No Harm review put into effect: compensation for women avoidably harmed by pelvic mesh, and ‘Sunshine legislation’ to improve transparency around industry payments in healthcare. They say these steps are vital to preventing future scandals and restoring public trust. Kath Sansom at Parliament (Image: Kath Sansom) Sharon Hodgson MP, co-chair of the First Do No Harm All Party Parliamentary Group, said: "The lack of progress sends a damaging message to patients that when healthcare systems fail, people can simply be left behind. "Women affected by the mesh and valproate scandals are still waiting for justice. "Those who suffered avoidable harm deserve accountability, proper support and fair redress. "Patient safety must be more than a slogan. "We must ensure that lessons are acted upon and that transparency and openness are placed at the heart of our healthcare system."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: RSPCA seeks quiet home for loving Martha after 67 per cent rise in mass cat rescues

A spokesperson for the centre said: “Martha is a loving and gentle girl who is looking for a quiet home where she can come out of her shell. “She can be a little cautious when meeting new people and may need a bit of time to settle into any new home. But once she feels comfortable, her loving personality really begins to shine. “Martha had previously lived in a household where cat flu was present. Due to this, she could be the only cat in the home. Martha could live with sensible secondary school-aged children depending on the introductions made at the centre.” Anyone who can offer Martha the right home can complete the RSPCA’s online application form. RSPCA centres are under mounting pressure as new figures show a 67 per cent rise in multi-cat rescues in one year. Figures released for the RSPCA’s Cruelty Hurts, Love Rescues campaign show it dealt with 1,752 mass-cat incidents last year, involving 10 or more cats in one property—almost five a day. That was a 67 per cent rise from 1,045 in 2024 and a 186 per cent increase from the 613 recorded in 2021. The charity said the incidents are placing unprecedented pressure on its resources in England and Wales. About 20,000 cats entered RSPCA care in 2025, and the charity fears that figure will be exceeded this year. Cat breeding peaks between May and September, bringing centres and branches unwanted kittens and pregnant mothers and putting further pressure on the charity’s limited space. Martha’s rehoming needs Martha needs access to the outdoors. Martha could live with secondary school-aged children. Martha would prefer to be the only pet in the home. Martha is quiet but full of love. The same centre has previously appealed for a home for a lurcher who spent 1,000 days in RSPCA care.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Young anglers catch and return 723 fish in confidence-building summer programme

The Dreamdrops Fishing Programme, run by children’s charity Dreamdrops in partnership with the Fly-Fishing Academy, took place every Tuesday in August at Rectory Farm in Great Addington, Northamptonshire. Up to eight young anglers attended each session, including graduates of an earlier life-skills angling course and two working towards the Angling Skills Activity Award. Roger Adams, an instructor from the Fly-Fishing Academy, said: "Where did August go? "It’s been tremendous fun, but my life has flashed before me – I have lost four weeks of it!" Richard Winser of the Fly-Fishing Academy said: "There have been some great sessions, they seemed to get incrementally better each time we ventured out; angling appeals on so many different levels and in so many personal ways, to different people. George Ward (Image: Dreamdrops Children's Charity) "It can enhance wellbeing and be very therapeutic just being outside and around water, in a safe and controlled environment." The young anglers caught and safely returned 723 fish during the programme. George Ward, a current participant, said: "I liked the way that the instructors had loads of time for you, and you didn’t feel rushed. "Everything was explained simply and they always told us what would be covered next. "The Zoom tutorials and Kahoot quizzes were serious fun. "It was great to have such a good course structure, and I learnt loads of new and different fishing techniques – amazing." Parent Michelle Quail praised the programme. She said: "For us personally, the fishing days have been such good fun and have stood out as a highlight of our summer, it has given us an opportunity to do things we would otherwise not have had a chance to do and to make some really lovely family memories along the way." Dreamdrops committee chair Christine Luckham congratulated the two young anglers who completed the course and will receive Gold Award Level certificates at a ceremony at Huntingdon Town Hall on September 12. She also thanked the Fly-Fishing Academy team, saying: "Once again, my thanks to the Fly-Fishing Academy team who have ploughed a new furrow and extended the boundaries further for our fishing programme and angling initiative." The Angling Skills Activity Award - Foundation (Gold) course includes three online tutorials and four additional fishing days, with participants required to demonstrate competency in 17 areas.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire care home has been rated good overall after previously being judged to require improvement by the Care Quality Commission (CQC). Montague House, in Keeling Lane, Brampton, was assessed between July 30 and August 19, with the report published September 8. The home provides accommodation, nursing and personal care for 52 residents, including people living with dementia. Montague House was awarded ‘Good’ ratings across four out of five criteria (Safe, Effective, Responsive and Well-led) and an 'Outstanding' rating for Caring. At the previous inspection in March 2023, inspectors found the provider breached regulations on safe care, treatment and governance. The CQC said the provider had made “sufficient improvements” and was no longer breaching the regulations. The care home no longer 'requires improvement' (Image: Montague House) Home Manager Paula Yorkston Toy said: “We are delighted with the CQC report and to have received an ‘Outstanding’ rating in ‘Caring’. “I want to thank every member of the team here for helping us to achieve this result and for their contribution to Montague House. “The residents and their wellbeing are at the heart of everything we do, and it’s terrific that the inspectors have recognised our dedication and care.” The latest inspection report reads: "People experienced personalised care from staff who understood them well and supported them to live meaningful and fulfilling lives. "Staff demonstrated a detailed understanding of people's individual needs, preferences and life histories. "There were many examples of compassionate, person-centred care, particularly for people living with dementia." Montague House in Brampton was rated 'good' in its latest inspection (Image: Montague House) Inspectors identified areas for further work, including safeguarding recognition and reporting, records showing repositioning had taken place as assessed, care planning and medicines oversight. There was no evidence of avoidable harm and the provider responded positively to feedback and took action. Residents took part in activities, therapies and community links, including exercise programmes, dementia activities and religious services. Inspectors found visible, approachable leaders and a positive culture at the home. Inspectors said residents had positive experiences, with staff acting calmly, patiently and respectfully and adapting to their emotional and wellbeing needs. A person told inspectors: "I like it here and I'm happy to be here."

Dorothy Hinton She married William “Bill” Hinton and had two daughters, Christine and Yvonne, two grandchildren, Lucy and Catherine, and two great-grandchildren, Anna and William. During the Second World War, Dorothy supported the war effort by writing to soldiers and knitting them socks. A keen cyclist, she often rode between villages to visit family and get to work. She also cycled regularly to RAF Tempsford to help at the NAAFI (Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes) canteen, a social hub for the base. After moving to Gamlingay in 1962, Dorothy threw herself into community life. At St Mary's Church, she taught Sunday School, helped launch a coffee morning, formed a fundraising sewing group and ran a marmalade stall. She even dressed as a St Trinian's schoolgirl on a gala float. Dorothy enjoying Elvis Dorothy's husband died in 2000, and she moved into Potton View in October 2024. Her family says Dorothy’s sense of humour remains intact and credits laughter as one key to her long life. Dorothy will celebrate her milestone birthday at the home with family, friends and fellow residents. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Charity offers free training to break workplace barriers for neurodivergent staff
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire charity is offering businesses free training on supporting neurodivergent employees. Red2Green will host the online session on Thursday, September 24, to help organisations identify and remove hidden workplace barriers. The session will examine how communication, workplace environments and established practices can affect neurodivergent staff. Liz Taylor, chief executive of Red2Green and neurodivergent herself, said: "Many workplace barriers are not created deliberately. "They are often found in the everyday things organisations have always done. "Small, thoughtful changes can make a significant difference. "They can help neurodivergent employees feel more confident and remain in work, while often making the workplace better for everyone." The charity’s Encompass programme turns awareness of neurodiversity into practical workplace change. It promotes changes that support autistic people and those with learning disabilities. Government research shows that only around three in ten working-age autistic people have jobs. That compares with five in ten disabled people and eight in ten non-disabled people. Liz said: "We are proud that Encompass has been developed by a local charity, based on our experience of supporting autistic people and those with learning disabilities. "We understand the barriers employees can face, but we also see the skills and potential that organisations can miss when their workplaces are not designed inclusively. "This free session is an opportunity for local organisations to begin looking at their own practices and identify changes they can make." Red2Green has supported autistic people and people with learning disabilities across Cambridgeshire for more than 25 years. The training is free, but places must be booked in advance. Register at https://fundraising.red2green.org/event/encompass-free-taster-training-session. Inclusive workplace policies should allow employees to discuss health needs openly and make reasonable adjustments where required, helping create a more supportive working environment.

On Tuesday (September 15), at Cambridge Crown Court, Andrulionis, of Balding Close, Wisbech, was jailed. He pleaded guilty to one count of rape before the case went to trial. He was also ordered to spend six years on extended licence, handed an indefinite restraining order against the victim. Andrulionis was placed on the sex offenders register for life and must pay a victim surcharge of £228. Sentencing, Judge Andrew Hurst described him as “dangerous”, that he was only “faintly familiar” with the concept of consent and a “substantial risk” to other women. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Disgraced ex-Cambs police sergeant jailed over 'toxic' Whatsapp culture
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A disgraced former Cambridgeshire Police officer who created a “toxic” WhatsApp culture has been jailed for four years after asking for a female suspect’s sex video. Ex-Cambridgeshire Constabulary police sergeant Paul Street, 41, engaged in “salacious gossip” with former PC Josh Williams after he found intimate pictures and footage on the woman’s personal phone. On Wednesday, the woman told of her “overwhelming sense of shock, violation, anger and humiliation”. Street also encouraged colleagues to “bully” a teenage detainee in WhatsApp messages. Following an Old Bailey trial in June, Street, of Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office. He admitted two offences of unlawful disclosure of personal data relating to confidential information and screenshots he sent to his partner in 2020. In a televised sentencing at the Old Bailey, Street was jailed for four years. Williams, 38, also of Huntingdon, who had pleaded guilty to misconduct in public office, was handed 16 months in prison and waved to family in the public gallery as he was sent down. Judge Mark Lucraft KC said: “The public should expect to be able to trust police officers to act fairly in the execution of their powers to prevent, detect and solve crime – anything less does great harm to the public faith in police forces and individual police officers. “The public expects, and rightly so, the highest of standards from police officers. I am sure there will be many thousands of officers in police forces in this country and abroad utterly horrified by your actions and by the attitude you have each displayed here. It is both appalling and inexplicable.” The judge noted the “collateral impact” of Street’s offending with 67 cases he was connected with – or via the contents of his phone – being discontinued and a further 14 under review. Street found fame in television crime shows on the BBC and Channel 4 and was known for getting “impressive results” through his “robust” style. However, anti-corruption officers began investigating him and uncovered his two WhatsApp groups in 2021 after a new police officer reported him. The offences were committed while working at Cambridgeshire Constabulary leading a unit at Cambourne police station, mainly dealing with county lines drug supply and organised crime. During the trial, prosecutor Anne Whyte KC had described how Street created a “toxic culture” which led to investigations into 11 other officers. After a junior officer raised concern about WhatsApp use, Street messaged colleagues: “Just a shame we have snakes as we are all such good mates.” In April 2020, Street called on his team to “bully” 17-year-old detainee Robiul Islam, encouraging them to “please hit him” and “smash his head in”. In the autumn of 2020, Williams was tasked with examining the phone of a female suspect he told Street was “quite fit”. Street asked him if there were “any nudes”, and Williams replied there was a video of the woman committing a sexual act. Williams went on to send Street a photo from the woman’s phone depicting her in underwear. The following year, Street asked on WhatsApp if Williams still had the intimate private video because he wanted to show it to “the lads from footy”. Williams responded that he doubted he still had it and there was no evidence the video was shared. Reading her victim personal statement in court, the woman said: “The photographs and videos on my phone were deeply private and intimate. “They were never intended to be viewed or shared by anyone without my consent. Learning that people in positions of authority deliberately accessed and circulated these images has left me feeling exposed, degraded and powerless. “Something that was entirely personal to me was taken and treated as if it had no value or dignity. “Members of the public are taught to trust the police and believe that officers will act with integrity and respect for the law. “In my case these individuals entrusted to safeguard my property and uphold the law abused their position in order to invade my privacy in an extremely personal and humiliating way. “I feel violated by these individuals who were in a position of power over me at the time. The abuse of that power has and continues to make this experience particularly difficult to come to terms with.” Mitigating, Jennifer Dempster KC said Street “enormously regrets his behaviour”. Father-of-two Street made a significant contribution to disrupting the drug trade before his 17-year career came to a “crashing end”, she said. Ms Dempster said: “He recognises he has not only let the public down, he has let the police down and he has let his family down.” For Williams, Robert Morris said: “He recognises what he did was deeply inappropriate, driven by misguided and stupid desire to engage in salacious gossip.” Eleven other officers were investigated over their conduct arising from the culture Street had fostered. Of those, two resigned, one was dismissed for gross misconduct, one received a final warning, two received written warnings, and five others were dealt with for low-level performance issues. Senior specialist prosecutor Lisa Rose, from the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “This case exposed a sustained pattern of unacceptable conduct by a police officer who abused his position of trust. “Police officers are entrusted with significant powers and are expected to uphold the highest standards at all times. “Members of the public should have confidence that any personal material obtained during an investigation will be handled lawfully and appropriately. “The actions of Paul Street and Joshua Williams represented a serious breach of that trust.” Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) director of engagement Emily Barry said: “Paul Street’s behaviour was appalling and a complete abuse of his position as a police officer. “He fostered a toxic culture in his team and instead of leading by example, he encouraged others to join in exchanging inappropriate messages – creating an environment that junior officers would find very difficult to challenge. “However, this investigation shows that officers must be courageous and call out this sort of behaviour and forces must make sure that they support and protect those that do report. The officer who reported Street should be acknowledged for standing up for what is right. “The public would also be shocked at knowing officers shared intimate photos from a woman’s phone without any policing purpose and that Street made a video threatening a child who was detained in custody.”

Huntingdonshire District Council has refused a retrospective bid to turn part of a Turkish restaurant complex in St Ives into staff accommodation. The application sought to turn a former storage building behind Vadi Kitchen, at 40 The Broadway, into a three-bedroom house in multiple occupation with a shared kitchen and bathroom. The accommodation had already been created and was being used as staff accommodation. Planning officers accepted residential use in St Ives town centre but recommended refusal over the building’s layout and poor living conditions. Planning officer Kevin Simpson said the scheme had a "contrived layout" that failed to provide an acceptable standard of living for future occupants. Officers said the shared kitchen had no natural light and doubled as the corridor to both bedrooms and the bathroom. Environmental Health officers warned that cooking facilities had been placed in the escape route. They feared residents could brush against hot pans or spill liquids while walking between the bedrooms and bathroom, risking burns and scalds. Read more Hunts MP's rescue dog wins public vote at Westminster Dog of the Year competition Godmanchester Town Show draws over 400 entries Disgraced ex-Cambs police sergeant jailed over 'toxic' Whatsapp culture St Neots prostate screening event could set world record with 122 men tested St Neots special school is making progress after being told it needed to improve The council also warned that water from the bathroom could make the area near the cooking equipment slippery and force rescuers through an escape route containing cooking facilities. Planners also criticised the lack of communal living space, saying the three bedrooms were the only rooms residents could live in. Officers also raised concerns about the bedrooms facing directly on to George Yard. They said windows opening straight on to the pedestrian route could allow people to see inside and reduce residents’ privacy. Officers said revised plans failed to address the concerns. The report said the amendments made "very little change" and failed to resolve the fundamental issues raised by Environmental Health and planning officers. The council also refused the application because the applicant failed to agree to provide wheeled bins for the development. St Ives Town Council also objected, calling the scheme an overdevelopment and criticising the accommodation’s size, layout and location in Flood Zone 3. Despite those objections, officers found the scheme acceptable on flood risk, heritage, parking and highway safety. But they concluded the scheme breached local and national planning rules on living conditions and should be refused. Huntingdonshire District Council formally refused planning permission on September 16. In May, Vadi Kitchen operator Bora Demir also applied to vary the restaurant's premises licence to allow alcohol sales for consumption on site.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs fraudster stole £40,000 from employer and spent it on skiing holiday
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A second-time fraudster has been jailed for stealing more than £40,000 from her employer and spending it on a skiing holiday. Kirsty Payne, 44, of Taverners Drive, Ramsey, admitted defrauding her Cambridge-based employer, Marshall Thermo King, which trades as Marshall Fleet Solutions. In February 2025, she processed a £400,410 payment through the company system—£40,383 more than the legitimate amount. The extra funds were traced to an account belonging to one of Payne’s family members. The discrepancy went unnoticed until April, when Payne was signed off work because of her deteriorating mental health. During a wellbeing check with the company’s head of HR, she suddenly confessed to the fraud and resigned. She first claimed the money paid for a relative’s medical treatment, but later told police it funded a skiing holiday in the French Alps. Payne said the theft was a "spur of the moment" decision. However, she had a previous conviction for fraud by false representation and said she was experiencing financial difficulties despite earning around £80,000 a year. Payne told officers she had been struggling mentally, especially due to a family member’s terminal illness. But she could not explain why she took the money. Detective Constable Valentin Radulescu, who investigated the case, said: "Payne gave little thought to the impact of defrauding her employer out of tens of thousands of pounds. "By committing fraud for a second time she showed she had not learned her lesson, and this was looked on negatively by the courts, who imposed a custodial sentence which she had initially avoided. "I hope her time behind bars allows her to reflect on her actions and hopefully, this case also serves as a warning to anyone else hoping to turn a profit through deception." Payne pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation at Cambridge Magistrates’ Court in July. On September 10, she was sentenced to 18 months in prison at Peterborough Crown Court. The sentence included ten months for the latest fraud, plus extra time for breaching a suspended sentence for a previous similar offence.
